title: E0.5: From Reconstructive to Future-Predictive 3D Foundations for Robotic World-Action Modeling
summary: World-action models (WAMs) offer a promising framework for embodied intelligence, yet mainstream approaches remain centered on video foundation models or vision-language models. Even when geometric features extracted by 3D models such as VGGT are incorporated, they are typically passed into a video model or VLM that serves as the primary backbone, leaving 3D geometry as an auxiliary input or prediction target rather than the native foundation for world modeling. We present E0.5, a geometry-native world-action model built directly on 3D foundation models. E0.5 introduces two key innovations. First, it adopts a 3D foundation model as the primary backbone, making 3D geometry the native representation for both world modeling and action prediction. Second, it explicitly predicts future 3D states together with actions, enabling the model to capture geometric world dynamics beyond action-only modeling or future video prediction. Experiments on RoboTwin 2.0 first demonstrate the effectiveness of E0.5 without embodied-data pretraining, achieving success rates of 89.90\% and 50.09\% under clean and randomized settings, respectively. Building on these results, we further pretrain E0.5 on more than 160k robot trajectories from AgiBotWorld-Beta, jointly learning robot actions and future geometry within the pretrained 3D foundation. This embodied pretraining improves mean real-world manipulation success rates by approximately 15 and 7 percentage points on AgileX Piper and Zerith H1, respectively. Together, these results demonstrate the potential of geometry-native foundations to acquire robot interaction knowledge and transfer it to physical manipulation. E0.5 embodies this geometry-native approach as a member of the VWA family of world-action models.
full_text: sec:introduction Robotic manipulation requires understanding not only the current spatial structure of a scene, but also how that structure may change as the robot acts. World-action models (WAMs) provide a framework for learning this relationship by jointly modeling robot actions and future world states~ song2025physical,ye2026world . A central design question is therefore what kind of representation should underpin this joint modeling of actions and their physical consequences. Mainstream WAMs build on video foundation models or vision-language models, leveraging their capabilities in visual generation and semantic understanding. Although these models can incorporate geometric information, their primary computation remains organized around a video or vision-language backbone, rather than a native geometric foundation. This distinction motivates us to investigate an alternative: building WAMs directly on 3D foundation models, so that action generation and future-state prediction are learned within a shared geometric backbone. Introducing 3D information into an existing model only partially addresses this requirement. Recent methods incorporate features extracted by geometric models into a vision-language or video backbone, or use these features as auxiliary supervision for the backbone’s representations~ yang2026understanding,guo2025glad . Such approaches enrich spatial understanding, but retain a vision-language or video foundation model as the primary backbone, rather than building directly on a 3D foundation model. More generally, geometry can serve as an additional input or prediction target without becoming the representational foundation for world modeling and action generation. We investigate a complementary approach: making a 3D foundation model the core backbone, training it to predict geometric futures together with actions, and expanding its capacity within this geometric modeling framework. We present E0.5, a geometry-native world-action model built directly on 3D foundation models. Following this principle, E0.5 brings together two key innovations: 3D foundation backbones that provide native geometric representations, explicit future 3D state prediction coupled with action generation. These components jointly define the model's representational basis and predictive objective. Figure~ fig:e05_overview summarizes these distinctions, contrasting E0.5 with video and VLM-centered models. First, E0.5 adopts a 3D foundation model as its primary backbone, placing geometric representations at the center of both world modeling and action prediction. The geometric backbone serves as the core model on which these capabilities are learned, extending the role of 3D models beyond front-end feature extraction or auxiliary supervision. Our implementation uses VGGT-Omega~ wang2026vggtomega as an example of a pretrained 3D foundation model. While such models recover the geometry of observed scenes, E0.5 develops this foundation into a predictive geometric backbone that learns future world states jointly with robot actions. Second, E0.5 explicitly predicts future 3D states together with actions. Reconstructing current geometry provides information about the scene at the time of observation; predicting future geometry additionally requires modeling how its spatial configuration evolves during interaction. This distinction aligns the geometric objective with the predictive role of a WAM. It also offers an alternative to future video prediction, whose targets encompass both geometric changes and variations in visual appearance. Our hypothesis is that directly supervising future 3D states encourages the backbone to learn spatial structure and dynamics that remain useful across environments, supporting generalization when observations differ from those encountered during training. This design also advances the use of 3D backbones beyond current-state reconstruction and restricted adaptation. VGA~ song2026robotic uses a native 3D backbone with current-scene geometric supervision and LoRA adaptation; its ablations report substantial degradation under full-parameter training. E0.5 instead unfreezes the geometric backbone and jointly optimizes it for future 3D prediction and action generation. Our experiments demonstrate that backbone optimization is effective in this formulation, allowing pretrained geometric representations to adapt to predictive world-action modeling. Thus, the distinction concerns both what the backbone predicts and how its representations are learned. These findings further motivate us to investigate whether a geometry-native foundation can acquire broad robot interaction knowledge while retaining its pretrained geometric representations. The strong performance observed in simulation, achieved without large-scale embodied pretraining, suggests that 3D foundation models provide an effective starting point for robot action learning. Building on this observation, we extend E0.5 to large-scale pretraining on AgiBotWorld-Beta, where robot actions and future geometric states are jointly modeled. Rather than adapting the backbone solely for action prediction, we continue to supervise future geometry throughout pretraining, allowing the geometric foundation to learn manipulation-relevant dynamics under explicit spatial constraints. We subsequently evaluate this pretrained model on distinct physical robot embodiments to examine how large-scale robot knowledge improves real-world manipulation. Experiments on widely used simulation benchmarks and real-robot tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of E0.5. Predicting future 3D states improves the average success rate by 9.43 percentage points over the variant without geometric reconstruction and by 7.93 percentage points over current-state reconstruction, highlighting the benefits of predictive geometric supervision. The advantage is especially pronounced under distribution shifts: in our evaluated out-of-distribution (OOD) setting, E0.5 achieves approximately 30 times the accuracy of the video-prediction-based WAM baselines. Together, these results establish 3D foundation backbones and future geometry prediction as an effective basis for generalizable world-action modeling. Our contributions are twofold: World-action models built on 3D foundations. We introduce E0.5, which adopts 3D foundation models as its primary backbones and develops their geometric representations for joint world modeling and action prediction. Explicit future 3D state prediction. We jointly learn future geometry and actions while optimizing the geometric backbone, achieving approximately 10-percentage-point improvement over current-state reconstruction and strong OOD generalization relative to video-prediction-based WAMs. sec:related_work Vision-Language-Action and Video-Based World-Action Models. Vision-language-action (VLA) models transfer pretrained visual and linguistic representations to robot control zhan2026e0,zhan2026stable,zhou2026tag,li2026vla . OpenVLA~ kim2024openvla adapts a vision-language backbone using large-scale robot demonstrations, while ~ physicalintelligence2025pi05 combines heterogeneous robot data, web data, and semantic supervision to improve open-world generalization. These approaches demonstrate the value of broad pretraining and multimodal knowledge transfer, with vision-language models providing the principal representational foundation for action generation. Despite these advances, strong benchmark performance does not necessarily translate into robust real-world generalization, with recent evaluations revealing sensitivity to physical perturbations and limitations in spatial reasoning~ chen2026radar . A complementary line of research couples action learning with future visual prediction. Unified Video Action Model~ li2025unified learns a shared video-action latent representation with separate diffusion decoders, while Video Policy~ liang2025video jointly trains video and action generation and leverages action-free videos for policy generalization. PAR song2025physical,song2026physics and DreamZero~ ye2026world builds a world-action model on a pretrained video diffusion backbone, jointly predicting future video and actions to transfer learned dynamics to new tasks and environments. These methods establish visual prediction as a useful source of supervision for embodied behavior. E0.5 shares the objective of learning actions together with future world states, but changes both the representational foundation and the prediction target: a 3D foundation model serves as the primary backbone, and future states are explicitly modeled through geometry rather than video appearance. Geometric Foundations and Future 3D Prediction. Learning 3D structure from visual evidence is an important foundation for spatial intelligence wang2023sparsenerf,shen2024geometry,he2026sceneexpander,zhao2026structsplat,wang2024perf,feng2025objfiller3d,chen2026style4d,xiang2025distilled . More broadly, geometric foundation models learn transferable spatial representations. DUSt3R~ wang2024dust3r regresses point maps from image pairs to reconstruct scene geometry. VGGT~ wang2025vggt and VGGT-Omega wang2026vggtomega jointly estimates multiple geometric quantities from visual observations. Their reconstruction-oriented pretraining offers a geometric starting point for embodied learning. E0.5 builds on this class of models, extending their role from recovering observed geometry to learning geometric futures jointly with robot actions. Several approaches introduce these geometric priors into existing VLA architectures. yang2026understanding investigate geometric feature fusion and representation alignment within VLAs, while GLaD~ guo2025glad distills features from a frozen geometric teacher into the language backbone's visual-token representations. Such methods incorporate geometric knowledge while retaining a vision-language-centered policy architecture. Geometry also appears as a generative target: 3D-VLA~ zhen2024vla connects a 3D-aware language model with diffusion models that generate goal images and point clouds. Thus, using 3D information or generating geometric goals is distinct from making a geometric foundation model the primary, trainable backbone for world-action modeling. VGA~ song2026robotic is more closely related in its use of a native geometric backbone for action generation. Its geometric supervision reconstructs the observed scene, and it uses LoRA adaptation to preserve pretrained backbone weights; its ablations report substantially lower performance with full-parameter training under the evaluated configuration. E0.5 instead explicitly predicts future 3D states and actions while unfreezing and jointly optimizing the geometric backbone. The distinction is therefore not simply the presence of a 3D backbone, but its transformation into a trainable predictive world-action model. Our comparison of future-state prediction with current-state reconstruction directly evaluates this distinction, while the OOD experiments examine its implications for generalization. sec:method E0.5 is designed around a single principle: the foundation used to generate actions should itself learn to anticipate geometric change. This principle unifies our two key contributions. A 3D foundation model provides the primary representation for world-action modeling, while future geometry supervision adapts this representation to anticipate spatial changes induced by robot actions. We therefore develop E0.5 as a future-predictive geometric foundation that jointly supports world modeling and action generation. title: Rollback: Experience Backtracking in World Models for Policy Improvement
summary: Action-conditioned world models offer a scalable alternative to costly real-world interaction for improving robot policies. However, existing world-model-based methods largely treat world models as forward-only surrogates of the physical environment, leaving untapped a capability no physical environment affords: rewinding to past decision points to explore counterfactual futures. We introduce Rollback, a policy improvement paradigm that turns world models from passive simulators into counterfactual engines: it rolls back to critical decision points, branches into alternative actions, and contrasts their outcomes to attribute success to individual decisions. This concentrates imagination where it matters most and distills counterfactual outcomes into fine-grained, action-level supervision without a separately learned value model. We build a scalable training system that unifies distributed world-model search with asynchronous real-robot execution, forming a self-reinforcing cycle: real-world experience continually sharpens the world model, and a sharper world model in turn drives further policy improvement. We term the world-model side of this cycle test-time physics grounding, a capability that hand-built physics simulators lack: while the world model serves as the training environment, real transitions from the policy it trains correct its dynamics through a lightweight LoRA pipeline. Experiments on three challenging real-world tasks show that Rollback improves success rates over the strongest baseline by an absolute 10.67%, 11.11%, and 11.85% on block extraction, ball tossing, and tabletop curling, respectively, while achieving more stable improvement throughout training. Although initialized from teleoperated demonstrations far below human level, Rollback surpasses the average success rate of human players on both ball tossing and tabletop curling within 8 hours of training.
full_text: Experiments sec:experiments =-1 We evaluate on three real-world manipulation tasks to assess policy performance and data efficiency. We investigate the contributions of experience-backtracking search (through the comparison with RISE w/ GE-Sim2, our reproduction of RISE on the same world model without backtracking), tree-structured supervision, and world-model adaptation to iterative policy improvement. Specifically, we ask whether outperforms existing baselines in the real world, how much each component contributes, whether it improves stably and reaches human-level performance, and how faithful its world model is. Experimental Setup sec:setup Tasks and Evaluation. We evaluate our proposed and baselines on the AGIBOT Genie-02 robot~ agibotg2 across three real-world tasks spanning contact-rich manipulation, precise control, and competitive interaction: [leftmargin=*] Block Extraction. The robot removes wooden Jenga blocks one at a time from a stacked tower without collapsing it, testing precise manipulation under stability constraints. Ball Tossing. The robot throws a ball into a bucket, with success determined by whether the ball lands inside. This task tests precise control of the throwing motion and release timing. Tabletop Curling. =-1 A human and the robot each deliver two stones. Later shots can displace earlier stones, and the winner is determined by the score based on proximity to the target center. This task tests strategic selection and precise execution against an opponent. The policy observes three RGB views, from one head-mounted camera and two wrist cameras, together with the robot's proprioceptive state, and controls 16 action dimensions, comprising seven arm joints and one gripper per side, at 30\,Hz. For each task, we select six initial positions (nine for Tabletop Curling) and run 15 trials per position (25 for Block Extraction); per-position results are in Appendix~ app:per-position . Implementation Details. (1) World Model Training. We initialize the world model from pretrained GE-Sim 2.0~ qiu2026ge and train it in two stages: supervised fine-tuning followed by distribution matching distillation~ dmd . We fine-tune the model on task-specific data for 10K steps using 32 NVIDIA H200 GPUs with a global batch size of 128. We then perform DMD on the same dataset for 2,500 steps using 16 NVIDIA H200 GPUs with a global batch size of 16. (2) Policy Warm-up. We initialize the policy from ~ pi05 and pre-train it on task-specific expert-collected data using RECAP-style quality conditioning~ recap . We use five quality bins, assigning successful trajectories to the highest bin and failed trajectories to the lowest bin . Training runs for 100K steps on 16 NVIDIA H200 GPUs with a global batch size of 64. (3) Reward Model Training. We use the world judge of GE-Sim 2.0~ qiu2026ge as the reward model and fine-tune it on task-specific robot videos annotated with success labels. Conditioned on visual observations and the task instruction, the model predicts task completion using a binary classification head trained with binary cross-entropy loss. (4) Policy Improvement in World Models. We run policy improvement with one physical robot and 48 NVIDIA H200 GPUs, allocating 40 GPUs to world-model-based tree search and 8 to policy training with DDP. Following world-model warm-up, all processes run asynchronously; each world-model adaptation adds newly collected real trajectories to the replay dataset and adapts the world model through 400 steps of LoRA-based~ lora SFT followed by 100 steps of DMD. Baselines. =-1 We compare with imitation learning, reinforcement learning, and world-model-based baselines. All methods use the same initialization and comparable compute budgets; RECAP and RISE w/ GE-Sim2 are trained for a similar duration of about 8 hours with one physical robot and a similar number of NVIDIA H200 GPUs. Execution-level details and hyperparameters are provided in Appendices~ app:details and~ app:hparams . (1) SFT. We fine-tune ~ pi05 on task-specific expert demonstrations using supervised learning. (2) RECAP. We adapt RECAP~ recap to , using a learned value model to estimate advantages for conditioned policy training on collected real-world data. (3) RISE w/ GE-Sim2. RISE~ rise learns from imagined interactions with a compositional world model that couples action-conditioned dynamics with a learned progress value model. We reproduce RISE on GE-Sim 2.0~ qiu2026ge , the same world model that uses, with five RECAP-style advantage bins, and denote this reproduction RISE w/ GE-Sim2. All RISE results in this report come from this reproduction rather than from the original paper. Because the two methods share the world model, the comparison isolates experience-backtracking search and tree-structured supervision from world-model quality. Main Results =-1 Table~ tab:main-results compares with the baselines across three real-world tasks. achieves the highest success rate on all tasks, reaching 69.33 on Block Extraction, 40.00 on Ball Tossing, and 64.44 on Tabletop Curling. 's average success rate exceeds SFT, RECAP, and RISE w/ GE-Sim2 by 17.63 , 13.71 , and 11.21 , respectively. Compared with RISE w/ GE-Sim2, which also learns through interaction with the same world model, improves success rates by an absolute 10.67 , 11.11 , and 11.85 on the three tasks. This corresponds to a relative improvement of 24.0 in average success rate over RISE w/ GE-Sim2. On average, real-world RL with RECAP adds 3.92 over SFT and forward world-model rollouts with RISE w/ GE-Sim2 add another 2.49 , whereas experience backtracking with the same world model adds 11.21 on top of RISE w/ GE-Sim2, more than the two previous gains combined. The largest relative gain is on Ball Tossing (38.5 over RISE w/ GE-Sim2), where the outcome is decided by the release, so comparing sibling actions from the same context directly identifies better releases. These gains span contact-rich manipulation, precise throwing, and competitive interaction, indicating that the benefits of search-based training transfer to physical execution without requiring world-model search at deployment. Ablation Studies sec:ablation We conduct ablations on Block Extraction to examine the contributions of world-model adaptation and tree-structured value estimation; frozen-world-model results on the other two tasks are reported in Appendix~ app:per-position . We report three metrics over all evaluation trials: Target Contact measures whether the pushing motion hits the target block; Task Success measures complete extraction without collapsing the remaining structure; and Consecutive Extractions counts the average number of blocks extracted in a row before failure. (1) Frozen World Model. We retain the world model obtained after initial task-specific training and disable subsequent updates from real interaction, which disables test-time physics grounding. (2) Direct Reward Supervision. We replace subtree-aggregated values with individual rollout rewards for quality-conditioned policy training while retaining tree search. All variants use the same policy initialization and computation budget. As shown in Table~ tab:ablation , removing either component degrades all three metrics; direct reward supervision lowers task success most (59.33 ), and a frozen world model reduces consecutive extractions from 2.60 to 1.90. Target contact also falls from 89.33 to 78.67 with a frozen world model and to 77.33 with direct reward supervision. With direct reward supervision, each label depends on a single stochastic rollout rather than a subtree average, and with a frozen world model, prediction errors accumulate over the long sequences of contact-rich decisions that block extraction requires. Training Dynamics sec:training-analysis Figure~ fig:training-curves tracks the real-world success rate of and RISE w/ GE-Sim2 on Ball Tossing and Tabletop Curling over 8 hours of training. Starting from the RECAP policy, improves Ball Tossing steadily from 25.56 to 40.00 , whereas RISE w/ GE-Sim2 fluctuates and ends at only 28.89 . This is a relative improvement of 56.5 within 8 hours using a single physical robot, while RISE w/ GE-Sim2 first drops to 24.44 after 2 hours. Keeping the world model frozen instead yields only 26.67 , indicating that continually refining the world model with real experience is essential for sustained improvement. On Tabletop Curling, rises from 51.11 to 64.44 over the same period, while RISE w/ GE-Sim2 stays close to its initialization and ends at 52.59 , only 1.48 above its starting point. On Tabletop Curling, the gap between the two methods widens at every evaluation; on Ball Tossing, it widens steadily after 4 hours. Qualitative Results sec:qualitative =-1 Figure~ fig:qualitative visualizes experience-backtracking search on Tabletop Curling: panel (a) shows the search tree, and panels (b, c) show continuations from a branch point inside imagination and from a rollback on a real attempt. Rather than restarting from the initial state, rolls back to two intermediate decision points of a real attempt and branches from the restored contexts. At step 200 (control steps at 30\,Hz), during the second push, the recorded push brings the red stone into the house, whereas an imagined alternative from the same context leaves it short of the house. Comparing continuations that share everything up to this point isolates the second push as the decision that determines the outcome. Branching also happens inside imagination: from the same imagined state at step 50, both continuations push the first stone alike, but one releases the second stone fast enough to reach the house and the other releases it slowly, so it stops in front. More examples for all three tasks are provided in Appendix~ app:qualitative . Surpassing Human Performance sec:human We compare with human players performing each task by hand and with teleoperated data collection, both under the same initial positions and success criteria; each is averaged over three people. On Ball Tossing, human players and teleoperation achieve 31.48 and 16.53 , respectively, and surpasses the human average after 6 hours of training (33.33 ), reaching 40.00 after 8 hours (Figure~ fig:human ). On Tabletop Curling, human players and teleoperation achieve 58.39 and 38.94 , and surpasses humans after 4 hours, reaching 64.44 after 8 hours. Although is initialized from teleoperated demonstrations far below human level, it surpasses human players on both tasks by learning from counterfactual imagination. At the end of training, exceeds the human average by 8.52 and 6.05 on the two tasks, and teleoperation by 23.47 and 25.50 . The RECAP initialization already exceeds teleoperation on both tasks (25.56 vs.\ 16.53 and 51.11 vs.\ 38.94 ), but only training with lifts it above human players. The policy never observes the human players, so the margin over them comes from comparing the robot's own alternative actions in imagination. World-Model Fidelity and Reward Reliability sec:fidelity To measure how far imagined rollouts drift from reality, we replay the recorded actions of eight failed real Block Extraction episodes open-loop in the co-evolved world model, five times each, and compare the predictions with the real recordings (Table~ tab:app-fidelity ). The average PSNR is 21.6\,dB, highest for the head camera (23.4\,dB), whose static background is easier to predict than the wrist views. title: Task-Utility IQA: Rethinking Image Quality Assessment in Embodied Tasks
summary: Image quality assessment (IQA) underpins embodied imaging pipelines by judging whether visual quality satisfies downstream tasks, yet most existing methods learn task-agnostic scores aligned with generic human ratings on static benchmarks. This objective mismatches embodied and interactive settings, where image adequacy depends on task goals, context, and action requirements that shape an agent's decisions. We argue that IQA should shift from score regression to goal-conditioned judgment defined by embodied task utility. To this end, we propose an MLLM-based embodied IQA agent framework that reasons about task requirements, grounds quality evidence, and produces decision-facing assessments. A compact VisDrone evidence study shows that conventional perceptual metrics and generic MLLM-based IQA scores are weak proxies for downstream VLM task success, while a task-conditioned utility score better predicts whether visual input supports the target task. These findings support a task-utility-oriented reframing of IQA for embodied, explainable, and decision-aware visual perception.
full_text: Image quality assessment (IQA) underpins embodied imaging pipelines by judging whether visual quality satisfies downstream tasks, yet most existing methods learn task-agnostic scores aligned with generic human ratings on static benchmarks. This objective mismatches embodied and interactive settings, where image adequacy depends on task goals, context, and action requirements that shape an agent's decisions. We argue that IQA should shift from score regression to goal-conditioned judgment defined by embodied task utility. To this end, we propose an MLLM-based embodied IQA agent framework that reasons about task requirements, grounds quality evidence, and produces decision-facing assessments. A compact VisDrone evidence study shows that conventional perceptual metrics and generic MLLM-based IQA scores are weak proxies for downstream VLM task success, while a task-conditioned utility score better predicts whether visual input supports the target task. These findings support a task-utility-oriented reframing of IQA for embodied, explainable, and decision-aware visual perception. Code and processed evidence-study results will be released at: . Introduction Image quality assessment (IQA) is a foundational problem in computer vision, concerned with determining whether visual signals are suitable for downstream use zhang2023blind,li2025q,zha2025aircopbench . IQA underpins a broad range of vision pipelines, including image acquisition and enhancement, compression and streaming, video frame selection, and the evaluation of restoration and generation models wang2004image,hore2010image,saad2012blind,mittal2012no,ma2025survey . With the emergence of embodied intelligence, the role of IQA extends beyond perceptual fidelity to embodied perception, where visual observations directly influence perception, reasoning, planning, and action in vision--language--action systems. Existing IQA research has progressed from classical full-reference metrics, such as PSNR hore2010image and SSIM wang2004image , to no-reference methods saad2012blind,mittal2012no and deep models optimized on human opinion scores bosse2017deep,ma2025survey,li2025image . While these advances have substantially improved perceptual quality prediction, the underlying paradigm remains largely centered on task-agnostic scalar scoring. In embodied settings, however, image quality cannot be fully characterized by perceptual fidelity alone; instead, it should be evaluated according to downstream usability, interpretability, and decision relevance for intelligent agents zhang2024embodied,zhu2025agenticiqa . Existing IQA protocols primarily assess alignment with human subjective judgments on static benchmarks, implicitly assuming that perceptual preference correlates with practical utility. Dilemma of Traditional IQA. In embodied settings, traditional IQA fails when quality requirements vary across tasks, when task-relevant regions occupy only part of the image chen2024topiq,song2025segmenting , and when semantic coverage matters more than pixel-level fidelity kerkouri2025modeling . In unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) infrastructure inspection, a task-agnostic metric can assign similar penalties to blur regardless of where it occurs, although blur in sky or background regions is often irrelevant while blur over the inspected surface can make an image unusable. In robotic manipulation, noise or compression may be tolerable for coarse navigation but harmful when edges, keypoints, or depth cues are needed for grasp planning. These cases reveal a fundamental evaluation misalignment: a single quality score optimized for generic human ratings cannot capture diverse embodied task requirements. 6pt gray!10 Primary position: IQA should embrace MLLM-based embodied agents, reframing image quality assessment as goal-conditioned, explainable, and adaptive judgment that is evaluated by task utility rather than by correlation with task-agnostic scores. The Turning Point. IQA stands at an inflection point driven by two converging trends. First, embodied AI agents, including UAVs, mobile robots, and AR systems, create new demands for context-aware quality assessment morgenthal2014quality,zhang2024embodied,lv2025ar . Second, multimodal large language models (MLLMs) liu2023visual combine visual perception with language-conditioned reasoning, enabling systems that understand context, generate explanations, and adapt to diverse tasks. Recent work shows that MLLMs can express quality judgments in natural language wu2023q,huang2024visualcritic , support comparative evaluation zhu2024adaptive,wu2024towards , and provide localized rationales you2024depicting,chen2024q . The missing step is to integrate IQA into the embodied loop, conditioning judgments and explanations on specific perception tasks and context so they can drive actionable decisions. Why This Position Paper? As AI systems transition from passive predictors to agents that perceive and act, visual quality should be defined relative to goals, constraints, and actions. Existing IQA objectives and benchmarks do not capture this dependency, and they provide little support for explanation, interaction, and policy-level decisions such as retake, reposition, or proceed. The maturation of MLLMs and the deployment of embodied systems make it timely to articulate a principled research agenda for embodied IQA agents. Contributions. This position paper makes four contributions: (1) We propose an MLLM-based embodied IQA agent framework that reframes image quality assessment from task-agnostic score regression to goal-conditioned, explainable, and utility-aware judgment; (2) We analyze failure modes of scoring-based IQA in embodied settings and motivate a task-utility view of quality, where visual adequacy depends on task goals, context, and action requirements; (3) We review MLLM-based IQA and recent embodied IQA efforts, highlighting the gap between generic or robot-oriented quality scoring and downstream task-utility alignment; (4) We provide compact empirical evidence on VisDrone~ zhu2018vision,du2019visdroneDet showing that task-agnostic perceptual and generic MLLM-based IQA scores are weak proxies for downstream task success, while a task-conditioned utility score better aligns with task utility. We provide an extended literature taxonomy and supplementary formulation details in Appendix~ app:literature_review and Appendix~ app:training_formulations . Background: MLLM-based IQA and Related Work Recent work has begun to recast IQA using multimodal foundation models, offering richer outputs than scalar scores. We summarize this line of work along three themes: (1) single-image assessment, (2) comparative and relational evaluation, and (3) grounded quality analysis. While these directions improve interpretability and flexibility, they still rarely model the task-conditioned nature of quality required by embodied agents. Detailed concept definitions are provided in . highlights the gap between current MLLM-based IQA and embodied requirements. Single-Image IQA with MLLMs Early work leveraged pre-trained vision-language models (VLMs) for IQA, establishing foundations for MLLM-based quality assessment. CLIP-IQA wang2023exploring demonstrates that CLIP embeddings can assess quality without task-specific training, achieving reasonable performance on general quality assessment. This zero-shot approach reveals that VLMs capture quality-relevant features. Q-Instruct wu2024q moves beyond zero-shot prompting by constructing instruction-tuning datasets that teach MLLMs to perform low-level visual quality judgments through natural language reasoning. By aligning quality assessment with instruction-following capabilities, it demonstrates that instruction tuning substantially improves MLLM performance on IQA-related tasks. Q-ALIGN wu2023q further advances this line of work by replacing continuous quality scores with discrete, text-defined quality levels that better reflect subjective evaluation categories such as excellent, good, and fair. Framing IQA as a classification problem rather than regression, Q-ALIGN achieves state-of-the-art results on KonIQ-10K lin2018koniq . Other recent work includes PromptIQA chen2024promptiqa , which uses prompts to boost performance and generalization, and multi-modal prompt learning approaches pan2024multi that enhance blind image quality assessment. Teaching-based methods zhang2025teaching,you2025teaching explore how to train LMMs for image quality scoring and interpreting. Next Token approaches li2025next demonstrate realistic image quality and aesthetic scoring with MLLMs. Align-IQA yang2024align addresses diverse human preferences through customizable guidance, enabling more flexible quality assessment aligned with different user needs. A comprehensive study wu2024comprehensive systematically investigates psychophysical experimental designs (single-stimulus, double-stimulus, and multiple-stimulus methods) combined with prompting strategies (standard, in-context, and chain-of-thought) for MLLM-based IQA, revealing that while GPT-4V provides reasonable quality assessment, it struggles with fine-grained quality discrimination and multi-image comparison tasks. Despite these advances, these methods treat IQA as an isolated task without considering task context. CLIP-IQA provides no task-specific reasoning, Q-Instruct focuses on general quality improvements, and Q-ALIGN, while more interpretable, still produces task-agnostic assessments. They do not integrate with embodied decision-making pipelines where quality judgments should inform actions and adapt to changing mission requirements. The gap between general quality assessment and task-aware judgment represents a fundamental challenge that these methods do not address. Comparative and Relational IQA Beyond single-image IQA, comparative and relational methods align quality assessment with human judgment by enabling relative, context-aware reasoning across multiple images. Compare2Score zhu2024adaptive uses adaptive soft comparison to estimate pairwise preferences. Q-Insight li2025q employs group relative policy optimization for ranked image sets. Co-Instruct wu2024towards enables open-ended visual quality comparison and introduces MICBench, a benchmark for multi-image comparison tasks. The advances in comparative assessment enable richer judgments than scalar scores but remain detached from task context. Pairwise comparison is more informative than assigning a single score, yet task-conditioned comparison is more meaningful for embodied applications; for example, an image should be judged by whether it supports obstacle avoidance rather than by generic visual preference alone. Bridging this gap between general and task-aware comparison is a key opportunity for embodied IQA. Grounded Quality Assessment Recent quality assessment work incorporates spatial grounding, recognizing that quality issues are often localized. Q-Ground chen2024q detects and describes local distortions via multi-scale feature learning and introduces the QGround-100K dataset, while DepictQA you2024depicting generates descriptive quality comparisons across image pairs. However, these explanations are not task-grounded: they identify what is wrong, but not why it matters for a specific task. Q-Ground can localize blur but cannot assess its task relevance (e.g., structural surfaces vs. sky for crack detection). DepictQA provides descriptive comparisons but cannot relate them to task requirements. As a result, they offer limited actionable guidance for embodied systems where explanations need to inform decisions. Embodied IQA. Recent work has begun to explicitly connect IQA with embodied AI. zhang2024embodied propose an embodied image quality assessment setting for robotic intelligence, with an embodied preference database and a dedicated no-reference IQA model. More recently, li2026embodiediqa formulate IQA for embodied AI as a benchmark problem and construct a larger E

title: Learning Multi-Phase Robot Loco-Manipulation via Phase-Conditioned Policy Optimization
summary: Complex whole-body loco-manipulation requires executing diverse maneuvers, such as crouching, grasping, and locomotion, within a single long-horizon task. While performing simple pick-and-place behaviors is well-established, scaling to complex, long-horizon tasks remains difficult. Currently, this challenge is addressed by relying on human motion data and correspondingly humanoid platforms, which limits platform independence and introduces substantial data processing overhead. Instead, we extend proximal policy optimization (PPO) to train a single policy for multi-phase tasks across diverse robotic hardware, leveraging prior task structure to shape behavior. Our method adapts PPO using a phase-conditioned critic, phase-gated reward functions, and a multi-phase reset curriculum to guide exploration. To support varied hardware, we employ a decoupled hierarchical control architecture that separates lower-level balancing dynamics from high-level phase execution. We demonstrate multi-stage loco-manipulation skills on hardware on both the Unitree G1 and a Boston Dynamics Spot equipped with a manipulator arm, and validate our design choices through ablations. Our approach enables the acquisition of complex loco-manipulation behaviors purely through environment interaction while directly incorporating high-level task structure into policy learning.
full_text: Learning Multi-Phase Robot Loco-Manipulation \ Phase-Conditioned Policy Optimization Simone Manni , Annika Wollschläger , Dario Bellicoso , Abel Gawel ,\\ Marco Hutter , Simon Le Cleac'h , and Jan Brüdigam Robotic Systems Lab (RSL), ETH Zurich, Zurich, Switzerland. Robotics and AI Institute (RAI), Zurich, Switzerland. Multi-Phase Loco-Manipulation. Our framework synthesizes a single, unified policy per environment capable of executing complex, multi-phase loco-manipulation behaviors, including: (a) a box pick-up and carrying sequence on the Unitree G1 humanoid; (b) a full tire-manipulation sequence (uprighting, rolling, and tilting) on Boston Dynamics Spot; and (c) a dynamic box pushing task with G1. fig:teaser Complex whole-body loco-manipulation requires executing diverse maneuvers, such as crouching, grasping, and locomotion, within a single long-horizon task. While performing simple pick-and-place behaviors is well-established, scaling to complex, long-horizon tasks remains difficult. Currently, this challenge is addressed by relying on human motion data and correspondingly humanoid platforms, which limits platform independence and introduces substantial data processing overhead. Instead, we extend proximal policy optimization (PPO) to train a single policy for multi-phase tasks across diverse robotic hardware, leveraging prior task structure to shape behavior. Our method adapts PPO using a phase-conditioned critic, phase-gated reward functions, and a multi-phase reset curriculum to guide exploration. To support varied hardware, we employ a decoupled hierarchical control architecture that separates lower-level balancing dynamics from high-level phase execution. We demonstrate multi-stage loco-manipulation skills on hardware on both the Unitree G1 and a Boston Dynamics Spot equipped with a manipulator arm, and validate our design choices through ablations. Our approach enables the acquisition of complex loco-manipulation behaviors purely through environment interaction while directly incorporating high-level task structure into policy learning. Introduction Loco-manipulation is an essential capability for deploying mobile robots in real-world environments, where they must navigate, interact with, and reconfigure their surroundings. Although reinforcement learning (RL) methods have been increasingly employed with success in short-horizon pick-and-place tasks tang2025deep, jung2026learning , they usually struggle in long-horizon settings due to the large exploration space and complex contact mechanics pmlr-v270-zhou25a, pmlr-v305-mao25a . Additionally, complex loco-manipulation tasks, such as lifting and carrying a box, mandate coordinating distinct physical modes (walking, crouching, rising) within a unified policy. This poses a major challenge for standard reward tuning, which might cause training to collapse into unwanted local minima, such as learning to kick or drag a box instead of lifting and carrying it. To bridge this gap, recent work increasingly relies on human motion datasets yang2025omniretarget and demonstrations, driving the widespread adoption of humanoid platforms in research. While effective, this paradigm requires substantial data processing overhead and results in platform-specific methods that fail to generalize to diverse robotic hardware. More recent approaches have successfully solved humanoid loco-manipulation tasks by learning through autonomous environment interaction, without human guidance byrd2026adaptmanip, leziart2026learning, zheng2025embracing . However, they only focus on simple table-to-table object transportation, ignoring the distinct physical transitions, such as low crouching and rising, required to pick up or deposit an object directly from the ground. Crucially, long-horizon tasks are inherently compositional and naturally break down into a sequence of distinct behavioral stages, each demanding specialized local control. For example, a box-lifting policy can be split into approaching, crouching and lifting phases. Exploiting this inherent multi-phase structure provides a promising route to tackle the exploration challenge without demonstration data. While traditional methods often rely on finite state machines to chain independently trained sub-policies sequentially---a strategy previously applied also to humanoid box-lifting dao2024sim ---managing transitions across highly dynamic regimes can be problematic. In contrast, consolidating these stages into a single policy natively manages inter-phase transitions and eliminates external orchestration. This strong multi-phase structure and the advantage of having a single policy to handle the entire task highlight the need for an RL framework that can explicitly leverage phase transitions to guide exploration and training. To this end, we introduce a variant of the popular PPO schulman2017proximal algorithm that incorporates the sequential nature of the task. A state machine segments the task into manageable behavior windows and masks MDP terms. The actor is forced to internalize task progression by predicting the current phase, and the critic is conditioned on the active phase to better capture local value changes. We evaluate our framework across two distinct platforms and multiple tasks, including a Spot quadruped maneuvering a tire and a Unitree G1 humanoid carrying a box. For the latter, we also resolve several sim-to-real issues to enable stable, prolonged grasping. Finally, through targeted ablations, we validate the impact of our core algorithmic choices. Our contributions are as follows. Unified Control Interface: To ensure compatibility, we first establish a common control interface across both platforms, extending the hierarchical RL framework originally developed for the quadruped to the humanoid. Multi-Phase RL Framework: We design a multi-phase RL training framework built on top of PPO that conditions value estimation and the MDP on task phases, allowing a single unified policy to coordinate complex multi-stage tasks. Related Work We provide a brief overview of related work on low and high-level policies for robotic manipulation, with a focus on long-horizon tasks. ReLiC for Hierarchical Loco-Manipulation Our framework builds on the hierarchical loco-manipulation architecture introduced in ReLiC~ pmlr-v305-zhu25a , itself grounded in earlier hierarchical RL approaches for quadrupedal loco-manipulation~ jeon2023learning . ReLiC uses a decoupled hierarchy in which a low-level whole-body controller tracks locomotion and posture commands while a high-level policy specifies task-dependent behaviors. We adopt this architecture as the control interface for our framework. For the Unitree G1, we train a new low-level whole-body controller with the same general design, adapting the interface to the humanoid's kinematics and balancing dynamics. For the Boston Dynamics Spot experiments, we directly use the ReLiC controller. Building on this established hierarchical architecture, our contribution focuses on the high-level learning problem: training a single policy to execute a long-horizon sequence of distinct behaviors. Humanoid Whole-Body Control Whole-body control for humanoids has shifted from model-based optimization 1642100, murooka2021humanoid, settimi2016motion to learning-based policies trained in simulation gu2026humanoid . This shift, however, has largely traded one bottleneck for another: rather than hand-designing controllers, the field is now dominated by demonstration-driven, motion-tracking approaches that imitate human motion capture or teleoperated data at increasing scale zhang2025natural, ji2024exbody2, pmlr-v305-ze25a . Driven to the extreme, this culminates in foundation-scale efforts such as SONIC luo2026sonic , trained on over 100 million frames of motion data. These methods produce highly natural motion but demand substantial data curation and compute. Closer to our approach, ULC sun2025ulc trains a single unified policy from scratch using large-scale parallel reinforcement learning, without motion references, to jointly track root velocity, root height, torso rotation, and dual-arm joint positions. We adopt the same demonstration-free, single-policy philosophy, but consider a narrower control objective tailored to our architecture and use cases. Following the decoupled upper- and lower-body control framework introduced in pmlr-v331-zhang26a , our policy is trained to track velocity, height, and torso pitch, while observing but not controlling the arms joints, removing the additional torso-rotation and dual-arm tracking objectives considered in ULC. Moreover, while ULC addresses the complexity of its high-dimensional command space through sequential skill acquisition and an adaptive curriculum, we instead constrain commands to feasible regions and use keyframe-based exploration to facilitate learning. Reinforcement Learning for Long-Horizon and Multi-Stage Tasks The decomposition of complex, long-horizon tasks builds upon the foundational principles of hierarchical reinforcement learning and the options framework introduced by Sutton and Barto sutton1999between . This paradigm relies on learning multiple sub-policies alongside an orchestrator that determines when to switch policy, enabling the agents to operate across distinct levels of abstraction and temporal scales. Subsequent extensions have explored designing the orchestrator as a finite state machine to chain sub-policies for deployment dao2024sim, konidaris2009skill, chen2023sequential . However, while traditional skill-chaining methods have succeeded primarily in quasi-static tabletop manipulation, applying them to dynamic loco-manipulation breaks down: defining stable initial and terminal states for sub-policies becomes difficult due to continuous momentum and shifting contacts, which in turn makes both sub-policy training and inter-policy transitions brittle. Hence, they typically require precise state observability at deployment or specialized training regimens lee2021adversarial, chen2024scar, lee2019composing to guarantee reliable policy transitions. To handle transitions autonomously, alternative approaches combine sub-policies at training time via distillation harish2024reinforcement, rudin2025parkour , although this introduces additional setup overhead. Similarly, our method uses the same idea of splitting a long task into multiple phases but directly optimizes a single policy over them. Our formulation also connects to the idea of reward machines icarte2018using and their applications in robotic manipulation baert2024reward , where individual policies are trained with sub-task-specific rewards. Similarly, our approach allows for phase-dependent rewards, but rather than training separate policies, it leverages this task-splitting intuition to train a single unified policy, utilizing a phase-conditioned value network to correctly capture phase-specific behavior. Method We introduce our phase-conditioned policy optimization method. We first formulate the reinforcement learning (RL) problem, then provide details on the low-level controllers, and finally describe the high-level phased policy learning. Reinforcement Learning Problem We formulate the long-horizon loco-manipulation task as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) defined by the tuple , where denotes the state space, represents the observation space, is the action space, models the stochastic transition probability density, is the reward function, and is the discount factor. At each discrete time step , the agent perceives an observation derived from the underlying environment state , and samples an action according to its policy , generating a trajectory . The objective is to maximize the expected discounted return: To mitigate the intractable exploration space of end-to-end high-dimensional motor control, we adopt a two-level hierarchical RL paradigm. title: ASPEN: Adaptive Semantic Reasoning via Command Persistence Prediction for Efficient Navigation VLAs
summary: Navigation vision-language-action (VLA) policies repeatedly invoke costly semantic reasoning even when the next command remains unchanged. Command reuse can reduce computation but risks missing instruction-dependent turns or stops. We introduce ASPEN, an event-triggered scheduler based on command persistence prediction: estimating whether the frozen base policy would reissue its previous command. A lightweight multimodal predictor combines temporal observations, language instructions, execution history, and cached VLA confidence. At eligible command boundaries, sufficient predicted persistence permits command reuse. Otherwise, ASPEN triggers fresh semantic reasoning from the VLA. Evaluated with frozen NaVILA on cross-dataset RxR-CE val-unseen, ASPEN reduces VLA calls by 9.5% and estimated inference time by 8.1%, including scheduling overhead. It maintains comparable navigation performance and preserves identical baseline action sequences on 92.1% of episodes.
full_text: Navigation vision-language-action (VLA) policies repeatedly invoke costly semantic reasoning even when the next command remains unchanged. Command reuse can reduce computation but risks missing instruction-dependent turns or stops. We introduce ASPEN, an event-triggered scheduler based on command persistence prediction: estimating whether the frozen base policy would reissue its previous command. A lightweight multimodal predictor combines temporal observations, language instructions, execution history, and cached VLA confidence. At eligible command boundaries, sufficient predicted persistence permits command reuse. Otherwise, ASPEN triggers fresh semantic reasoning from the VLA. Evaluated with frozen NaVILA on cross-dataset RxR-CE val-unseen, ASPEN reduces VLA calls by 9.5 and estimated inference time by 8.1 , including scheduling overhead. It maintains comparable navigation performance and preserves identical baseline action sequences on 92.1 of episodes. Introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) policies connect visual observations and language instructions to robot behavior~ palme, rt2, openvla . In navigation, these policies can generate high-level commands that are executed through a downstream action interface~ waypoint, etpnav, navillm, navid, navila . However, repeated invocation of a large VLA incurs substantial cost when successive decisions produce the same command. We study when this semantic reasoning can be omitted while retaining the behavior of a frozen navigation policy. Existing efficiency methods use action-sequence prediction~ act, diffusionpolicy, octo , selective computation and compression~ molevla, efficientvla , temporal caching~ vlacache, gatedcache , and adaptive execution~ flashvla, spvla, ffdcwam . FlashVLA~ flashvla combines action-history consistency and visual-token overlap to trigger reuse, whereas SP-VLA~ spvla schedules between a VLA and a lightweight action generator using motion history. In navigation, substantial visual change can accompany continued forward motion, while the current view alone may not establish whether an instructed landmark has already been passed. The relevant scheduling question is therefore not simply whether the scene or motion has changed, but whether the base policy's next command would change given the instruction and execution history. We introduce ASPEN, which predicts this command persistence from temporal observations, language, execution history, and cached VLA confidence. Following the event-triggered principle~ tabuada2007, heemels2012 , the scheduler chooses between repeating the previous command and refreshing NaVILA. Unlike a lightweight replacement controller, its predicted command distribution is used to schedule the base policy, not to select a different executable command. Our contributions are (i) command-persistence-based scheduling for a frozen navigation policy, (ii) a context-conditioned predictor with explicit eligibility check, and (iii) cross-dataset evaluation from R2R-CE to RxR-CE~ vlnce, rxr , demonstrating reduced estimated inference cost with similar observed success and high action-sequence agreement. ASPEN: Command Persistence Prediction sec:method ASPEN operates at high-level command boundaries, not individual simulator steps (Figure~ fig:overview ). At boundary , the preceding command has completed and observation is available. Before feature extraction, an eligibility check restricts predictor invocation to parsed forward commands with fewer than eight consecutive reuses. Lightweight multimodal command predictor. Frozen SigLIP encodes the episode's first view and the two most recent historical decision-point views. Each view is pooled into a token grid and projected to width 256. Frozen Llama-3 encodes the instruction text once per episode, projecting its final hidden states to the same width. For each historical decision, a learned state vector encodes the executed command, magnitude, step count, repeat flag, episode-progress features, and cached NaVILA confidence. Confidence is refreshed only when NaVILA is invoked. Following DINO-WM~ dinowm , the state vector is added to the corresponding visual tokens and also included as a separate state token. Two width-256 transformer layers with four attention heads apply causal self-attention over visual and state tokens, instruction cross-attention~ lcvn , and feed-forward processing. Instruction tokens serve as keys and values. The resulting state output queries the separately encoded current view through attention pooling. The current view's 81 tokens do not pass through the transformer. An MLP outputs over NaVILA's ten canonical commands. Command-persistence trigger. Let denote eligible forward commands and the consecutive reuse count before boundary . The scheduler uses The persistence score is the learned probability mass on the previous canonical command and is computed only when . Ineligible boundaries invoke NaVILA directly. The reference command is generated from the current execution history only on a refresh, not to verify reuse. Both branches share the downstream execution interface, and NaVILA's observation history continues updating during reuse. This score predicts reference-command agreement rather than certifying task correctness. Training and trigger calibration. We train ASPEN with ten-class next-command cross-entropy on frozen NaVILA rollouts. The R2R-CE training split is divided into disjoint training, checkpoint-selection, and calibration sets: 42/6/13 buildings and 2,536/405/1,685 episodes, respectively. Training includes additional examples collected after incorrect command reuse. We use AdamW with learning rate and batch size 32, training three seeds for up to 100 epochs with 15-epoch early-stopping patience. For each seed, we retain the checkpoint with the lowest checkpoint-selection loss. Deterministic replay on the calibration set selects the threshold maximizing call savings subject to an empirical divergence rate of at most . We deploy the median seed by replay savings, yielding , and evaluate it without RxR-specific tuning. This source-domain selection criterion provides no target-domain divergence guarantee. Experimental Results sec:experiments Evaluation and comparators. We evaluate the selected scheduler on 1,223 RxR-CE val-unseen episodes without target-dataset training or tuning. Comparators include frozen NaVILA, navigation adaptations of FlashVLA's FlashTrigger~ flashvla and SP-VLA~ spvla using published default thresholds, and two diagnostic alternatives. Free Rule repeats a preceding 75\,cm forward command once. Full Gate uses a recurrent classifier, with threshold , after each forward command to choose between an additional 25\,cm forward step and a NaVILA call. We report success rate (SR), oracle success (OS), normalized dynamic time warping (nDTW), and navigation error (NE) as navigation performance metrics. Efficiency is reported by VLA calls and estimated inference time per episode. Exact agreement is the percentage of episodes with the same complete executed action sequence as baseline NaVILA. This measures fidelity to the reference policy, not whether its trajectory succeeds. Inference-cost estimation. We combine logged invocation counts with fixed unit costs measured on a dedicated NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU over 241 ASPEN gate calls across 20 profiling episodes. ASPEN's estimated gate cost is 19.45\,ms, the sum of component-wise median costs for image decoding, preprocessing, visual encoding, pooling, prediction, and communication. The predictor alone accounts for 1.5\,ms, while the shared SigLIP visual encoding accounts for 10.5\,ms. Episode-averaged estimates include scheduling overhead and once-per-episode instruction encoding, with the same estimation procedure used for all methods. Reported results are estimated inference costs, not measured end-to-end navigation runtimes. Efficiency--performance trade-off. Table~ tab:rxr shows that ASPEN maintains comparable SR, OS, nDTW, and NE to baseline NaVILA while reducing estimated inference time by 8.1 . Compared with FlashTrigger, ASPEN uses 3.3 fewer calls per episode, but agreement decreases from to . The additional savings therefore involve an efficiency--agreement trade-off rather than improvement on navigation performance. SP-VLA has slightly lower estimated inference time than ASPEN (38.0 versus 38.2\,s), but its success rate falls to . Free Rule offers the largest call and estimated-time reductions of by utilizing its simple refresh condition. However, its success rate falls to , and exact agreement to . Full Gate reduces calls by yet estimated time by only , emphasizing the need to include scheduling overhead. Efficiency--performance trade-off for all methods shown in Appendix app:add_details Figure~ fig:baseline_compare illustrates ASPEN's adaptive scheduling. It reduces unnecessary semantic reasoning while maintaining the reference trajectory, achieving successful navigation with 9 estimated inference-time savings. Figure~ fig:example_trigger illustrates how ASPEN's context-conditioned predictor triggers semantic reasoning when necessary. At point 1, the instruction calls for a right turn, and a walkway is visible. ASPEN refreshes semantic reasoning and turns right, whereas SP-VLA continues forward. Conclusion sec:conclusion ASPEN enables efficient, event-triggered semantic reasoning in navigation VLAs through command persistence prediction. Its lightweight multimodal command predictor combines navigation context with cached VLA confidence to determine when the previous command can be reused. Cross-dataset evaluation with frozen NaVILA shows reduced reasoning cost while maintaining comparable navigation performance and high agreement with baseline action sequences. Future work will examine transfer to other navigation VLAs and measure latency and energy savings on physical robots. Additional Results app:add_details Figure fig:trade-off shows that ASPEN offers the best efficiency--performance trade-off. It offers 3.8 more inference time savings compared to FlashTrigger while achieving 4 points higher success rate and 85 points higher exact agreement compared to Free Rule.

title: SG^2SLAM: Spatial Geometry-Informed 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM for Monocular Outdoor Navigation
summary: Monocular outdoor navigation requires robust camera motion estimation and a dense, navigable map, where 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM serves this task through an explicit differentiable parameterization and closed-form projection. However, typically, the geometry is recovered by associating 2D pixels with 3D points, so a modular SLAM system absorbs tracking error into the map, leading to cascading degradation. To address these gaps, we present SG^2SLAM, which couples streaming spatial geometry with a ray-conditioned 3DGS kernel. Streaming spatial geometry replaces the per- frame cross-dimensional correspondence with a chunk-level metric prior that supervises tracking and mapping from one source. A ray-conditioned kernel extends each primitive with a viewing-direction subspace that senses the monocular camera viewpoints. The joint optimization over spatial geometry and poses ensures a globally consistent map and trajectory outcome. Experiments on the KITTI and Waymo Open datasets show that our SG^2SLAM surpasses the per-frame association baselines in the monocular outdoor navigation task. Code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.
full_text: Monocular outdoor navigation requires robust camera motion estimation and a dense, navigable map, where 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM serves this task through an explicit differentiable parameterization and closed-form projection. However, typically, the geometry is recovered by associating 2D pixels with 3D points, so a modular SLAM system absorbs tracking error into the map, leading to cascading degradation. To address these gaps, we present SLAM, which couples streaming spatial geometry with a ray-conditioned 3DGS kernel. Streaming spatial geometry replaces the per-frame cross-dimensional correspondence with a chunk-level metric prior that supervises tracking and mapping from one source. A ray-conditioned kernel extends each primitive with a viewing-direction subspace that senses the monocular camera viewpoints. The joint optimization over spatial geometry and poses ensures a globally consistent map and trajectory outcome. Experiments on the KITTI and Waymo Open datasets show that our SLAM surpasses the per-frame association baselines in the monocular outdoor navigation task. Code will be made publicly available upon acceptance. Introduction Recovering camera motion and creating a dense, navigable map of the environment from a monocular RGB stream remain core capabilities for autonomous navigation. Coupling 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) with visual Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) has rapidly become a mainstream research direction, as its explicit, differentiable parameterization is naturally compatible with online tracking and mapping patle2025ad-gs . However, in monocular outdoor navigation, which is the deployment scenario of practical interest, the 3DGS SLAM suffers from an undetermined global scale and further exposes two concrete gaps that we identify below. Existing SLAM systems recover geometry through the 2D–3D matching paradigm, in which 2D pixel observations are associated with 3D points deng2025gigaslam, feldmann2026diskchungs, murai2025mast3rslam, yu2026kilogs, cheng2025outdoor . The 2D–3D association is, however, intrinsically cross-dimensional. The 3D to 2D projection irreversibly discards depth, and the inverse recovery is a non-convex problem that is sensitive to outliers, reprojection noise, and mismatched feature scales. Under the conditions of outdoor monocular navigation, these sensitivities compound. Within a modular SLAM architecture, tracking errors from 2D–3D correspondences are absorbed into the 3D map, which then provides a degraded reference for the next round of matching, producing a slow but unbounded drift that is particularly hard to localize and correct. The 3DGS map becomes geometrically ambiguous while absorbing tracking errors. 3DGS is mainly optimized against a photometric loss for novel view synthesis, which admits multiple geometrically distinct Gaussian configurations that produce indistinguishable renderings. In outdoor sequences, this manifests as floating Gaussians, broken thin structures, and inconsistent surface normals huang20242dgs . These artifacts are tolerable for view synthesis but are directly harmful for navigation due to the pollution of depth information, where downstream tasks such as collision checking and traversability estimation consume the map. To mitigate these gaps in outdoor monocular conditions, we propose SLAM, a 3DGS SLAM built on streaming spatial geometry and a monocular-depth-aware ray-conditioned 3DGS kernel, where the frontend streams poses, point maps, and per-pixel confidence from windows of frames to form chunking, with a metric depth network supervising the metric scale. Then, the backend refines the 3DGS map, conditioning each primitive on the viewing ray with spatial geometric supervision and keeping the mapping consistent and aware under monocular camera conditions. Chunks are then fused by a joint global graph optimization over spatial geometry and poses. Our contribution is as follows: We present a 3DGS SLAM built on streaming spatial geometry. Compared to the baselines based on pairwise 2D pixel matching and cross-dimensional correspondences, our SLAM improves both frontend tracking and backend mapping. We render 3DGS through a ray-conditioned kernel in closed form, where the mean and covariance span a spatial block and a viewing-direction subspace, thus removing the blending at grazing angles that may produce floating primitives. We fuse chunks through joint global graph optimization over the spatial geometry and poses, which keeps the map and trajectory globally consistent and settles the fusion of all chunks in a single solve. Related Work Classical and Learning-Based Monocular SLAM MonoSLAM~ davison2007monoslam showed that a single camera is enough to track and map in real time with an extended Kalman filter, and PTAM~ klein2007ptam made keyframe-based bundle adjustment practical by running tracking and mapping in two parallel threads. The ORB-SLAM family~ murartal2015orbslam, murartal2017orbslam2, campos2021orbslam3 was built on this design using ORB features, a covisibility graph, and bag-of-words place recognition~ galvez2012bags . Methods such as LSD-SLAM~ engel2014lsd skip keypoints and minimize photometric error. DROID-SLAM~ teed2021droid iterates dense optical flow updates through a differentiable bundle adjustment layer and generalizes well across datasets. DPVO~ teed2023dpvo replaces dense flow with sparse patches to cut memory and runtime. All of these systems recover depth indirectly by associating 2D observations with 3D points, and the quality of representation determines both the accuracy and the cost of the association. SLAM with 3D Foundation Models Another direction uses 3D foundation models that regress 3D structures directly from images. DUSt3R~ wang2024dust3r predicts point maps for an image pair in a shared frame, without known intrinsics, and MASt3R~ leroy2024mast3r adds a matching head that provides dense and accurate correspondences. Spann3R~ wang2025spann3r processes images pairwise and maintains a spatial memory in a recurrent state, allowing the whole video to be reconstructed online. VGGT~ wang2025vggt goes further and predicts cameras, depth maps, and point maps for multiple views in a single feed-forward pass. Several SLAM systems are built on these models. MASt3R-SLAM uses two-view MASt3R predictions for tracking and local fusion, and it runs in real time on uncalibrated video murai2025mast3rslam, leroy2024mast3r . SLAM3R~ liu2025slam3r reconstructs dense scenes from monocular RGB with a sliding window of frames that are registered into a global map. VGGT-SLAM builds submaps with VGGT and aligns them with a 15 degree of freedom homography on the SL(4) manifold, since an uncalibrated reconstruction is only defined up to a projective transformation maggio2025vggtslam, wang2025vggt . VGGT-Long~ deng2025vggtlong targets kilometer-scale driving sequences by splitting the video into overlapping chunks, aligning neighboring chunks, and correcting the result with loop closure. This direction replaces correspondence with regression, predicting the 3D structures directly by the network rather than by the camera model. But such systems recover geometric similarity only after submap registration, sliding windows, or explicit alignment in a pairwise manner. 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM 3D Gaussian Splatting~ kerbl20233dgs represents the scene with explicit anisotropic Gaussians that are rasterized at high frame rates, and it quickly became the preferred map for dense SLAM. MonoGS~ matsuki2024gaussian optimizes camera poses directly against the Gaussian map and works with monocular or RGB-D input. SplaTAM~ keetha2024splatam and GS-SLAM~ yan2024gsslam rely on depth sensors, while Photo-SLAM~ huang2024photoslam and CaRtGS~ feng2024cartgs leave tracking to ORB-SLAM3 and spend the GPU budget on mapping. Splat-SLAM~ sandstrom2024splat and HI-SLAM2~ zhang2025hislam2 pair a learned dense tracker with monocular depth priors, and they deform the 3D Gaussians when the trajectory is corrected by global optimization. LoopSplat~ zhu2025loopsplat closes loops by registering submaps made of 3D Gaussians directly. S3PO-GS~ cheng2025outdoor anchors MASt3R point maps to the Gaussian map, which keeps the scale consistent across frames and limits scale drift. GigaSLAM~ deng2025gigaslam stores 3D Gaussians in a hierarchical sparse voxel map, tracks with a metric depth network together with epipolar geometry, and corrects drift with bag-of-words loop closure. DiskChunGS~ feldmann2026diskchungs boosts performance by optimizing the I/O: it splits the scene into spatial chunks, keeps only the active ones on the GPU, and moves the rest to disk. KiloGS-SLAM~ yu2026kilogs combines a multi-tier tracker with chunk-based densification and pruning of 3D Gaussians. Across these systems, the 3DGS map is dominated by image evidence rather than spatial geometry, so the cross-dimensional cost of 2D–3D matching persists beneath the recent progress. Methodology Our SLAM couples streaming spatial geometry with monocular-depth-aware 3DGS based on ray-conditioned kernels to deliver globally consistent mapping and tracking in monocular outdoor navigation. title: PrinGS: Privacy Preservation in Gaussian Splatting
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has rapidly become the preferred representation for high-fidelity novel view synthesis and 3D scene reconstruction. However, the learned representation encodes sensitive visual information including human faces, license plates, documents, and computer screens, raising significant privacy concerns when trained splats are shared or deployed. In this work, we address the underexplored problem of privacy preservation in Gaussian Splatting by proposing a representation-level anonymization framework that directly anonymizes a trained splat. Given a trained splat and a user-provided reference view identifying sensitive content, our method localizes the corresponding regions in the underlying 3D representation and directly anonymizes them, ensuring that the sensitive information is absent from all subsequently rendered novel views while preserving the overall scene geometry and visual fidelity. We achieve this post-training anonymization in less than 1 second. Furthermore, we extend our framework with a privacy-by-design training strategy that prevents sensitive content from being embedded into the representation during optimization, enabling the generation of privacy-preserving splats directly from training images. Our method achieves a remarkably low Face Similarity Measure (FSM) of 9.79% at a retained Face Detection Rate (FDR) of 39.47% and makes sensitive text completely unreadable with an OCR Character Error Rate of 1.00. Our work aims to serve as the primary stepping stone towards privacy-aware 3D representations and motivates further research along these directions.
