While these representations excel at preserving visual fidelity, they also make it possible to recover information that users may expect to remain private, creating new challenges for the safe sharing and deployment of learned scene representations. Since this information is embedded within the learned 3D representation it remains accessible from arbitrary novel viewpoints, introducing significant privacy risks and raising challenges for compliance with regulations such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)~ EU_GDPR_2016 and the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act~ DPDPA2023 . An increasing number of splats are being publicly shared and deployed across real-world applications. A challenge arises when an individual notices their identity captured in a scene without consent and requests its removal to comply with privacy regulations. Retraining from scratch is computationally infeasible. Additionally, in many scenarios, the original training images used for reconstruction are unavailable, inaccessible, or prohibitively expensive to reacquire. Consequently, there is a pressing need for techniques that can anonymize existing splats without requiring access to the original training data. A straightforward solution is to anonymize rendered images after novel-view synthesis. However, such image-space anonymization is inherently view-dependent and leaves the underlying 3D representation unchanged, allowing sensitive information to remain visible when the scene is rendered from different viewpoints. This limitation motivates a representation-level approach that directly anonymizes the learned splat, ensuring that sensitive information is removed across all novel views. We present , a framework for post-training privacy preservation in Gaussian Splatting. Given a trained splat and user-selected reference views containing sensitive content, our method localizes the corresponding Gaussians in the underlying 3D representation and directly anonymizes them. By operating on the representation itself rather than rendered images, sensitive information is removed from the splat, preventing its recovery from arbitrary novel viewpoints while preserving scene geometry and fidelity as shown in Figure~ fig:teaser . While post-training anonymization is essential for existing splats, the rapid adoption of 3DGS is expected to result in an ever-growing number of new 3D scene representations. This presents an opportunity to incorporate privacy preservation directly into the reconstruction pipeline rather than addressing it retrospectively. Motivated by this, we further introduce a privacy-by-design framework that integrates our representation-level anonymization mechanism into the optimization process, preventing sensitive information from being encoded into the splat during training. Existing 3DGS benchmarks predominantly lack privacy-sensitive content like faces, creating a critical gap that hinders the evaluation of privacy aware 3D scene reconstructions. To address this, we construct, , a dataset of synthetic indoor scenes containing human subjects across varying demographics like skin tones and genders, establishing the first benchmark for systematic evaluation of privacy preservation of faces in Gaussian Splatting. Furthermore, conventional rendering metrics primarily assess visual fidelity and do not capture privacy preservation. We therefore quantitatively evaluate our privacy-by-design approach using novel task-specific metrics based on Face Similarity Measure (FSM) and Face Detection Rate (FDR) for faces and OCR Character Error Rate to quantify the removal of textual sensitive information. In terms of facial privacy, our method achieves a Face Similarity Metric (FSM) of only , representing a substantial reduction ( ) compared to standard 3DGS ( ). Furthermore, for textual content, our approach attains a Character Error Rate (CER) of , indicating complete unreadability of private text, significantly outperforming baseline 3DGS, which yields a CER of . We present the first framework for post-training privacy preservation in Gaussian Splatting that directly anonymizes the learned representation without requiring the original training images, preventing sensitive information from being recovered from novel viewpoints in just second. Privacy-by-Design. We introduce a privacy-by-design extension that incorporates anonymization into the Gaussian Splatting optimization process, preventing sensitive information from being encoded during training. . To address the lack of static scenes with humans due to privacy reasons, we construct a benchmark of synthetic indoor scenes containing human subjects across varying demographics, enabling systematic evaluation of privacy-preserving Gaussian Splatting methods. This formulation bypasses costly volumetric ray marching, enabling real-time rendering and interactive scene exploration. Building upon the foundational 3DGS framework, subsequent research has branched into multiple directions to enhance rendering quality and efficiency. Notable quality improvements include anti-aliased formulations such as Mip-Splatting~ yu2024mip and specialized regularizations like AbsGS~ ye2024absgs that handle unbounded scenes and reduce artifacts. Another direction modifies the densification strategy such as 3DGS-MCMC~ kheradmand20243d . To bridge the gap toward resource-constrained settings, methods like Taming 3DGS~ mallick2024taming introduce controlled densification to curb primitive redundancy. Building upon these efficiency measures, compact variants like Mini-Splatting~ fang2024mini, fang2024mini2 introduce memory-efficient pruning and compression mechanisms. Despite these rapid developments in performance and visual fidelity, existing literature predominantly focuses on optimization efficiency and rendering quality while largely overlooking the security and privacy implications of capturing real-world environments. Since these attributes must be learned during optimization, such methods cannot be applied to an already-trained splat that does not carry them. instead localizes sensitive Gaussians directly from the rasterizer's transmittance-weighted contributions, and anonymizes them. To mitigate the exposure of personally identifiable information (PII), regulatory frameworks have accelerated research into automated anonymization; however, existing efforts remain predominantly confined to the 2D domain. For images, anonymization is achieved as a two-step process: detection or segmentation followed by blurring. For detection and segmentation, frameworks such as YOLO~ hurtik2022poly, wang2024yolov1 , Faster R-CNN~ ren2016faster , Mask R-CNN~ he2017mask , and SAM~ kirillov2023segment are utilized to accurately localize sensitive regions. Following detection, privacy is enforced by applying conventional filtering and obfuscation mechanisms such as localized spatial blurring, pixelation, masking, or identity scrambling to protect sensitive regions~ ribaric2016identification . In videos, privacy preservation builds upon these image-based techniques by incorporating temporal consistency through multi-object tracking algorithms~ ciaparrone2020deep, senior2005enabling to prevent identity leakage across successive frames. title: Ground Sample Distance Constrained k-Coverage Viewpoint Planning via Set Multi-Cover Formulation
summary: Drone-based 3D reconstruction and inspection require viewpoints that satisfy image-quality constraints while observing each surface region multiple times, which overlap-based planning heuristics do not guarantee. We study ground sample distance (GSD)-constrained $k$-coverage viewpoint selection for structures represented by surface voxels. Candidate viewpoints are generated along outward surface directions, screened with distance, viewing-angle, field-of-view, and occlusion tests, and augmented for voxels with insufficient visibility. Selection is then posed as set multi-cover with per-voxel coverage demands. We propose a dynamically weighted greedy heuristic that prioritizes remaining coverage deficits and scarce viewing alternatives, and compare it with sequential overlap-based pruning and an integer linear programming (ILP) formulation on the same candidate pools. Across two structures, four voxel resolutions, and three coverage requirements, the proposed approach achieves full or near-full $k$-coverage with compact viewpoint sets, using only 3.00--16.39\% more viewpoints than ILP while offering an interpretable selection process based on coverage deficits and viewpoint availability.

Introduction Autonomous aerial inspection and 3D reconstruction require a set of camera viewpoints that observe all surface regions and satisfy image-quality constraints governing reconstruction fidelity. In such applications, image resolution is commonly expressed through ground sampling distance (GSD), which directly determines the recoverable surface detail in the reconstructed model wilkinson2014elements,Schenk2005,Kraus2011 . Photogrammetric flight planning commonly recommends -- image overlap to support reliable reconstruction wilkinson2014elements,Forstner2016 . Under idealized strip-imaging assumptions, a forward overlap implies that a surface point appears in approximately consecutive images, motivating multi-view redundancy. However, overlap is a global acquisition heuristic and does not directly enforce that each surface region is observed a prescribed number of times under sensing constraints, particularly in the presence of self-occlusions and complex geometry. In this study, we address the viewpoint generation and selection problem for aerial inspection of structures with known geometry (in a world coordinate frame). Specifically, we aim to generate a compact set of camera viewpoints, each defined by a waypoint and a camera orientation, that satisfies prescribed GSD and -coverage requirements. The GSD constraint enforces a spatial-resolution bound under the adopted sensing model, while the -coverage requirement seeks observations of each surface region from at least distinct viewpoints to support multi-view observation. We formulate inspection viewpoint planning as a GSD-constrained -coverage problem over a voxelized surface representation. Surface voxels represent discrete observable regions, and candidate viewpoints are generated to satisfy geometric constraints derived from a prescribed GSD bound and maximum oblique viewing angle. Each candidate viewpoint observes a subset of surface voxels, yielding a set multi-cover formulation that seeks at least observations per voxel, subject to the visibility available in the candidate set. We construct a sensing-compliant candidate set and select a smaller subset of viewpoints using a globally informed greedy -coverage heuristic, evaluated against an integer linear programming (ILP) reference formulation over the same candidate set. Viewpoint selection is explicitly decoupled from downstream tour generation, allowing discrete coverage requirements to be evaluated independently of trajectory optimization. The resulting framework enables explicit evaluation of sensing-constrained multi-view coverage under the adopted geometric sensing model. Related Work sec:related Coverage path planning (CPP) ensures a robot observes or traverses all regions of an environment. Early work established complete coverage through geometric decomposition and topological reasoning acar2002sensor , with surveys formalizing CPP taxonomies and coverage--efficiency trade-offs choset2001coverage,galceran2013survey,tan2021comprehensive . These approaches provide spatial coverage guarantees but primarily reason about traversal completeness rather than image (sensing) quality or multi-view observations. Modern inspection planners extend CPP to sensing-driven tasks by jointly selecting viewpoints and motion plans under geometric and robotic constraints faigl2011sensor . Aerial inspection planners generate candidates through iterative or adaptive sampling to reconstruct complex structures bircher2015structural,almadhoun2018coverage , while recent works incorporate sensing constraints such as field-of-view limits, incidence angle, and overlap heuristics lee2022ceo,liang2025optimized . Reconstruction-oriented planners further improve imaging quality through continuous trajectory optimization or topology-aware planning zhang2021continuous,shang2023topology . Several systems have been proposed that couple viewpoint generation with trajectory optimization lu2023tmstc,tripicchio2023smooth,mitra2025online . While such integrated approaches consider both sensing and motion objectives, our work focuses specifically on viewpoint selection, allowing per-surface-region coverage requirements to be examined independently of trajectory optimization. Sequential redundancy reduction has been used in viewpoint planning, where candidate viewpoints are discarded if their visibility regions overlap substantially with previously selected views bircher2015structural,almadhoun2018coverage . However, overlap-based pruning does not, by itself, enforce a prescribed number of observations for each surface region, and its outcome can depend on viewpoint ordering and overlap thresholds. Recent work has formulated viewpoint planning as a combinatorial set-cover problem. Adaptive spatial subdivision combined with ILP optimization has been used to obtain minimum-cardinality viewpoint sets with complete feature coverage spensieri2025unified,ramesh2024approximate . Related multi-cover formulations have also been studied in geometric coverage problems, demonstrating the use of explicit redundancy constraints in combinatorial optimization. These formulations establish mathematical approaches to coverage selection. Our work builds on this perspective by incorporating GSD-constrained candidate generation, coverage-driven viewpoint augmentation, and per-surface-region multi-cover requirements. Voxel representations are widely used to simplify visibility reasoning in complex environments. Voxelized planners generate viewpoints around clustered surface regions prior to trajectory optimization hagmanns2024path , and enriched voxel maps support planning in dynamic environments golpour20254d . Existing work has addressed geometric coverage, sensing-constrained viewpoint generation, and combinatorial viewpoint optimization through different formulations. Building on these approaches, this work considers their integration for GSD-constrained -coverage over voxelized surfaces. Specifically, we combine sensing-aware candidate generation, targeted augmentation of undercovered surface regions, and set multi-cover optimization to select compact viewpoint sets satisfying prescribed coverage requirements when feasible. title: GRAFT: Geometry-Aware Residual Adaptation for Foundation Trackers
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures, 3 tables. Project page: https://graft-humanoid.github.io/
summary: Humanoid behavior foundation models (BFMs) provide reusable whole-body motion priors: given a kinematic reference, they generate coordinated joint commands for motion replay, teleoperation, and VLA control. However, trained primarily on flat-ground motion, BFMs lack an explicit mechanism to adapt foot placement, swing clearance, and contact timing to local terrain. Many terrain-aware BFM approaches address this limitation by retraining or fine-tuning the tracker together with perception, incurring substantial data and computation costs while coupling ordinary tracking to the perception pathway. To bridge this gap, we propose GRAFT, a geometry-aware residual adaptation framework for frozen behavior trackers. GRAFT preserves the BFM parameters and motion-reference interface, while a lightweight adapter adds terrain-conditioned corrections only to lower-body execution targets. The adapter is trained with task and foot-geometry rewards, regularized to suppress unnecessary corrections on flat ground, and distilled from privileged terrain observations to onboard depth. Because the frozen BFM already provides whole-body reference tracking and nominal locomotion, GRAFT reduces terrain learning to a focused execution-adaptation problem. We instantiate the framework on four frozen trackers and evaluate stairs, gaps, and platforms in simulation. We further validate it through real-world deployment on a Unitree G1, where the adapted SONIC tracker traverses terrain with onboard depth and unmodified references.

Humanoid behavior foundation models (BFMs) provide reusable whole-body motion priors: given a kinematic reference, they generate coordinated joint commands for motion replay, teleoperation, and VLA control. However, trained primarily on flat-ground motion, BFMs lack an explicit mechanism to adapt foot placement, swing clearance, and contact timing to local terrain. Many terrain-aware BFM approaches address this limitation by retraining or fine-tuning the tracker together with perception, incurring substantial data and computation costs while coupling ordinary tracking to the perception pathway. To bridge this gap, we propose GRAFT, a geometry-aware residual adaptation framework for frozen behavior trackers. GRAFT preserves the BFM parameters and motion-reference interface, while a lightweight adapter adds terrain-conditioned corrections only to lower-body execution targets. The adapter is trained with task and foot-geometry rewards, regularized to suppress unnecessary corrections on flat ground, and distilled from privileged terrain observations to onboard depth. Because the frozen BFM already provides whole-body reference tracking and nominal locomotion, GRAFT reduces terrain learning to a focused execution-adaptation problem. We instantiate the framework on four frozen trackers and evaluate stairs, gaps, and platforms in simulation. We further validate it through real-world deployment on a Unitree G1, where the adapted SONIC tracker traverses terrain with onboard depth and unmodified references. Introduction A behavior foundation model (BFM) learns a single whole-body tracking policy from a large corpus of human motion: given a kinematic reference, it outputs joint commands~ sonic,humanoidgpt,holomotion . Motion references form its sole upstream command interface. The same BFM can therefore be driven by a recorded clip, an online teleoperator, or a high-level policy such as a vision-language-action (VLA) model, without retraining for each source. This shared reference interface is what lets one released tracker serve several upstream command sources. These corpora, however, are recorded almost entirely on flat, empty ground, and the environment enters neither the policy's observation nor its reward. A BFM therefore learns how to approximate a reference kinematically, not how to place its feet on the surface it is actually crossing. Changing the reference does not supply what is missing. Given a clip of a person climbing stairs, the policy reproduces the motion in the air but does not actually climb the stairs, because the foot placement, swing clearance and contact timing the steps require were never part of what it was trained to produce. Current approaches give BFMs scene-interaction ability by pairing motion with reconstructed scene geometry and retraining~ gigabrain , or by fine-tuning a pretrained model together with a terrain encoder~ grail,pbfm . These approaches are effective, but they change the deployed tracker and couple ordinary tracking to the terrain-perception pathway. Constructing terrain-paired motion data requires annotation and processing at scale, together with the compute to retrain on it. Fine-tuning a behavior prior on a narrow new task can also degrade the reusable prior, which motivates residual adaptation on a frozen backbone elsewhere~ mosaic . To address this problem, we propose GRAFT. The frozen BFM processes the unmodified reference, while a separately trained adapter adds geometry-conditioned corrections to the lower-body execution targets; the upper-body targets remain those of the frozen tracker, since they are what a teleoperator or a VLA is commanding. A deployment gate controls whether the correction is applied at all. The key idea is to separate reusable whole-body motion generation from terrain execution adaptation. The BFM retains responsibility for reference tracking, nominal locomotion, and whole-body coordination; the adapter learns only the terrain-dependent deviation from this nominal execution. We train it with foot-clearance and placement penalties and suppress its output on flat ground, then distill a teacher trained under privileged terrain observations into a student that reads onboard depth. This decomposition turns terrain adaptation into a focused execution problem without rewriting the upstream reference or modifying the released tracker. Our contributions are: We introduce GRAFT, a terrain-adaptation framework that adds geometry-conditioned lower-body corrections to a frozen behavior tracker while preserving its parameters and its motion-reference interface, with a gate that can be switched off at deployment; mid-run disabling and re-enabling are verified in simulation. We propose GRAFT as a general framework for adapting frozen behavior foundation trackers to terrain interaction. We instantiate the framework on four distinct trackers, training a separate adapter for each, and show that the same residual structure and reward family acquire terrain traversal while keeping flat-ground corrections small. We validate GRAFT through real-world deployment on a Unitree G1. The SONIC adapter is distilled from privileged terrain observations to onboard depth, and the resulting tracker traverses terrain with unmodified references; a separate composite-course simulation verifies mid-run residual disabling and re-enabling. Related Work sec:rw Whole-body motion tracking and behavior foundation models Whole-body motion tracking has expanded from single-clip imitation to learning from large, heterogeneous motion corpora~ gmt . Behavior foundation models encode that motion diversity in a reusable prior. The bases we adapt in this work span the two dominant forms this takes. SONIC exposes a latent command interface to upstream modules and is trained to track references supplied at run time, so a planner, a teleoperator or a VLA can drive the same controller~ sonic . Humanoid-GPT instead distills a generalist tracker for zero-shot use on unseen motion, without a task-specific latent~ humanoidgpt . HoloMotion~ holomotion and further work on prompting and scaling these priors~ bfmzero,scalingbfm follow the same interface. Other approaches reach hardware-ready tracking through minimal reward formulations~ beyondmimic , real-time retargeting for teleoperation~ twist , and alternative representations of motion priors~ motionpriors . Accepting a reference from any upstream source is what makes these models reusable as an interface rather than as a skill. Their training distribution, however, is free-space motion on flat ground in empty scenes~ gigabrain : the policy observes proprioception and a reference window, and the environment enters neither the observation nor the reward. However far the corpus is scaled, foot placement and contact behavior on terrain do not emerge from it. Terrain-aware whole-body control Terrain geometry was addressed earlier along the perceptive-locomotion line: elevation-map and depth-based policies traverse stairs, gaps and parkour terrain~ dpl,perceptiveloco,php,extremeparkour , with separate lines on surefooted placement~ ssr , on robustness when exteroception degrades~ rpl , and on sparse footholds~ beamdojo ; related parkour controllers exist on quadrupeds~ puma . Their command channel, however, is a velocity direction or a navigation goal, which specifies where the base should go rather than what the whole body should do~ gigabrain . Three routes bring terrain into a reference-driven BFM. GigaBrain-WBC recovers the geometry each motion must have been performed on and trains a world-model tracker on the resulting terrain-paired corpus. Terrain-interactive motion becomes trackable, but the deployed policy reads only proprioception, the previous action and a latent command~ gigabrain . GRAIL specializes a pretrained BFM for two task families, and its terrain-aware branch fine-tunes the controller together with a height-map encoder~ grail . Perceptive BFM is the closest to our setting: it keeps the raw kinematic reference as the deployment command and injects terrain features from a torso-depth height grid through an identity-initialized residual path. The tracking prior is fine-tuned with PPO at the same time, the residual acts on the whole-body actor mean, terrain supervision needs references rewritten to conform to the terrain, and the identity gate is a training initialization rather than a deployment switch~ pbfm . These three routes each pay a price in how perception and tracking are coupled. The deployed policy of GigaBrain-WBC consumes no exteroception, so its tracking does not depend on perception, at the cost of never measuring the geometry in front of it. GRAIL and Perceptive BFM bring perception in, but the terrain skill and the base weights sit in the same parameters, so a degradation in perception costs more than terrain traversal. These routes motivate a complementary question: how much terrain capability can be obtained without modifying the foundation tracker or adding a task-specific perception-and-control architecture? GRAFT studies this adaptation-side trade-off. Its central claim is that a frozen whole-body prior can reduce the task-specific structure required for terrain adaptation, while preserving the upstream reference interface. Residual and parameter-efficient adaptation of a frozen policy Learning a residual correction on top of a fixed policy has developed as a separate line. ResMimic conditions whole-body corrections on object and contact state for loco-manipulation~ resmimic , MOSAIC uses a residual adapter to close an interface gap, explicitly motivated by avoiding the forgetting that continual fine-tuning causes~ mosaic , and a cerebellum-inspired controller supplies inference-time corrections for recovery from actuator and dynamics faults~ cerebellar . In all of them the frozen policy remains runnable once the residual is taken away, and ResMimic evaluates that base-only mode as a baseline. GRAFT differs in what conditions the correction and in what it writes: local terrain geometry rather than object, interface or fault state, and the lower body rather than the whole body. We additionally evaluate disabling and re-enabling the adapter within a single continuous simulation run, which none of them reports. Related approaches project commands onto a learned competence manifold~ cmp , modify the weights themselves~ lorapolicy,safelora , adapt a frozen backbone through learned masks~ maskadapt , or absorb dynamics shifts on a fixed controller~ residualctrl . Table~ tab:capability places GRAFT against these lines: it keeps the frozen-base, additive-residual structure, conditions it on terrain geometry, and treats plug-and-play as a deployment property. Method sec:method GRAFT separates whole-body motion generation from terrain execution adaptation. The frozen BFM provides a reusable motion prior, including reference tracking, nominal locomotion, and whole-body coordination. A lightweight residual policy then learns the terrain-dependent deviation from this nominal execution. At each control step the frozen BFM maps the kinematic reference and proprioception to nominal whole-body joint-position targets . A residual policy runs at the same control rate and produces corrections in the same units, and the combined targets are executed by a joint-level PD controller, where the mask confines the correction to the lower-body joints. The output of carries a fixed per-joint scale and is expressed in the same units as , so is the correction actually added. Channels outside the mask are identical to the base output, and zeroing the residual makes the executed target equal 's output at every step. Only is trained; stays frozen. The trainable problem is therefore focused on terrain-dependent execution rather than relearning the nominal gait or whole-body reference-following behavior. The adapter observes propriocept

title: A generalist policy for muscle-driven control across individual musculoskeletal models
comment: 17 pages, 7 figures. Project website: https://woodater-thu.github.io/MyoAcross/ Bozhao Wang and Yinglei Zhu contributed equally to this work
summary: Differences in musculoskeletal morphology challenge policy reuse across individual models. Here we present MyoAcross, a framework that combines individual musculoskeletal model construction, morphology-conditioned policy learning and virtual model augmentation to enable muscle-driven reference-motion tracking without individual fine-tuning. Across 31 held-out individual models, MyoAcross achieves 99.24% completion and reduces tracking error by 22.60% relative to an unconditioned multilayer perceptron. Policy reuse extends to models of 22 held-out individuals constructed from single-image shape estimates, measured height and body mass, and, with asymmetry augmentation, to models with unilateral lower-limb shortening. Comparisons with measurements from 120 additional individuals show agreement in vertical ground reaction force waveforms and channel-dependent agreement between simulated muscle activations and electromyography. These results establish a common control framework for comparative simulations of movement across individual musculoskeletal models.
full_text: Differences in musculoskeletal morphology challenge policy reuse across individual models. Here we present MyoAcross, a framework that combines individual musculoskeletal model construction, morphology-conditioned policy learning and virtual model augmentation to enable muscle-driven reference- motion tracking without individual fine-tuning. Across 31 held-out individual models, MyoAcross achieves 99.24 completion and reduces tracking error by 22.60 relative to an unconditioned multilayer perceptron. Policy reuse extends to models of 22 held-out individuals constructed from single-image shape estimates, measured height and body mass, and, with asymmetry augmentation, to models with unilateral lower-limb shortening. Comparisons with measurements from 120 additional individuals show agreement in vertical ground reaction force waveforms and channel-dependent agreement between simulated muscle activations and electromyography. These results establish a common control framework for comparative simulations of movement across individual musculoskeletal models. Project website: . Introduction sec:introduction Differences in body dimensions and mass alter the mechanical demands of movement~ zajac1989muscle . Musculoskeletal simulations link muscle forces to whole-body dynamics, providing a framework for examining how these differences affect movement. Comparing movement across individual musculoskeletal models requires controllers that accommodate the dynamics of each model. A central challenge is whether one muscle-driven policy can track reference motions across these models without individual fine-tuning. Such a policy would provide a common control strategy for comparative simulations across individuals. Advances in individual model construction and muscle-driven control provide complementary foundations for this capability. Marker-based and image-based workflows adapt musculoskeletal geometry to individual measurements~ opensimScaleTool,werling2023addbiomechanics,valente2017nmsbuilder . The Skinned Multi-Person Linear (SMPL) body model~ loper2015smpl represents individual body shape, while the anatomically informed parametric skin-and-skeleton model (SKEL)~ keller2023skel links body shape to skeletal geometry. Together, these models provide skeletal measurements for constructing individual musculoskeletal models. This route also raises the question of whether shape estimated from a single image, together with measured height and body mass, can support policy reuse. In parallel, reinforcement learning has enabled full-body muscle-driven tracking of diverse reference motions~ lee2019scalable,feng2023musclevae,wei2026msemulator,li2026musclemimic . Differences in skeletal proportions, muscle geometry and mass change the dynamics that these controllers encounter. Whether a policy trained on a generic template can accommodate this variation is therefore a key question for transfer to individual models. Morphology-conditioned control offers a way to accommodate differences between models within a single policy. Studies of robot and human character control have demonstrated policies that operate across different bodies~ huang2020shared,gupta2022metamorph,bohlinger2024urma,doshi2025crossformer,won2019bodyshape,luo2022uhc . In muscle-driven systems, related advances include anatomy-conditioned gait generation, morphology-adaptive locomotion and control across heterogeneous models~ park2022gaitnet,kim2025freemusco,an2025arnold . Building on these advances, we ask whether morphology conditioning supports muscle-driven tracking of time-resolved reference motions across individual musculoskeletal models, including those of individuals excluded from training. We further examine how variation among training models contributes to this capability. Unilateral lower-limb shortening provides a clinically motivated test of policy reuse under structural variation. Clinical studies of hemiplegic cerebral palsy report length differences between affected and unaffected lower limbs~ riad2010discrepancy,kim2022discrepancy , motivating simulated models with corresponding geometric changes. Retaining the original reference motions tests whether the policy can sustain prescribed movements across these altered models. This setting also allows us to examine whether greater asymmetry in the training models improves transfer. A complementary question concerns sensitivity to inaccuracies in the morphology features and reference-motion inputs supplied to the policy. Perturbing these inputs separately and jointly, while keeping the physical model fixed, distinguishes input sensitivity from the effects of structural variation. Here we introduce MyoAcross, a framework that combines individual musculoskeletal model construction with generalist muscle-driven policy learning. Regional scaling fits skeletal proportions to individual measurements, while mass calibration and geometry-based rules update inertial and musculotendon properties within a common musculoskeletal topology. Model-derived morphology features condition the policy, and virtual model augmentation exposes it to additional variation in model dynamics. We evaluate policy reuse across held-out individual models and assess the biomechanical plausibility of simulated walking by comparing vertical ground reaction forces and muscle activations with measurements from the corresponding Gait120 subjects. Controlled comparisons examine the contributions of training across models, morphology conditioning and virtual model augmentation. Further tests assess transfer under unilateral lower-limb shortening and sensitivity to morphology feature and reference-motion input errors. Finally, we examine whether single-image shape estimates, together with measured height and body mass, support individual model construction and reuse of the pretrained policy. Results sec:results We evaluated policy reuse across held-out individual models and the contributions of morphology conditioning and virtual model augmentation. We assessed simulated walking through comparisons with measured vertical ground reaction forces and electromyography. Further experiments assessed transfer to asymmetric and image-derived models, together with sensitivity to morphology feature and reference-motion input errors. Individual musculoskeletal models support a common policy interface MyoAcross combines individual model construction with morphology-conditioned muscle control through a common policy interface (Fig.~ fig:framework ). We used SKEL to derive 17 target skeletal measurements from SMPL body shape. Skeletal-guided regional scaling fitted 13 regional scale factors of the MyoFullBody template to these targets, while mass calibration matched total mass to each individual's recorded body mass. The resulting individual models differed in geometry and associated physical parameters but retained a common topology and a 416-dimensional muscle excitation space. Across 141 individual models, regional scaling achieved a mean absolute skeletal measurement fitting error of 2.51\,mm (Fig.~ fig:framework c). Errors were averaged over 17 measurements within each model and then across models. Fitting a single global scale factor to the same targets yielded an error of 13.50\,mm, while the unchanged MyoFullBody template had an error of 24.97\,mm. Regional scaling therefore reduced fitting error by 81.38 and 89.94 , respectively, capturing individual skeletal proportions more accurately than either comparator. Retargeting 64 source motions from 8 locomotion categories to the 141 individual models produced 9024 reference motions (Fig.~ fig:framework a,b). Each model supplied its own 17 skeletal measurements and total mass as morphology features. A morphology encoder mapped these features to a morphology representation that conditioned the actor and critic through feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM). The actor used the policy observations and morphology conditioning to generate muscle excitations. Virtual model augmentation and multi-model simulations exposed the policy to variation in model dynamics during training (Fig.~ fig:framework d). Together, the reference motions and model-derived morphology features supported policy training across individual models through a common interface. A generalist policy enables reuse across held-out individual models We compared 4 policies to assess the contributions of multi-model training and morphology conditioning to policy reuse (Fig.~ fig:generalization a). The template-trained multilayer perceptron (MLP) used the MyoFullBody template and received no morphology features. The remaining policies were an MLP trained across individual models without morphology input (unconditioned MLP), the encoded morphology feature concatenation policy (Concat), and the FiLM-conditioned MyoAcross policy. Each policy was evaluated on 31 held-out individual models with 64 reference motions per model, yielding 1984 trials without individual fine-tuning. Each model used its corresponding reference motions, while policy parameters and normalization statistics remained fixed. The 3 multi-model policies used the same training model bank, reference motions and interaction budget, and were evaluated at 15,000 training iterations. The template-trained MLP completed 8.32 of reference motions. Completion reached 98.24 for the unconditioned MLP, 97.53 for Concat and 99.24 for MyoAcross (Fig.~ fig:generalization b). MyoAcross increased completion by 1.01 percentage points relative to the unconditioned MLP (95 confidence interval, 0.30--1.86 percentage points). Reference coverage measured the fraction of each motion executed, including trials that terminated early. It reached 45.53 for the template-trained MLP, compared with 99.42 , 99.20 and 99.76 for the unconditioned MLP, Concat and MyoAcross, respectively. With MyoAcross, 12 of the 15 incomplete trials occurred in a single individual model, which achieved 81.25 completion. These comparisons support training across model variation for policy transfer to held-out individuals, with morphology conditioning through FiLM providing a further improvement in completion. MyoAcross further improved tracking accuracy among the 3 multi-model policies, which all achieved high completion and reference coverage. Tracking error was 53.70\,mm for MyoAcross, compared with 69.39\,mm for the unconditioned MLP and 59.88\,mm for Concat (Fig.~ fig:generalization b). These differences corresponded to relative error reductions of 22.60 and 10.33 , respectively. Errors were computed over executed frames, including incomplete trials, and interpreted alongside completion and reference coverage. MyoAcross achieved lower tracking error than both the unconditioned MLP and Concat for each of the 31 held-out individual models (Fig.~ fig:generalization c). Across motion categories, it outperformed the unconditioned MLP in all 8 categories and Concat in 6, with mean tracking errors ranging from 43.23 to 75.55\,mm (Fig.~ fig:generalization d). The largest reductions relative to Concat occurred in clockwise circling (51.81 versus 70.75\,mm) and counterclockwise circling (48.89 versus 69.37\,mm). Concat achieved lower tracking error in slow walking (48.84 versus 50.52\,mm) and right turns (70.90 versus 75.55\,mm). The accuracy gains thus extended across all held-out individuals and most motion categories, supporting policy reuse across individual musculoskeletal models. title: SO-101 Bench: Accessible Spatial Manipulation
summary: Low-cost arms such as the SO-101 have become the most common entry point to robot learning, yet no released policy performs spatially constrained, language-conditioned tasks on them out of the box, and existing SO-101 benchmarks run only on physical hardware with simple tasks and few held-out objects. We introduce SO-101 Bench, a simulated benchmark for language-conditioned spatial manipulation built on an Isaac Lab digital twin of a real SO-101 setup. It has four tasks scored as five families, 138 objects in seen, unseen-instance and unseen-class splits, 916 evaluation episodes with subsets for held-out appearances, rotate-to-fit planning and occlusion memory, and 3,629 simulated demonstrations on which every learned policy is fine-tuned under an equal compute budget. The twin ranks policies as the real robot does: five policies trained without real data, four VLAs and an LLM agent, keep their exact ranking when the same weights run on the physical arm in an unseen environment with unseen objects (Spearman rho = 1.00, MMRV = 0.000), although simulation overestimates success. Across nine VLAs and world-action models, the best learned policies score near 61%, with spatial placement, unseen object classes and rotate-to-fit planning remaining open. An LLM agent that writes code and hands grasping to a learned policy scores 83.2%, and an ablation shows that this lead comes from the choice of harness and the choice of language model.

Introduction sec:intro Low-cost arms have become the most common entry point to robot learning. The open-source SO-101~ hf2026so101,therobotstudio2024soarm100 is a 3D-printed arm driven by six serial-bus servos; a follower arm costs about \ 4,900 for one ALOHA arm~ kawaharazuka2026mevion . LeRobot~ cadene2026lerobot supports it from teleoperation to deployment, and SO-family arms produce most of the community robot datasets on the Hugging Face Hub. Open models now train on these data: SmolVLA was pretrained on 481 community datasets~ shukor2025smolvla , and MolmoAct2 has a variant post-trained on 38k curated SO-100/101 episodes~ fang2026molmoact2 . These models, however, are starting points for fine-tuning on a user's own demonstrations: MolmoAct2-SO100/101 demonstrates out-of-the-box performance on basic tasks, and to our knowledge no released policy performs spatially constrained, language-conditioned tasks on an SO-101 out of the box in a new environment with new objects. Evaluation, too, has not kept pace: the SO-101 benchmarks released this year run only on physical hardware~ yu2026so101failure,huang2026vlareplica,selvaraj2026armnetbench,tiensmith2026spabench . Their tasks include insertion, pouring, wiping and spatial grounding; Spa-Bench tests relational placement, referential descriptions, ordinal position and counting, with familiar constituents in its primary evaluation and a separate novel-object pilot~ tiensmith2026spabench . They are also costly: real-robot studies typically afford tens of rollouts per condition~ arkhangelskiy2026phail , and results depend on the particular build (servo offsets differ between arms~ huang2026vlareplica ; one arm farm reports a misaligned camera and objects that wore down during evaluation~ selvaraj2026armnetbench ). Simulation removes these costs, but a simulated benchmark is useful only if its rankings hold on hardware. Widely used suites target other embodiments~ liu2023libero,nasiriany2026robocasa365,chen2025robotwin2 , the one simulated SO-101 task set we know of contains eight language-free cube and can tasks~ almuzairee2026squint , and the most cited suite is saturated: a 0.54M-parameter policy reaches 95.1 on LIBERO~ sendai2026minerva , where clean averages for three protocol-faithful vision-language-action model (VLA) and world-action model (WAM) evaluations span only 1.36 points~ wang2026industrialvlabench . Real2sim evaluation~ li2024simpler,jain2025polaris,sedlacek2025realm,ranawaka2026simfoundry shows that a carefully built digital twin can predict real-world rankings, but the prediction is specific to the simulator, policies and setup on which it was validated: in a five-policy study spanning 1,115 real rollouts across three simulators, SIMPLER showed weak ranking agreement with the real robot~ wang2026practical . These studies also mostly run in one direction, placing policies trained on real data inside a twin. As policies are increasingly trained on simulated data alone~ deshpande2026molmobot,yu2026oasis , a benchmark should also show that its ranking survives when the same sim-trained weights run on a real robot. Finally, it should measure what aggregate success hides: a policy can complete a task without understanding it: on LIBERO, a probe that replaces instruction text with a task-ID embedding nearly matches the best published results~ jiang2026benchmarking , and on a real SO-101, VLAs that manipulate reliably can fail to adapt to OOD spatial relations~ tiensmith2026spabench . We introduce SO-101 Bench, a simulated benchmark for language-conditioned spatial manipulation with a single SO-101 arm, built so that its rankings carry over to the real robot (Fig.~ fig:teaser ). Its core is an Isaac Lab~ mittal2025isaaclab digital twin of a real SO-101 setup with 138 household objects in three generalization splits: seen (in the training dataset), unseen object of a seen class, and unseen class, with 37 unseen-class objects kept private. Four tasks (place every object in a bin; place an object next to another; place it between two others; move it in a direction until it reaches the boundary object) are scored automatically from simulator state. They require the policy to pick out the named object among same-class distractors, grasp unfamiliar geometry and place it under spatial constraints. The primary evaluation has 916 feasibility-checked episodes over 15 task-family split cells, with subsets for held-out appearances (ROBUST), rotating an object to fit a tight space (PLAN) and remembering occluded objects (MEM). Every learned policy is fine-tuned on the same 3,629 simulated teleoperated demonstrations of seen objects under an equal 36\,h x 4 x A100 compute budget. Two studies test whether the twin can stand in for the real robot. Independently trained real-only and sim-only GR00T~N1.6 policies find the same conditions hard (Pearson across the 15 cells) and fail in the same ways (Sec.~ sec:correspondence ). Five policies that never saw real data from our setup, four VLAs and an LLM agent, then run with identical weights in the twin and on the physical SO-101 in an environment unseen in training, with objects from all three splits; SO-101 Bench policies work out of the box in unseen real environments with unseen objects. Simulation ranks them exactly as the real robot does (Spearman , MMRV , 95 CI ), although it overestimates every policy's success by 9 to 31 percentage points (Sec.~ sec:sim2real ). On the full leaderboard of nine VLAs and WAMs, the best learned policies, InternW0- ~ miao2026internw0 and Galaxea 0.5~ liu2026g05 , are statistically tied near 61; spatial placement and unseen classes are where they fail, and none exceeds 17 on PLAN. The strongest entry is an LLM agent: GPT-6.1 Sol~ openai2026sol writing code in the PyRUA-Lean harness~ si2026pyrua and handing grasps to Galaxea 0.5 scores 83.2 and solves 75 of PLAN. Its lead comes largely from the harness. On 60 paired episodes, Sol succeeds on 35 (21/60) with direct tool calls, 67 (40/60) with PyRUA-Lean and 85 (51/60) with the Galaxea 0.5 hand-off, against 53 (32/60) for Galaxea 0.5 alone, and the lead holds on the real robot, 64 (29/45) against 53 (24/45). Our contributions are: SO-101 Bench, a digital-twin benchmark for language-conditioned spatial manipulation on a low-cost arm, with instance- and class-level object splits, ROBUST, PLAN and MEM subsets and automatic scoring, released with the so101 bench sim (3,629 simulated episodes) and so101 bench real ( 4,400 real episodes) datasets. Evidence that the twin ranks policies as the real robot does: condition- and failure-level correspondence between independently trained real-only and sim-only policies, and an exact sim2real ranking of five policies, including an LLM agent, run with identical weights and no real data from our setup; these policies perform language-conditioned tasks out of the box in an unseen real environment with unseen objects. A leaderboard of nine VLAs and WAMs and two LLM agents, with every learned policy fine-tuned on the same data and compute, showing that spatial placement, unseen object classes and rotate-to-fit planning remain open. Harness and model ablations showing that, in our setting, a code-as-policy harness that hands grasping to a learned policy outperforms either on their own; Direct action generation by the agent proves expensive and ineffective, and 6.1 Sol compares favorably to other agents. Related Work sec:related Low-cost hardware and SO-101 benchmarks. Cheap hardware has repeatedly widened who can do robot learning. ALOHA showed that a low-cost bimanual rig can learn fine manipulation~ zhao2023aloha , and 2026 platforms push prices further, from a \ 1,100 kit reproduced across sites~ huang2026vlareplica , ArmnetBench scores 2,518 rollouts of seven policies on an arm farm~ selvaraj2026armnetbench , and Spa-Bench probes recombinations of familiar objects, spatial concepts and actions in its primary evaluation, with a separate novel-object pilot~ tiensmith2026spabench . All four use real robot demonstrations for task-specific adaptation and evaluate on physical hardware. In simulation, the SO-101 Task Set contains eight language-free tasks for visual reinforcement learning with sim2real transfer~ almuzairee2026squint , and LeIsaac provides SO-101 teleoperation and data-collection tooling in Isaac Lab~ lightwheel2025leisaac . To our knowledge, SO-101 Bench is the first language-conditioned SO-101 benchmark with held-out object splits whose simulated policy ranking is validated on the real arm. It also represents one of, if not the most, challenging task suites handled by an SO-101 up to this point. Real2sim evaluation and sim2real transfer. Whether simulated evaluation predicts real performance was studied early for navigation~ kadian2020sim2real ; for manipulation, SIMPLER~ li2024simpler showed that an aligned simulator can rank real-world policies and introduced the MMRV metric. Twins built from scans, neural reconstructions or generated assets now report strong score or ranking agreement within their validated settings~ jain2025polaris,sedlacek2025realm,yang2026robolab,ruan2026x2real,xiao2026h2rbench,wang2026reveal ; SimFoundry reaches Pearson 0.911 and MMRV 0.018 over five policy architectures~ ranawaka2026simfoundry . Two 2026 results temper this. Validity does not carry across setups: re-tested against new real rollouts, SIMPLER's agreement with the real-robot ranking is weak~ wang2026practical . Reconstruction quality also matters: an authored object-and-scene pipeline achieved sim--real correlation of 0.90 versus 0.51 for a default reconstruction in a ten-cell study~ verma2026measuring , consistent with our tuning of each reconstructed object against its physical counterpart (Appendix~ app:objects ). Learned world models are an alternative evaluator~ geminirobotics2025veo , but released models often predict success on verified failures~ xu2026worldmodelsdream . In parallel, policies trained only on simulated data now transfer to real robots: MolmoB0T reaches 79.2 on real pick-and-place without real demonstrations~ deshpande2026molmobot , OASIS pairs image-to-3D assets with teleoperation inside simulation~ yu2026oasis , and LEGS and Splat2Act fine-tune pretrained VLAs using only synthetic robot demonstrations~ kim2026legs,ye2026splat2act . title: RoboSTD: Zero-Shot Single-to-Dual Transfer via Sagittal Mirroring for Bimanual Learning
summary: Bimanual robot manipulation plays an important role in real-world robotic applications, but the high cost of collecting bimanual demonstrations limits the scalable development of bimanual policy learning. Meanwhile, existing single-arm manipulation data are difficult to directly transfer to bimanual systems due to the Single-to-Dual gap in action spaces, coordination requirements, and arm-side spatial preference. To address this issue, we propose RoboSTD, a zero-shot Single-to-Dual data construction method for bimanual robot learning. RoboSTD first applies sagittal-plane mirroring to observations, proprioception, and actions to construct executable contralateral pseudo-demonstrations. It then uses an LLM to generate structured spatio-temporal coordination constraints that guide the reconstruction of pseudo-bimanual supervision across workspace regions and task stages. We evaluate RoboSTD on the AgileX ALOHA platform in both RoboTwin simulation and real-world settings. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of RoboSTD for bimanual policy learning. Without requiring additional bimanual demonstrations, RoboSTD increases the average number of collected cups to 2.11x that of the single-arm baseline in the cup collection task. Project page: Introduction Bimanual robot manipulation enables complex tasks that are difficult to efficiently perform with single-arm systems through coordinated use of two arms, making it important for real-world robotic applications~ zhao2023aloha,fu2024mobilealoha . However, compared with single-arm learning, bimanual policy learning faces a more severe data bottleneck. Collecting high-quality bimanual demonstrations requires not only recording the trajectories of both arms, but also maintaining spatial relationships, execution timing, and task-role coordination, making data acquisition substantially more complex and expensive. Previous studies have identified demonstration collection cost and teleoperation burden as major bottlenecks for scalable robot learning ~ luo2024hajl,mandlekar2023mimicgen,jiang2024dexmimicgen . Therefore, reducing the dependence on real bimanual demonstrations is critical for scalable bimanual robot learning. Meanwhile, the amount of single-arm manipulation data accumulated by the robot learning community represents a valuable resource for robot learning. However, how to reuse such single-arm data for bimanual learning remains underexplored. This gives rise to a Single-to-Dual gap, involving differences in action spaces, coordination requirements, and spatial preferences across arm sides. An overview of this challenge and our approach is shown in Fig.~ fig:robostd_overview . To investigate this phenomenon, we randomly sample 10,000 trajectories from Open X-Embodiment~ oneill2023openx and compute the spatial locations of end-effector events. As shown in Fig.~ fig:introduction (a), only 35.7 of these events occur in the left workspace, whereas 64.3 occur in the right workspace, corresponding to a 28.6 percentage-point spatial imbalance. We further evaluate the pretrained ~ black2024pi0 and the non-pretrained ACT~ zhao2023aloha on 10 tasks in RoboTwin 2.0~ chen2025robotwin2 . As shown in Fig.~ fig:introduction (b), achieves average success rates of 66.3 and 75.9 on left- and right-arm tasks, respectively, corresponding to a Bias Gap of 9.6 percentage points. In contrast, ACT achieves 50.0 and 50.4 , with a Bias Gap of only 0.4 percentage points. The right-side preference observed in both the data distribution and the pretrained policy suggests that upstream spatial imbalance may be reflected in arm-side performance, potentially hindering balanced Single-to-Dual transfer. To address this gap, we propose RoboSTD, a zero-shot Single-to-Dual data construction method for bimanual robot learning. Here, zero-shot denotes requiring no additional task-specific bimanual demonstrations, rather than zero-shot policy inference. RoboSTD consists of two stages. First, sagittal-plane mirroring transforms observations, proprioception, and actions ~ ordonez2024morphological,zhuang2025mirrorduo to construct executable contralateral pseudo-demonstrations. Second, LLM-guided spatio-temporal reconstruction infers arm assignment, precedence, and conflict constraints from context to compose original and mirrored skills into pseudo-bimanual supervision. We evaluate RoboSTD using the AgileX ALOHA platform in both the RoboTwin 2.0 simulation environment~ chen2025robotwin2 and real-world settings. In the simulation effectiveness experiments over 10 RoboTwin tasks, policies trained with 100 native bimanual demonstrations per task achieve an average success rate of 67.6 , while those trained with RoboSTD-generated supervision from only 50 single-arm demonstrations per task achieve 66.5 . The small 1.1 percentage-point gap shows that RoboSTD can construct effective bimanual supervision from fewer single-arm demonstrations. In the spatial generalization task, RoboSTD extends skills originally limited to a unilateral workspace to the full bimanual workspace, achieving a increase in the average number of collected cups over the single-arm baseline. In the long-horizon sandwich-making task, RoboSTD further improves the task success rate and average completion, demonstrating stronger temporal coordination. These results demonstrate that sagittal-plane mirroring and LLM-guided spatio-temporal reconstruction can effectively extend single-arm demonstrations into useful bimanual supervision. The main contributions are summarized as follows: We identify and analyze arm-side spatial preferences in robot data and pretrained policies, and reveal their potential impact on balanced bimanual learning. We propose RoboSTD, a zero-shot Single-to-Dual data construction method that converts existing single-arm demonstrations into bimanual supervision. We demonstrate RoboSTD's effectiveness for Single-to-Dual transfer, improving workspace coverage and long-horizon coordination in real-world bimanual tasks. Related Work Unimanual and Bimanual Robot Datasets. Large-scale robot datasets have become an important foundation for learning generalizable manipulation policies. Open X-Embodiment~ oneill2023openx aggregates large-scale cross-embodiment robot data, while DROID~ khazatsky2024droid and BridgeData~ walke2023bridgedata provide diverse real-world manipulation data across tasks and environments. However, most existing large-scale resources are dominated by unimanual interaction. For bimanual manipulation, ALOHA~ zhao2023aloha provides a low-cost dual-arm teleoperation platform for collecting coordinated demonstrations, while Mobile ALOHA~ fu2024mobilealoha extends data collection to mobile bimanual manipulation. RoboCOIN~ wu2025robocoin further provides real-world bimanual manipulation data for learning and evaluating coordinated policies. In simulation, RoboTwin 2.0~ chen2025robotwin2 provides scalable bimanual task environments and data-generation pipelines. Despite these efforts, large-scale, high-quality real-world bimanual data remain substantially more difficult and expensive to acquire than unimanual data. Unimanual and Bimanual Policy Learning. Recent imitation-learning methods have substantially improved robot manipulation through sequence modeling~ zhao2023aloha , diffusion-based action generation~ chi2023diffusion , and large-scale generalist or vision-language-action pretraining ~ black2024pi0,kim2024openvla,ghosh2024octo . Compared with unimanual manipulation, bimanual policy learning must jointly model the actions of both arms together with their spatial and temporal coordination, introducing additional challenges in role assignment and long-horizon execution. ALOHA~ zhao2023aloha and Mobile ALOHA~ fu2024mobilealoha demonstrate bimanual policy learning from coordinated demonstrations. These methods highlight the importance of jointly modeling both arms together with their spatial and temporal coordination in complex bimanual tasks. Robot Data Augmentation and Bimanual Transfer. Another line of work improves data efficiency by augmenting or reusing robot demonstrations. MimicGen~ mandlekar2023mimicgen and DexMimicGen~ jiang2024dexmimicgen automatically generate demonstrations from a small number of source demonstrations, while D-CODA~ liu2025dcoda and ROPA~ chen2025ropa improve the utilization of existing bimanual demonstrations through offline data augmentation. AnyBimanual~ lu2024anybimanual transfers pretrained unimanual policies to bimanual manipulation, but still relies on additional bimanual demonstrations for adaptation. Other studies exploit morphological symmetry to improve sample efficiency and bilateral generalization~ ordonez2024morphological,li2025symdex . As summarized in Table~ tab:related_work_comparison , existing approaches differ in their source supervision, dependence on additional bimanual demonstrations, and ability to support Single-to-Dual transfer and spatio-temporal coordination. title: TOPS: Reshaping Flow Source and Transport for Multi-Task Robot Manipulation
summary: Flow-based policies for language-conditioned multi-task manipulation commonly share a single $\textit{Gaussian}$ source prior and a common linear transport path across tasks. However, reliably executing multiple tasks with distinct motion requirements remains challenging for a shared policy. We introduce $\textbf{TOPS}$ ($\textbf{T}$ask-$\textbf{O}$riented $\textbf{P}$riors and $\textbf{S}$chedules), which adapts the flow source prior and interpolation schedule to each task without modifying the network architecture. TOPS first constructs multimodal task sources from reverse-mapped expert action sequences, allowing language instructions to select where generation begins. Guided by source-target covariance mismatch, it then slows the transition toward expert actions early in denoising and accelerates it later along directions requiring expansion. Under a $\textit{Gaussian}$ endpoint model, our analysis shows that this schedule adjustment can lower an upper bound on velocity-prediction risk. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and CALVIN demonstrate improved performance across in-distribution, perturbation and cross-environment settings, alongside better data efficiency. Using one integration step, TOPS raises LIBERO-10 success from $53.44\%$ to $69.67\%$ compared with ten-step Standard Flow Matching (FM), while reducing inference time to approximately one-sixth of the baseline. TOPS also yields consistent gains when transferred to the large-scale flow-based $π_{0.5}$ policy across all four evaluated settings. Real-world experiments further demonstrate improved task success, including an increase from $20\%$ with standard FM to $80\%$ with TOPS on the upper-drawer opening task.
full_text: Introduction Real-world manipulation exhibits substantial behavioral diversity. Different tasks require distinct motion patterns, and even a given goal can be achieved through different contact strategies, motion trajectories, and temporal execution patterns. Diffusion and flow-matching models~ actionflow,diffusion_policy,riemannian capture such multimodal action distributions directly and have become widely used in imitation learning. This expressive power has also carried the generative paradigm from task-specific visuomotor control to language-conditioned multi-task and generalist robot policies~ dnact,pi0,pi05 . In this setting, a shared policy must accommodate the motion requirements of different tasks and execute each task reliably. However, a shared policy can perform well on some tasks yet struggle to execute others reliably~ baku,libero,disc . A shared policy must capture multiple action modes within a task and substantially different action distributions across tasks~ discrete_policy,flexible_policy . Existing approaches introduce or redesign policy components to improve multi-task performance, using feature modulation~ baku , visual selection~ otter , instruction-generated parameters~ disc , and expert routing~ smodp . In flow policies~ flow_matching , the network must recover distinct task-specific action distributions from a shared Gaussian source under a common linear transport path. Before changing the policy architecture as in prior work, we step back to the generative process itself and ask: could adapting the source prior and transport to each task improve multi-task performance without changing the policy architecture? To investigate, we reverse a trained multi-task flow policy and trace expert actions back to their source samples~ reversal_steer . As shown in Figs.~ fig:raft_reverse_geometry (a,b), reverse-mapped expert actions exhibit task-dependent organization under the warm-up policy, with further subclusters within individual tasks. These patterns motivate us to investigate whether fitting task-specific sources to the reverse images and directly denoising from the corresponding region can improve policy learning. To further understand what changes are needed to reach expert actions, we analyze the covariance mismatch between these sources and the corresponding expert-action distributions using a Gaussian optimal-transport map. Its eigenvectors define orthogonal axes, each representing a weighted combination of action components across timesteps. We find expert actions have substantially greater standard deviation than source samples only along a few axes. We refer to this source-to-target increase as expansion. Yet conventional flow matching~ flow_matching,pi05 starts every task from a single task-independent Gaussian and applies the same linear interpolation schedule along every axis. This leaves the network to recover task-specific action structure from shared noise, while interpolation timing remains unchanged despite the unequal source-to-target changes revealed by our analysis. Motivated by these findings, we introduce (Task-Oriented Priors and Schedules) for multi-task flow policies. It fits a Gaussian mixture with low-rank covariance structure~ MPPCA to each task's reverse-mapped samples, allowing language instructions to select the source. Along expansion axes, slows interpolation toward expert actions early and accelerates it later, retaining linear interpolation elsewhere. Under a Gaussian endpoint model~ stochastic , we show that adapting interpolation can lower an upper bound on velocity-prediction risk. This risk captures the irreducible error that arises when the same interpolated action sequence corresponds to different velocity targets. On LIBERO-10, our schedule reduces estimated time-integrated directional risk on expansion axes by relative to linear interpolation (Fig.~ fig:risk-validation ). In controlled 2D experiments with few integration steps, it also places more samples in target regions than linear or fast-then-slow schedules (Fig.~ fig:toy_exp ). Together, these choices support efficient few-step action generation. We evaluate on LIBERO~ libero , LIBERO-Plus~ LIBERO-Plus , CALVIN~ calvin , and three real-world multi-task suites. With the same backbone as the baselines, achieves the highest mean performance across two in-distribution and two out-of-distribution settings, covering perturbations and unseen environments, using one schedule-aware step. Compared with ten-step Standard FM~ flow_matching , it raises LIBERO-10 success from 53.44 to 69.67 while reducing inference latency to approximately one-sixth. Limited-data evaluations also show gains across all simulation benchmarks: on CALVIN ABC D, trained on 30 of demonstrations outperforms all evaluated baselines trained on 50 . These gains also extend to the large-scale flow-based policy in all four settings, raising LIBERO-Plus success from 64.4 to 69.0 and CALVIN ABC D average chain length from 3.033 to 3.744. Real-world gains include 80 success on upper-drawer opening, compared with 20 for Standard FM. To recap, our contributions are threefold: =0.1cm \ We construct task-specific sources by fitting Gaussian mixtures with low-rank covariance structure to reverse-mapped expert action chunks, enabling language-guided source selection. =0.1cm \ We introduce slow-then-fast scheduling along expansion directions identified by Gaussian optimal transport, motivated by an upper bound on velocity-prediction risk under independent Gaussian endpoints. =0.1cm \ Experiments show that achieves the highest mean performance across the main in- and out-of-distribution simulation settings with one schedule-aware step, while reducing latency and improving data efficiency. Gains also extend to the large-scale policy and real-world tasks. Related Work Language-conditioned multi-task policies. Language-conditioned multi-task policies aim to execute diverse behaviors with a shared model~ pi0,pi05,baku . Prior work supports task-specific behavior through visual feature modulation or selection~ baku,otter , instruction-generated parameters~ disc , and semantic expert routing~ smodp . adapts source distributions and interpolation schedules to task-specific action structure while preserving the policy backbone and its original conditioning. Source distributions for generative policies. Existing sources use action histories~ a2a,jia2026marspolicy,bai2026flash or conditioning representations~ Cocos , while LeaP~ leap learns proprioception-conditioned diagonal Gaussians. MM-FM~ MM-FM combines a mixture fitted to target image latents with mode-dependent coupling. Flow reversal steering~ reversal_steer uses inverted actions for direct steering or learning observation-conditioned noise policies while keeping the base flow frozen. fits low-rank Gaussian mixtures to each task's reverse images pooled across observations and trains the velocity field under adapted sources and paths. Coupling and path design in flow matching. Prior work optimizes endpoint couplings~ OT-CFM,COT_policy or straightens trajectories by retraining on flow-generated pairs~ reflow . MeanFlow~ meanflow learns interval-averaged velocity for one-step generation. Other methods approximate geodesics under data-induced metrics~ metric_flow_maching or adapt global schedules to velocity profiles or regression difficulty~ vsfm,dcfm . retains independent endpoint sampling and uses Gaussian OT to identify task-specific expansion directions for slow-then-fast scheduling. title: ClusterSplat: Semantic Cluster Selection for 3D Visual Grounding in Gaussian Splatting
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 as a Spotlight paper. Project page: https://jaesung8.github.io/clustersplat/
summary: We study 3D visual grounding in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), where a referring expression should identify a target object as both a rendered 2D mask and a set of explicit 3D Gaussians. Prior methods typically extract 3D targets by applying heuristic thresholding or top-ratio filtering to dense primitive-level relevance scores. However, these scores often vary substantially across scenes and prompts, making such heuristics sensitive and leading to unstable targeting. ClusterSplat addresses this by reframing 3D target selection as cluster-level selection over scene-adaptive candidates. The method first learns instance-aware Gaussian features, forms feature-aware seed voxels, and merges neighboring seed voxels when a description-length criterion decreases, producing a scene-specific set of cluster candidates. Given a referring expression, a query-conditioned cluster scorer ranks the cluster candidates with a lightweight MLP, and the selected cluster directly defines the explicit 3D target while its cluster score is rendered for the 2D mask. On ScanRefer, ClusterSplat achieves the best rendered 2D segmentation and explicit 3D target metrics among the compared 3DGS baselines. It also obtains the best average Ref-LERF scores, supporting the same trend under fine-grained referring descriptions. On ScanNet v2 class name queries, ClusterSplat achieves the strongest rendered 2D results and the highest 3D matching accuracy, while maintaining competitive 3D IoU. Our project page is available at https://jaesung8.github.io/clustersplat/ .
