Our project page is available at . Introduction 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has recently emerged as a compelling explicit alternative to neural radiance fields mildenhall2020nerf . It offers photorealistic novel-view synthesis with real-time rendering capabilities~ kerbl20233d . Beyond visual rendering, 3DGS is rapidly evolving into a general-purpose 3D representation capable of structural modeling~ lu2024scaffold, guedon2024sugar and semantic understanding qin2024langsplat,wu2024opengaussian,li2025scenesplat,zhu2025objectgs . A pivotal direction in this evolution is language grounding. This capability enables natural-language querying of 3D scenes through referring expressions. While recent approaches have successfully lifted vision-language embeddings into 3D space for open-vocabulary querying~ kerr2023lerf, qin2024langsplat , explicitly extracting the precise 3D extent of a target object remains a significant challenge. The core difficulty lies in the continuous nature of the relevance fields used in prior works. Existing methods typically compute dense, primitive-level relevance scores and isolate the target by applying heuristic discretization, such as global thresholding or top- filtering~ wu2024opengaussian,drsplat25,qu2024goi . However, these heuristics are highly sensitive in open-vocabulary settings. Relevance score distributions often vary substantially with the scene context and the complexity of the prompt (e.g., compositional attributes or spatial relations). Consequently, relying on scale-sensitive hyperparameters often leads to unstable targeting. Figure~ fig:teaser illustrates this failure mode: top-ratio filtering can scatter selected primitives across the referred object and nearby distractors rather than producing one coherent 3D target. As shown by the top-ratio analysis in Appendix~ sec:app_sensitivity , dense relevance fields often lack clear decision boundaries, causing the target to be missed or merged with background under a fixed selection ratio. Moreover, indoor scenes vary substantially in object count, object scale, clutter, and same-class distractors, so cluster candidates should adapt their granularity to the scene structure. To overcome this instability, we design ClusterSplat as a cluster-level targeting framework (Figure~ fig:overview ) that shifts the selection granularity from individual primitives to scene-adaptive cluster candidates. We view the cluster index as the coarse decision variable for a single referred target and construct these candidates with a scene-adaptive merge procedure guided by description length. These observations, together with the scattered primitive selections in Figure~ fig:teaser , motivate formulating 3D target selection as a discrete selection problem over coherent object-level candidates rather than as a filtering task over millions of unstructured primitives. The framework can be viewed as two stages that align with the offline scene preparation and query-conditioned grounding blocks in Figure~ fig:overview . First, we optimize instance-aware Gaussian features and construct feature-aware seed voxels. We then build a candidate graph over seed-voxel descriptors and merge adjacent components only when the description length decreases, producing a scene-specific number of clusters. Second, during target selection, a query-conditioned cluster scorer ranks the candidates with a lightweight MLP to select the target cluster. The selected cluster directly defines the explicit 3D target, and its cluster-level scores are rendered to produce the 2D mask. Furthermore, we observe that the advancement of 3DGS grounding is hindered by the lack of evaluation protocols that jointly assess rendered 2D masks and explicit 3D target sets. Current benchmarks like Ref-LERF~ he2025refersplat are limited in scene diversity, while standard semantic segmentation metrics fail to capture the nuances of compositional language grounding. Class name prompts provide category-level grounding, but they cannot uniquely specify one target when multiple objects from the same category appear in a scene. Referring expressions address this ambiguity through attributes and spatial relations, making ScanRefer a more demanding test of object-level targeting. To bridge this gap, we define a reproducible evaluation protocol that combines official ScanNet v2 annotations with ScanRefer expressions~ dai2017scannet,chen2020scanrefer . Our main comparison uses the subset of 10 scenes adopted by recent 3DGS open-vocabulary baselines for reproducibility. This enables class name grounding and referring expression segmentation to be reported on the same ScanNet v2 scenes. In summary, our contributions are as follows: We introduce a scale- and granularity-aware formulation for 3D visual grounding in 3DGS. By transforming primitive-level score filtering into cluster-level selection over scene-adaptive candidates, we avoid per-query score thresholds while allowing the cluster granularity to follow the scene structure. We propose ClusterSplat, a two-stage framework that first learns instance-aware Gaussian features and constructs scene-adaptive clusters with a description-length criterion, followed by query-conditioned cluster scoring for explicit target selection and 2D mask rendering. We evaluate ClusterSplat with a reproducible protocol combining ScanNet v2 annotations and ScanRefer expressions that reports class name grounding and referring expression segmentation on the same ScanNet v2 scenes. On the ScanRefer benchmark, experiments show state-of-the-art referring segmentation among the compared 3DGS baselines. Ref-LERF further confirms consistent gains in fine-grained scenes, while ScanNet v2 class name evaluation shows improved rendered 2D masks and competitive 3D object matching. Related Work sec:related 3D Gaussian Splatting and Language Grounding Neural rendering first achieved high-quality novel-view synthesis with implicit radiance fields~ mildenhall2020nerf , while recent explicit representations such as 3DGS provide real-time rasterization-based rendering~ kerbl20233d . Explicit primitives also support faster optimization and direct geometric manipulation compared with fully implicit scene encodings. Subsequent work improves 3DGS through structural regularity, filtering, surface-aligned primitives, and alternative optimization strategies~ lu2024scaffold,yu2024mip,huang20242d,kheradmand20243d . Beyond rendering, explicit Gaussian primitives have become a substrate for semantic and language-aware feature fields learned through language embeddings, 2D foundation-model distillation, or cross-modal rasterization~ qin2024langsplat,shi2024legaussians,zhou2024feature3dgs,peng2025vlgss,li2025scenesplat,zhu2025objectgs . However, view-consistent semantic rendering does not by itself define a reliable single-object 3D target. Dr.~Splat directly registers language embeddings to Gaussians~ drsplat25 , interaction-oriented methods lift 2D prompts into Gaussian space~ gaussian_grouping,cen2025segment , and instance-level Gaussian representations recover object-level subsets~ li2024instancegaussian,piekenbrinck2025opensplat3d . Yet many pipelines still extract targets from continuous relevance scores using thresholding, top- selection, or related discretization rules~ qu2024goi,wu2024opengaussian,drsplat25 . These rules remain sensitive to scene- and prompt-dependent score scales, which makes explicit 3D targeting unstable. This sensitivity has also motivated alternatives to fixed similarity cutoffs, such as hyperplane-based selection of Gaussians of Interest~ qu2024goi . Referring tasks in 3D Gaussian scenes make this limitation more apparent. ReferSplat introduces the Ref-LERF benchmark and obtains supervision from reliable Grounded-SAM candidates~ he2025refersplat,ren2024grounded , but view-wise mask cues can still under-specify whether a prediction forms one coherent 3D instance when the Gaussian representation admits ambiguous groupings~ wu2024opengaussian . Related 3DGS methods use grouped or instance-aware structure for point-level open-vocabulary understanding, view-dependent semantic aggregation, or dense open-vocabulary 3D segmentation~ wu2024opengaussian,cen2025laga,zhu2025cos3d . These objectives are complementary to our setting, where a referring expression should select one referred target. This motivates grouping primitives into stable candidates and performing discrete selection in the grouped space. In ClusterSplat, clusters serve as the decision domain for single-target referring expressions, and the selected cluster directly determines the explicit 3D target. 3D Visual Grounding 3D visual grounding aims to localize a language-specified target within a 3D scene. It is commonly separated into comprehension tasks, which predict a coarse target location such as a box, and segmentation tasks, which predict a precise point- or mask-level region~ chen2020scanrefer,he2024refmask3d . ScanNet v2 scenes and ScanRefer expressions have been instrumental in this area by providing RGB-D reconstructions with rich, compositional language descriptions~ dai2017scannet,chen2020scanrefer . Related 3D referring-expression datasets further study language grounding beyond a single benchmark family~ achlioptas2020referit3d . Building on these datasets, point-cloud methods have improved language-geometry alignment and relational reasoning~ he2024refmask3d,zhao2021dvgtransformer,wu2023eda . Open-vocabulary 3D scene understanding has also been explored with CLIP-aligned point features and class-agnostic 3D mask proposals before the recent shift toward 3DGS representations~ peng_openscene_2023,takmaz2023openmask3d . Foundation-model supervision further improves scalability, with AugRefer generating diverse synthetic supervision~ wang2025augrefer and SeeGround enabling zero-shot grounding by bridging 3D scenes with 2D vision-language models~ li2025seeground . Adapting this progress to 3DGS requires care because 3DGS optimizes unstructured primitives primarily for rendering. Unlike explicit point clouds, Gaussian primitives are not directly organized as semantic units, so pixel-level parsing can hide failures in the underlying 3D target set. OpenGaussian highlights this 2D-3D discrepancy when improving feature association and discretized 3D selection~ wu2024opengaussian . Since relevance scores in open-vocabulary 3DGS vary across scenes and prompts, robust evaluation should report both rendered 2D segmentation and discrete 3D

title: Making Self-Driving Laboratories Auditable:A Unified Framework for Hybrid Actions,Measurements, and Safe Execution
summary: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) are laboratory systems that couple experimental planning, automated execution, and measurement feedback in a closed loop. Integrating flexible robot control with the typed application programming interfaces (APIs) and continuous measurements exposed by laboratory instruments remains an execution-interface challenge. To address this challenge, we propose a traceable framework comprising four components: LAM (Lab Action Model), OpenSDL, Safe-SDL, and L3-Bench. LAM is a proposed measurement-conditioned policy architecture that extends vision-language-action paradigms to generate both continuous robot trajectories and typed instrument API calls. OpenSDL is an execution substrate with an initial control implementation, designed to map role-level operations to heterogeneous devices, coordinate execution, and record timestamped causal events. The proposed Safe-SDL runtime gate combines pre-dispatch schema and resource checks with signal temporal logic monitoring during execution, including extended waiting periods. L3-Bench (Level-3 Laboratory Benchmark) specifies an episode-level evaluation protocol covering physical outcomes, timing, reproducibility, safety violations, and fault recovery. Together, these components provide an end-to-end design for linking hybrid action generation, monitored device execution, measurement feedback, and experimental evaluation, addressing coordination and traceability challenges in SDL workflows.
full_text: Making Self-Driving Laboratories Auditable:\\ A Unified Framework for Hybrid Actions,\\ Measurements, and Safe Execution Introduction introduction Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) are laboratory systems that couple experimental intent and planning to automated execution and measurement feedback in a closed loop~ abolhasani2023 . This approach can accelerate materials discovery and reaction optimization while reducing the need for repeated manual intervention~ abolhasani2023,slattery2024,szymanski2023 . Their defining operation is a repeated decision cycle: (i) a machine-readable objective is translated into experimental operations; (ii) those operations are executed by instruments and robots; (iii) measurements and device states are collected; and (iv) the resulting evidence is used to inform the next decision. Through this cycle, experimental throughput can be increased and condition search or hypothesis testing conducted systematically across many trials~ king2004,steiner2019,slattery2024,szymanski2023 . To implement this cycle, practical SDLs combine planning tools for step (i), device control for step (ii), sensing and data acquisition for step (iii), and data analysis and decision-making for step (iv). Data and provenance management link these stages, while human supervision supports oversight and intervention throughout the cycle~ abolhasani2023 . Representative developments have showcased how experimental procedures and robot actions can be represented, executed, and recorded. In 2019, Steiner et al. described Chemputer, which encoded chemical procedures as executable programs, separating hardware-independent procedures from platform-specific connectivity and device drivers~ steiner2019 . In 2023, Boiko et al. introduced Coscientist, which combined language-model reasoning with documentation search, code execution, and laboratory APIs to plan and perform chemical experiments~ boiko2023 . In 2024, Kim et al. introduced OpenVLA, a vision-language-action (VLA) model connecting visual observations and language instructions to learned robot control~ kim2024 . In the same year, Bai et al. developed a dynamic knowledge graph framework for distributed SDLs that supports shared ontologies and cycle-level provenance, with limited granularity for exact operation timing under hardware constraints~ bai2024 . In 2026, Ren et al. introduced LabVLA, which applied VLA policies to laboratory protocols while acknowledging that measurement-driven protocol revision had not yet been demonstrated~ ren2026 . IvoryOS provides an interoperable web interface for orchestrating Python-based SDLs~ zhang2025 . Established standards address device connectivity and provenance. SiLA 2 (Standardization in Lab Automation) describes instrument capabilities through typed Features, Commands, and Properties, supporting discovery, command execution, and property subscriptions~ juchli2022 . Provenance standards provide a formal basis for representing auditable records. The World Wide Web Consortium's PROV Ontology (W3C PROV-O) represents entities, activities, and agents through generation, usage, attribution, and qualified relations carrying roles and time information~ lebo2013 . PROV-CONSTRAINTS defines validity, equivalence, and event-ordering constraints for provenance records~ cheney2013constraints ; the companion PROV-SEM Working Group Note provides first-order semantics for the PROV data model~ cheney2013semantics . ProvONE extends PROV with scientific workflow structure and execution provenance~ cao2016provone , while Research Object Crate (RO-Crate) packages research artefacts with Schema.org-based structured metadata~ soilandreyes2022rocrate . These approaches establish provenance representation and consistency rules. Our execution-interface contribution concerns their coupling to measurement-conditioned hybrid actions, pre-dispatch gating, clock-domain-aware timestamping, and timed safety monitoring. We position SDL-Traj as a proposed PROV-O-aligned laboratory profile, reusing core provenance relations and adding application-specific terms for device capabilities, monotonic-clock metadata, and signal temporal logic (STL) robustness. Explicit vocabulary mappings, PROV-O export, SiLA 2 adapters, and conformance tests remain implementation targets. For example, reaction and cooling waits require monitoring to remain active and link fresh or stale measurements, pending calls, verified completion events, and gate decisions. Such execution records must preserve both scientific context and the conditions under which physical actions were admitted. These requirements motivate a shared interface linking measurement-conditioned action generation with execution, monitoring, and evaluation. We therefore propose a traceable framework comprising LAM (Lab Action Model), OpenSDL, Safe-SDL, and L3-Bench. LAM is designed to generate a hybrid output consisting of continuous robot trajectories and typed instrument API calls from task instructions, visual observations, robot states, and instrument measurements. Its proposed architecture extends the VLA framework with typed telemetry and shares multimodal context between a continuous motion expert and a discrete function-calling head. OpenSDL, with an initial control implementation, is designed to map role-level operations to heterogeneous devices and coordinate operations according to their dependencies, waiting requirements, and completion conditions. Its event model links measurements, device states, and execution outcomes to dispatched commands and runtime decisions in timestamped causal records. In the proposed loop, updated observations and confirmed events provide context for subsequent LAM action proposals. Safe-SDL is the proposed runtime gate for schema and resource checks before dispatch and monitoring of formalized temporal constraints throughout execution, including extended waiting periods. Timeouts, degraded measurement quality, or insufficient safety margins are intended to trigger action blocking and predefined degradation or safe-abort procedures. L3-Bench (Level-3 Laboratory Benchmark) specifies an episode-level evaluation protocol covering protocol-specific physical outcomes, timing, reproducibility, safety violations, and fault recovery. Here, L3 denotes measurement-conditioned adaptation within an experiment, as defined in the task-specific classification of Section~ autonomy-levels . End-to-end LAM training, cross-device transfer experiments, and systematic hardware and safety validation remain to be completed; improvements in throughput, adaptability, and fault recovery are hypotheses to be tested through the proposed evaluation. Problem Formulation and Control Interface problem-formulation-and-system-philosophy Autonomy Levels autonomy-levels We adopt a task-specific working L1--L4 autonomy classification that complements published SDL autonomy taxonomies~ tobias2025,hung2024 . These levels classify execution capability; SDLs additionally require the planning-and-feedback loop defined above. L1--L4 describe increasing adaptation: L1 denotes scripted execution or teleoperation, L2 visual protocol execution, L3 measurement-conditioned adaptation, and L4 hypothesis optimization across batches with multi-instrument coordination. We focus on implementable and measurable L3 behavior in the near term, leaving L4 for future work. Hybrid State--Action and Event Semantics hybrid-stateaction-space We represent the laboratory process as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP), a standard model for sequential decision-making when the physical state cannot be observed completely: \[ = , , , , , , . \] Here, is the latent physical state of the laboratory, is the hybrid candidate-action space, is the transition model describing how action changes state to , and is the task or operational reward. is the observation space, is the observation model, and discounts delayed reward. The notation captures temperatures, concentrations, device queues, and completion states that are partially observed and may be delayed or noisy; the current implementation leaves the transition and reward models unspecified. At time , the observation is , where contains synchronized visual frames, is the proprioceptive state, and contains measurement streams from heterogeneous instruments. The action space is the Cartesian product \[ = _ _ . \] The arm-action space includes a no-motion option, and the instrument-action space contains finite, possibly empty collections of calls. Feasible combinations depend on resource and safety constraints. A continuous action contains control steps and trajectory dimensions, with recorded coordinate frame, control period, and calibration version. An individual instrument call is a typed instrument call: Role identifies the capability, Op identifies the operation such as Set, Execute, or Read, and contains validated parameters and units. The two action types share a time base and event ledger. Empty outputs allow monitoring during waiting periods. To give this Cartesian product executable semantics, the output of a decision cycle is written as \[ a_t= ( A_ ,t:t+H_a-1 , _t ), _t=\ c_i\ _ i=1 ^ N_t , \] where each instrument call includes a role, an operation, parameters, a waiting policy, and an idempotency key: \[ c_i= r_i,o_i, _i, _i, _i . \] Here, is a semantic capability in the role dictionary, is the requested operation, contains typed parameters, specifies timeout, retry, and completion conditions, and supports deduplication and transaction association. The action compiler checks units, ranges, resource locks, and preconditions before mapping a role call to a concrete DeviceProvider (an adapter that implements a role for one physical or simulated device). Role-preserving substitution retains high-level action labels; device calibration, latency, and physical limits still require compatibility tests. States, actions, and events share a common timeline. Observations, candidate actions, and device returns are recorded as events , linked by episode IDs, timestamps, and causal parent events. The proposed ledger combines device timestamps, a runtime monotonic clock, and causal event IDs. Clock offsets and drift are recorded explicitly; receive order alone cannot establish cross-device causality. In this paper, an event is therefore the auditable record of one observation, proposal, gate decision, dispatch, return, or compensation step recorded in the event ledger. This design distinguishes an incorrect model proposal, a safety-blocked action, and a device execution failure, and allows replay to reconstruct the causal sequence from proposal through approval to completion. Design Requirements design-requirements We express the laboratory control interface as five checkable invariants. Semantic portability requires policies to depend on roles, capabilities, and units. Action composability requires continuous trajectories and discrete calls to carry preconditions, resource requirements, and completion signals so that they can form a directed acyclic graph (DAG) execution plan. Temporal consistency requires visual frames, proprioception, telemetry, and action events to share monotonic timestamps with explicit measurement delays and waiting intervals. Safety gating requires every action to pass through the same observable safety kernel before submission to the bus; device interlocks govern actions independently of model confidence. Replayability requires raw inputs, compiled device commands, return bytes, and safety decisions to be linked to the same episode for offline replay and difference analysis. These invariants define an auditable protocol contribution and establish module boundaries. LAM generates candidate actions from context, while OpenSDL checks their semantic, temporal, and safety properties; the modules exchange data only through a versioned schema. title: RouteDRAG: Learning to Route and Control Agentic Execution for Multimodal Document RAG
comment: Our code is now available at https://github.com/Ereshkigal1/RouteDRAG
summary: Web-based applications increasingly rely on understanding long multimodal documents, where answering questions often requires combining information across pages, tables, and figures. Agentic retrieval-augmented generation addresses these tasks through iterative retrieval and reasoning. However, Agentic execution is not always necessary, introducing additional computation and potentially incorrect answers. Our empirical analysis reveals that Agentic execution provides query-dependent benefits, while additional operations may improve, preserve, or degrade answer accuracy. These findings motivate controlling both Agent invocation and subsequent execution. To address these challenges, we propose RouteDRAG, a learning-based framework comprising four components. Unified Document Index organizes multimodal content into a graph-backed index and derives query representations from initial retrieval. Adaptive Path Routing preserves exact answering and predicts the relative benefit of Agent over shorter execution paths. Dynamic Agent Execution maintains an evolving workspace and refines Planner proposals to control tool use and termination. Sequential Policy Learning first trains operation control from observed outcomes and then trains path routing using the resulting Agent's performance. Across two benchmarks, RouteDRAG achieves an average accuracy improvement of 3.47 percentage points over shorter-path-only execution while assigning only 79.3% of queries to Agent. Notably, it also surpasses uniform Agent execution on both benchmarks while requiring fewer answering calls. Our code is now available at https://github.com/Ereshkigal1/RouteDRAG.
full_text: Zekai Chen* Hao Zhu* Yu Liu Xunkai Li Zejian Kang Rui Qian Quanjiang Li Rong-Hua Li Web-based applications increasingly rely on understanding long multimodal documents, where answering questions often requires combining information across pages, tables, and figures. Agentic retrieval-augmented generation addresses these tasks through iterative retrieval and reasoning. However, Agentic execution is not always necessary, introducing additional computation and potentially incorrect answers. Our empirical analysis reveals that Agentic execution provides query-dependent benefits, while additional operations may improve, preserve, or degrade answer accuracy. These findings motivate controlling both Agent invocation and subsequent execution. To address these challenges, we propose RouteDRAG, a learning-based framework comprising four components. Unified Document Index organizes multimodal content into a graph-backed index and derives query representations from initial retrieval. Adaptive Path Routing preserves exact answering and predicts the relative benefit of Agent over shorter execution paths. Dynamic Agent Execution maintains an evolving workspace and refines Planner proposals to control tool use and termination. Sequential Policy Learning first trains operation control from observed outcomes and then trains path routing using the resulting Agent's performance. Across two benchmarks, RouteDRAG achieves an average accuracy improvement of 3.47 percentage points over shorter-path-only execution while assigning only 79.3 of queries to Agent. Notably, it also surpasses uniform Agent execution on both benchmarks while requiring fewer answering calls. Our code is now available on . Introduction sec:introduction Web-based applications, such as financial analysis platforms~ chen2021finqa,zhu2021tatqa , government information portals, academic search engines~ dasigi2021qasper , and online technical support~ castelli2020techqa,feng2020doc2dial , increasingly rely on understanding long and visually rich documents. Answering questions often requires locating and combining information distributed across pages, tables, and figures. For example, explaining a company's financial performance may require examining numerical results in a table and their explanations on other pages. A single retrieval step may locate only part of the required information, leaving the question unanswered. Agentic retrieval-augmented generation (Agentic RAG) addresses this challenge through iterative retrieval, visual understanding, and multi-step reasoning, allowing information from different document regions to be located and combined. Recent studies have made Agentic RAG more adaptive through multimodal retrieval, graph-based exploration and iterative reasoning~ wang2025vidorag,sourati2026ladrag,zuo2026magerag,ji2026taprag,liu2026opera . These methods allow Agents to dynamically select document content and adjust retrieval procedures. However, adapting how information is retrieved does not fully address how much Agentic execution is needed. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:motivation , some questions require multiple retrieval steps to locate and combine information across different pages, while others can be answered directly from the initial retrieval results without invoking an Agent. Unnecessary Agent invocation increases computational cost and may introduce irrelevant or conflicting information, leading to incorrect answers. Yet deciding whether to invoke an Agent is only the first step. As the Agent gathers more information, it must further decide whether to retrieve additional content, inspect visual regions, or terminate execution. This raises two fundamental questions: when should Agentic execution be invoked, and how should its subsequent operations be controlled? Our empirical analysis reveals three observations about Agentic execution. O1: Limited Overall Gains. Agent improves accuracy by 1.00 and 3.12 percentage points on DocBench and MMLongBench-Doc, respectively, but uses and as many answering tokens as Standard. O2: Query-Dependent Benefits. Agent alone answers 3.09 and 6.69 of questions correctly, while both Agent and Standard succeed on 69.24 and 44.18 . Conversely, Standard alone succeeds on 2.09 and 3.57 , indicating that Agent execution is not universally beneficial. O3: Non-Monotonic Operation Gains. Among 917 matched operation-level comparisons, 84.51 show unchanged correctness, while additional operations can improve or degrade answers. These observations motivate selective Agent invocation based on its expected benefit and adaptive operation control based on information collected during execution. To address these challenges, we propose RouteDRAG, a learning-based framework for selective Agentic document RAG. First, Unified Document Index organizes multimodal content into a graph-backed index and derives query representations from initial retrieval. Next, Adaptive Path Routing predicts the benefit of invoking Agent over a shorter path while preserving exact answering. When Agent is invoked, Dynamic Agent Execution maintains an evolving workspace and refines Planner proposals to control subsequent operations and termination. Finally, Sequential Policy Learning first trains operation control from observed outcomes and then trains path routing using the resulting Agent's performance. Together, these components adapt Agent invocation and execution to individual queries. Our Contributions. We identify limited overall gains, query-dependent benefits, and non-monotonic operation gains in Agentic document RAG, motivating execution decisions at both query and operation levels. We propose RouteDRAG, integrating Unified Document Index, Adaptive Path Routing, Dynamic Agent Execution, and Sequential Policy Learning to control Agent invocation and subsequent operations. We evaluate RouteDRAG against nine RAG methods on DocBench and MMLongBench-Doc, achieving 75.86 and 53.80 accuracy, respectively, while reducing answering calls by 16.4 and 14.9 compared with uniform Agent execution. Related Work sec:related_work Multimodal and Agentic Document RAG Document RAG has evolved from text-based retrieval toward richer multimodal and structural representations. LightRAG~ guo2025lightrag organizes entities and relations into a graph, while RAG-Anything~ guo2025raganything extends graph-based retrieval to multimodal documents. GraphReader li2024graphreader further employs graph-guided Agent exploration for long-text understanding. G -Reader du2026g2reader maintains evolving content and planning graphs for multimodal document question answering. VisRAG~ yu2025visrag and M3DocRAG~ cho2024m3docrag further explore visual retrieval for document understanding. AgenticOCR wang2026agenticocr enables query-driven parsing of relevant visual regions to reduce redundant document processing. ReAct yao2023react established a reasoning-and-acting paradigm that interleaves language-model reasoning with external actions. Recent Agentic approaches support more flexible information acquisition. ViDoRAG~ wang2025vidorag employs iterative exploration and reasoning, LAD-RAG~ sourati2026ladrag combines neural and structural document retrieval, and MAGE-RAG~ zuo2026magerag dynamically explores and prunes graph-based evidence. TAP-RAG~ ji2026taprag further adapts graph expansion and visual inspection to query requirements. These methods improve the acquisition and organization of multimodal information. RouteDRAG instead focuses on whether such Agentic execution is necessary for a given query and how its subsequent operations should be controlled. Adaptive Retrieval and Execution Selection Adaptive RAG methods adjust retrieval and execution according to query requirements. Self-RAG~ asai2024selfrag learns when retrieval is needed, while Adaptive-RAG~ jeong2024adaptiverag selects among no-retrieval, single-step, and iterative strategies based on query complexity. Active Retrieval Augmented Generation jiang2023active dynamically retrieves additional evidence during generation. MBA-RAG~ tang2025mbarag further uses bandit-based selection to balance retrieval quality and efficiency. More recent methods extend adaptation to multi-step execution. MAO-ARAG~ chen2025maoarag dynamically organizes retrieval agents into query-specific workflows, while SPARKLE~ fang2026sparkle learns a separate policy for controlling retrieval operations. These studies demonstrate the value of both query-level adaptation and step-wise control. RouteDRAG connects the two decisions by estimating Agent's benefit relative to a designated shorter path and refining subsequent operations based on the evolving workspace. Its sequential learning process further aligns path routing with the behavior of the resulting Agent. Problem Definition sec:problem Given a multimodal document and a query , let denote the unified document index. We consider four execution paths: where the first three provide shorter answering procedures, while Agent supports iterative retrieval and reasoning. Unlike execution-path selection alone, selective Agentic execution involves two related decisions. At the query level, a routing policy determines whether Agent is necessary or a shorter path is sufficient. Once Agent is invoked, its execution policy selects an operation from the legal action set based on the evolving workspace , including whether to continue acquiring information or terminate. Our objective is to maintain answer accuracy while avoiding unnecessary Agent invocation and subsequent operations. Empirical Study sec:empirical To understand when Agentic execution is necessary, we investigate its benefits from three perspectives. We use a standalone reference Agent for these analyses, distinct from the final RouteDRAG Actor evaluated in the main experiments. We first examine whether uniform Agent execution justifies its additional cost, then investigate how its benefits vary across queries, and finally assess whether additional operations consistently improve answers. O1: Limited Overall Gains. Does Agentic execution justify its additional computation? Fig.~ fig:empirical (a) compares Standard and Agent across five DocBench domains and seven MMLongBench-Doc document types. Agent improves accuracy by 1.00 and 3.12 percentage points on DocBench and MMLongBench-Doc, respectively, while consuming and the answering tokens. These results reveal a mismatch between overall accuracy gains and computational cost: uniformly invoking the Agent incurs substantial overhead for modest improvements. However, aggregate results cannot identify which queries justify this additional computation, motivating a closer examination of query-level benefits. O2: Query-Dependent Benefits. Which queries actually benefit from Agent execution? Fig.~ fig:empirical (b) compares the two paths on the same questions. Correctness remains unchanged for 94.83 of DocBench queries and 89.73 of MMLongBench-Doc queries. Meanwhile, Agent recovers answers missed by Standard on 3.09 and 6.69 of queries, but also turns correct answers into incorrect ones on 2.09 and 3.57 , respectively. Thus, Agent execution is neither universally necessary nor uniformly beneficial. Its value depends on the query, motivating Adaptive Path Routing to estimate the expected benefit of Agent execution over the designated short path. O3: Non-Monotonic Operation Gains. Even when Agent execution is warranted, does acquiring more information necessarily improve the answer? We examine 917 matched comparisons between immediate FINISH and executing one additional operation before FINISH. As shown in Fig.~ fig:empirical (c), 84.51 of comparisons leave correctness unchanged, while the remaining operations can either improve or degrade answers. In particular, VISUAL operations degrade correctness more often than they improve it, suggesting that additional information may introduce noise rather than useful evidence. title: RynnWorld-Latent: A Cross-Embodiment World Model Conditioned on Universal Latent Actions
summary: Learning controllable world dynamics from heterogeneous interaction videos is challenging because robot embodiments use incompatible action spaces, while human videos lack native control labels. We present RynnWorld-Latent, a cross-embodiment video world model that uses the 3D-grounded latent actions introduced by RynnLAM as a shared conditioning interface. This representation enables joint pretraining on human interaction videos, robot demonstrations, and simulation rollouts without requiring a common native action space. Built on a pretrained video transformer, RynnWorld-Latent combines global action tokens with an identity-initialized local pathway that aligns actions with future video latents. We pretrain on 23 datasets comprising approximately 553.5M frames and adapt the model to target robots through post-training. The framework supports two data-generation routes: digital teleoperation uses target robot commands to generate action-video demonstrations, while latent-action synthesis transfers source motion to an edited initial frame and pairs the resulting rollout with retargeted pseudo robot actions. Experiments show improved video prediction metrics on public benchmarks and two real-robot platforms, alongside qualitative action following when different action sequences share the same initial observation. Synthetic mid-training improves policy success rates on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, and both generation routes improve real-world policy success rates over real-demonstration-only training in the evaluated settings. These results support universal latent actions as a scalable interface for learning controllable visual dynamics across heterogeneous embodiments.
full_text: Introduction World models, which predict future states conditioned on actions, have long been theorized as a cornerstone of generalist robot intelligence~ sutton1991dyna,lecun2022path,richens2025general . The recent progress of large-scale video generation has catalyzed a new class of video world models, in which future dynamics are represented directly in visual space~ zhao2026rynnworld,zhao2026rynnworldteleop,agarwal2025cosmos,ali2025world,zhao2026towards,zhao2026high,zhao2025physsplat . These models achieve impressive visual fidelity and provide a promising substrate for learning physical dynamics from large-scale video corpora. However, when applied to robotic manipulation, language-conditioned video generators face an interface mismatch: their primary control signal is a task-level description, while physical interaction is governed by continuous, frame-level causal interventions. Language describes semantic intentions at a coarse temporal granularity. An instruction such as ``pick up the cup'' specifies a task outcome, but does not determine the precise trajectory by which the outcome is achieved. In contact-rich manipulation, small differences in timing, contact order, gripper state, or camera motion can lead to substantially different futures. Without fine-grained motion or action conditioning, a text-conditioned model must represent multiple plausible trajectories for the same instruction, making precise control over manipulation dynamics challenging. Moreover, natural language alone is not a convenient interface for specifying temporally precise interventions, such as closing the gripper earlier while maintaining the same preceding motion. These limitations motivate an explicit action-conditioning interface for controllable video world modeling. A natural solution is to condition world models on robot actions~ gao2026dreamdojo . However, directly using raw robot actions introduces a severe alignment bottleneck. Different embodiments operate in heterogeneous kinematic spaces, with different joint counts, coordinate conventions, control frequencies, and hardware limits. As a result, a world model conditioned on raw actions is difficult to scale across platforms. At the same time, large-scale human videos contain abundant interaction dynamics without robot-specific control labels, while simulation actions need not match a target robot's control space. What is needed is not a stronger action encoder for a particular robot, but a shared action interface that represents interaction-related visual change while abstracting away platform-specific control conventions. We argue that latent actions provide such an interface. Instead of representing actions as robot commands, latent actions describe what changed between observations. Distilled from video in a self-supervised manner, continuous latent actions provide a shared description of visual transitions without requiring identical hardware control interfaces. Human hands, robot grippers, and simulated agents may differ drastically in their low-level control signals, yet their visual transitions can share motion and interaction patterns. By encoding heterogeneous videos into a shared latent-action representation, a single world model can be pretrained on human interactions, robot demonstrations, and simulation rollouts under a unified action-conditioning objective, without requiring their native control spaces to be aligned. In this work, we introduce , a cross-embodiment video world model built upon ~ zhao2026rynnvla , the 3D-grounded latent-action representation introduced in RynnVLA-Latent~ zhao2026rynnvla . While RynnVLA-Latent~ zhao2026rynnvla uses these descriptors as supervision targets for policy pretraining, our work investigates their complementary role as conditioning signals for learning controllable visual dynamics. predicts future video from an initial observation and a sequence of continuous latent actions, without requiring text conditioning or a common native robot action space. Technically, we combine global action tokens with an identity-initialized, frame-aligned local conditioning pathway within a pretrained video diffusion transformer. The local pathway exploits the temporal correspondence between latent-action extraction and video-latent compression, allowing each action descriptor to condition its corresponding future video latent. A central idea of this work is that should not be viewed only as a future predictor, but as a data-generation engine for scalable robot learning. This leads to two complementary generation modes. First, after target-robot post-training, can be conditioned on target robot actions and support interactive digital teleoperation~ zhao2026rynnworldteleop : operator control signals are mapped to target actions and drive video generation, producing paired action-video data without requiring additional physical robot execution. Second, the latent-action-conditioned model enables data synthesis from existing videos. Given a source video, we extract its latent-action sequence, edit the first frame to replace the embodiment or environment, and generate a new rollout conditioned on the edited first frame and the original latent actions. First-frame editing specifies the new visual embodiment or environment, while the latent-action sequence guides the interaction dynamics. The resulting rollout has motion close to the source video, but appears under a new embodiment or environment. These generated rollouts can be paired with retargeted pseudo robot actions for downstream VLA training. We evaluate from three complementary perspectives. First, we assess action-conditioned video prediction on public world-model benchmarks and held-out demonstrations from two real-robot platforms, measuring prediction fidelity after target-robot adaptation. Second, we investigate latent-action controllability through qualitative comparisons that vary the supplied latent-action sequences while holding the initial observation fixed, and illustrate cross-embodiment motion transfer through first-frame editing. Third, we examine the utility of world-model-generated data for downstream policy learning. Synthetic mid-training improves success rates on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, while both latent-action-driven synthesis and digital teleoperation improve observed closed-loop policy success on the evaluated real-world manipulation tasks. These evaluations jointly characterize prediction fidelity, qualitative action following, and downstream training utility. Our main contributions are as follows: We present , a text-free, latent-action-conditioned video world model, which uses frozen descriptors as a shared conditioning interface for learning visual dynamics from human interaction videos, heterogeneous robot demonstrations, and simulation rollouts without aligning their native control spaces. We design an action-conditioning mechanism that combines global action tokens with locally identity-initialized, frame-aligned injection, associating transition descriptors with the corresponding future video latents. We enable latent-action-guided generation under edited robot embodiments and environments, and adapt the world model to native robot-action conditioning. The resulting latent-action synthesis and digital-teleoperation pipelines generate data that improves downstream policy learning in the evaluated settings. Related Work sec:related_work World Models World models predict how environments change under actions and support planning and policy learning through simulated experience~ finn2016physical,ebert2018foresight,hafner2019planet,hafner2020dreamer . Advances in video generation have enabled large-scale pretraining of visual dynamics models and their adaptation to interactive simulation~ agarwal2025cosmos,yang2024unisim,wu2024ivideogpt,rigter2024avid,huang2025vid2world . Language-conditioned video and image generation have also been used to produce visual plans and synthetic demonstrations for robot control~ du2023unipi,zhou2024robodreamer,black2024susie,jang2025dreamgen . However, task-level instructions leave the timing and trajectory of individual movements largely unspecified. To simulate fine-grained manipulation, action-conditioned world models incorporate robot controls into future prediction~ zhu2025irasim,guo2026ctrlworld,wang2025hma . Such predictions support policy evaluation~ li2025worldeval,quevedo2026worldgym,wang2026iws and planning~ ebert2018foresight,zhou2025dinowm,assran2025vjepa2,kim2026cosmospolicy , while related approaches combine future prediction with action learning to improve robot policies~ wu2024gr1,cheang2024gr2,zhu2025uwm,ye2026dreamzero,sun2026vlajepa . Extending action-conditioned modeling across embodiments requires handling differences in action dimensions, coordinate conventions, and control semantics. Existing approaches address this through heterogeneous action modeling~ wang2025hma or geometric motion representations shared by humans and robots~ wu2026oscar,zhao2026rynnworldteleop . For pretraining on diverse robot and human videos, a further challenge is that many data sources lack corresponding control labels. More closely related to our setting, latent-action pretraining infers conditioning variables from observed transitions, allowing videos without native action labels to contribute to world-model learning~ gao2025adaworld,garrido2026wild,gao2026dreamdojo,liu2026clapworld . Building on this direction, uses continuous latent actions as a shared conditioning interface for cross-embodiment world-model pretraining, without requiring direct alignment of embodiment-specific control spaces. Latent Action Learning Learning across embodiments requires representations that connect different forms of observation and control. Prior work studies shared policies trained on heterogeneous robot data~ o2024open,octo2024octo,kim2024openvla,wang2024hpt and action-space alignment using recorded controls~ zheng2025uniact,zhang2025ate . For videos without corresponding robot actions, transferable skills and geometric motion cues provide intermediate representations for learning~ xu2023xskill,kim2025uniskill,wen2024atm,bharadhwaj2024track2act,collins2025amplify . Latent action learning instead infers compact action variables from transitions between observations~ rybkin2019clasp,schmidt2024lapo . These variables have been used as supervision for policy pretraining and transfer~ ye2025lapa,chen2025moto,bu2025univla,chen2025villax,li2025latbot,tharwat2025lawm , as well as conditioning inputs for predicting future states~ menapace2021playable,bruce2024genie,alles2025latentworld,bi2025motus,garrido2026wild . Both discrete codes~ bruce2024genie,ye2025lapa,chen2025moto and continuous representations~ gao2025adaworld,liang2026clam,yang2026como,garrido2026wild,gao2026dreamdojo have been explored. Recent work further studies alignment with available action supervision~ zhang2026claplatent,luo2026jala , the separation of motion from appearance~ yang2026como,xu2026motionfocused,zhang2026dila , and geometric constraints on the learned action space~ yang2026lawm3d . These distinctions matter because visual changes can include camera motion, background variation, and other effects unrelated to the agent's control~ nikulin2025laom,zhang2025lamanalysis,garrido2026wild . Building on these studies, we use a pretrained and frozen encoder ~ zhao2026rynnvla to extract 3D-grounded continuous latent-action descriptors from heterogeneous visual transitions. Unlike methods that require native control annotations or explicit motion retargeting during world-model pretraining, our approach uses these descriptors as a shared conditioning interface for human, robot, and simulation videos. title: TAPESTRY: A Single Backbone for Video Generation and Robot Control
comment: Accepted to Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL) 2026
summary: Pretrained video generation models encode rich priors about physical interactions, but leveraging them for robot control typically requires either resource-intensive video generation at test time or action heads trained from scratch that do not fully utilize the pretrained backbone. We introduce Tokenizing Actions as Video Patches in a Shared Transformer Policy (TAPESTRY), a world action model that repurposes a pretrained video diffusion transformer into a robotic policy without requiring video generation at inference. Our key idea is to treat robot actions as single-patch tokens in the video model's latent space. A lightweight linear projection maps each action timestep to the patch dimensions of the pretrained VAE, and the resulting tokens are processed by the same patchifying layers and transformer backbone used for video. The shared backbone is optimized through three diffusion objectives sampled per minibatch element: Video diffusion uses VAE latents from robot and human videos to establish dynamics priors. Joint video+action diffusion trains on robot demonstrations using a coupled diffusion timestep and an asymmetric attention mask. Action-only diffusion denoises actions conditioned on clean image latents. At test time, the model generates a compact action token sequence in a single DDIM step from pure noise, producing smooth action chunks at 84 ms per action chunk on consumer hardware and avoiding the cost of full video generation. Across simulation benchmarks and real-robot experiments, TAPESTRY achieves strong performance with substantially lower inference cost than comparable joint video--action policies. More information can be found at https://tapestry-wam.github.io.

Pretrained video generation models encode rich priors about physical interactions, but leveraging them for robot control typically requires either resource-intensive video generation at test time or action heads trained from scratch that do not fully utilize the pretrained backbone. We introduce Tokenizing Actions as Video Patches in a Shared Transformer Policy (TAPESTRY), a world action model that repurposes a pretrained video diffusion transformer into a robotic policy without requiring video generation at inference. The shared backbone is optimized through three diffusion objectives sampled per minibatch element: Video diffusion uses VAE latents from robot and human videos to establish dynamics priors. Joint video+action diffusion trains on robot demonstrations using a coupled diffusion timestep and an asymmetric attention mask. Action-only diffusion denoises actions conditioned on clean image latents. At test time, the model generates a compact action token sequence in a single DDIM step from pure noise, producing smooth action chunks at \,ms per action chunk on consumer hardware and avoiding the cost of full video generation. Across simulation benchmarks and real-robot experiments, TAPESTRY achieves strong performance with substantially lower inference cost than comparable joint video--action policies. More information can be found at tapestry-wam.github.io . Introduction Video generation models have emerged as an effective method of distilling internet-scale knowledge about physical interactions into robotic policies. Trained on up to millions of hours of human and real-world video, these models learn rich priors over how the visual world evolves in response to actions, priors difficult to acquire from the limited robot demonstration datasets available today. The central question for robot learning is: how can we best transfer these priors to learn policies that generalize across tasks, environments, and embodiments? Existing approaches span a spectrum of coupling between the video model and the robotic policy, each with characteristic tradeoffs. At one end, methods such as UniPi~ du2023learning and DreamGen~ jang2025dreamgen use a video generation model to synthesize visual rollouts and then extract actions via a separately trained inverse dynamics model. This pipeline leaves the video model architecturally unmodified but compounds errors across two generative stages and requires expensive frame generation at test time, limiting real-time deployment. A lighter-weight alternative, exemplified by Video Prediction Policy~ hu2024video and mimic-video~ zhong2025mimicvideo , extracts intermediate latent representations from a pretrained video backbone and conditions a downstream action head on these features. This avoids full video generation but limits knowledge transfer, since the action head is trained from scratch and cannot directly access the backbone's pretrained weights. The most tightly coupled approaches share a single backbone across video and action diffusion. These include prior work UWM~ zhu2025unified , UVA~ li2025unified , and concurrent works Cosmos Policy~ kim2026cosmospolicyfinetuningvideo , DreamZero~ ye2026dreamzero , Fast-WAM~ yuan2026fastwamworldactionmodels , and GigaWorld-Policy~ ni2026gigaworld . These methods achieve the deepest integration, but each either trains from scratch without a pretrained video prior, pays a heavy inference-time token cost, or predicts actions with a separate module trained from scratch. Our insight stems from a simple observation: the dynamics priors useful for action prediction reside in the weights of the video backbone, not in the generated pixels. Although generating full video sequences is one way to access these priors, we identify that it is unnecessary if the end goal is fast, closed-loop action prediction. Specifically, by representing action tokens as patchified video tokens aligned with video pretraining, robot actions inherit the backbone's dynamics priors without the overhead of pixel-space generation, reducing online inference cost. We apply this idea in , a method that re-purposes a pretrained video diffusion transformer into an action-generating policy. The key mechanism is treating each action timestep as a single patch in the video VAE latent space: a lightweight linear projection maps the raw action vector to the VAE's patch dimensions, an affine-free layer normalization matches the per-token mean and variance of the VAE latents, and the resulting pseudo-patch is fed through the same patchifying convolution that the backbone uses for video tokenization. The backbone is then jointly fine-tuned on three diffusion objectives sampled per minibatch element: standard video diffusion on VAE latents from a large mixture of robot and human videos, joint video action diffusion on paired robot demonstrations, and action-only diffusion that denoises actions conditioned on clean image latents. At test time, only the action pathway is used: the model denoises a compact sequence of action tokens conditioned on the current observation and a language instruction, in a single DDIM step from pure noise. This produces smooth action chunks at \,ms per chunk on a single RTX~5090, faster than an optimized DreamZero~ ye2026dreamzero on the same GPU ( sec:efficiency ). We validate the approach on a challenging action-free variant of the LIBERO benchmark and on a real-world bimanual manipulator, demonstrating generalization to novel objects, novel motion primitives, and composed multi-step behaviors. Our key contributions are as follows: Action-as-VAE-patch tokenization. We design an action tokenizer that reuses the video VAE patchifying convolution and matches the per-token mean and variance of its latents, adding only parameters so the same DiT weights act on robot actions and video natively. Three-objective joint training with a shared backbone. A single pretrained video diffusion backbone is co-trained on video diffusion, joint video+action diffusion, and action-only diffusion. The joint branch uses an asymmetric attention mask and a coupled diffusion timestep across modalities. Single-step inference. Under our diffusion schedule, a single DDIM step from pure noise reduces inference to one forward pass on a short action token sequence, producing smooth, jerk-free action chunks. We analyze why this eliminates the high-frequency noise in world action models. Real-world bimanual deployment. We evaluate on a real bimanual manipulator, showing generalization to novel objects, novel motion primitives, and composed multi-step tasks. Method Problem Setup sec:setup We assume access to two types of data: a video dataset and a robot-interaction dataset , where is a clip of pixel video, is the RGB observation frame at the start of , is a language goal, and is an action chunk of length over a -dimensional action space. Our aim is to learn a visual control policy that, at deployment, maps the current observation and language goal to an action chunk, without producing video. The policy is implemented as a single diffusion backbone trained jointly on via video denoising and on via joint or action-only denoising (Sec.~ sec:three_objectives ), and deployed as a single denoising step on action tokens (Sec.~ sec:single_step ). Background and Preliminaries sec:background We build on a pretrained video diffusion transformer (DiT) for text-conditioned video generation. A frozen 3D-VAE encodes a pixel video into a latent tensor with temporal stride and spatial stride from pixel to latent dimensions, and channel count . Here counts latent frames and are the spatial dimensions of each latent frame. A 2D patchifying convolution with patch size maps each spatial patch of each latent frame to a token of hidden dimension , yielding a video token sequence with sequence length . The current observation frame is encoded by replicating it along the temporal axis, passing the result through the VAE, and patchifying with to produce observation image tokens , which together with the frozen T5-XXL~ t5 text token sequence form a clean conditioning prefix that is never noised. The DiT, denoted , is trained with the DDPM~ ho2020denoising -prediction~ salimans2022progressive objective and sampled at inference with DDIM~ song2020denoising . Diffusion timesteps are where is the final diffusion timestep, and the noise schedule has zero terminal SNR ( ): the fully-noised state for carries no information about , a property we exploit at inference ( sec:hf-investigation ). Throughout, we denote a clean token sequence by subscript and its noised version at timestep by subscript . Action Tokenization sec:action_tokenization The video patchifying convolution was pretrained on KL-regularized VAE patches that approximately follow statistics, and projecting raw action vectors directly into the DiT hidden space produces tokens far outside that distribution. In practice, a direct linear projection that bypasses exhibits instability early into training, and standard remediations (gradient clipping, NaN-skipping, normalization) delay but do not eliminate the divergence. Routing actions through removes it and lets the same DiT weights act on action and video tokens alike. We treat each action timestep as a single VAE patch, reusing as much of the pretrained tokenization pipeline as possible. The closest analogue in the literature is Cosmos Policy~ kim2026cosmospolicyfinetuningvideo , which expresses each action chunk as 112 redundant copies tiled into the existing video latent grid. We contrast its inference cost with ours in sec:efficiency . Concretely, we map each per-step action vector into a DiT token via a linear projection , an affine-free LayerNorm, and the backbone's shared patchifying convolution : The affine-free LayerNorm matches only the per-token mean and variance of the approximately unit-normal KL-regularized VAE latents that was pretrained on, and sharing rather than introducing a fresh action projection means action tokens and video tokens enter the DiT through the same learned linear map. The procedure yields one DiT token per action timestep, so the full action sequence has length , which is typically a much shorter sequence length than the spatial tokens per latent timestep required for video patch tokens. Action tokens receive the backbone's fixed 3D sinusoidal positional encodings with temporal indices on a spatial grid; in the joint mode, video and action tokens are each indexed from and then concatenated. After the DiT forward, the backbone's pretrained patch unembedding and the tied transpose of map each denoised action token back to action space: . The readout reuses and and adds no parameters. title: Trace-WAM: Learning to Act via 3D Motion Prediction for World Action Models
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) learn representations for robot control by coupling future visual prediction with action generation. Successful manipulation depends primarily on how the robot and task-relevant objects evolve, whereas future-video prediction must also reconstruct the appearance and background of the entire scene. We therefore propose Trace-WAM, which augments video-action learning with future 3D motion prediction as an auxiliary objective. This objective supervises temporal point correspondence together with image-plane displacement and depth change, directly describing the interaction dynamics and spatial changes involved in manipulation. To this end, we adopt a three-branch Mixture-of-Transformer (Tri-MoT) architecture to jointly learn video prediction, motion prediction, and action generation. The motion expert predicts future trajectories from current visual features, allowing motion supervision to shape the representations used for action generation. Because the action expert does not consume predicted trajectories, inference retains the current-observation policy path: a single visual forward pass followed by action denoising. Experiments on RoboCasa-GR1, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus demonstrate strong in-distribution performance and out-of-distribution generalization, with particularly clear gains over Fast-WAM under limited demonstrations and distribution shifts.
full_text: World Action Models (WAMs) learn representations for robot control by coupling future visual prediction with action generation. Successful manipulation depends primarily on how the robot and task-relevant objects evolve, whereas future-video prediction must also reconstruct the appearance and background of the entire scene. We therefore propose Trace-WAM, which augments video-action learning with future 3D motion prediction as an auxiliary objective. This objective supervises temporal point correspondence together with image-plane displacement and depth change, directly describing the interaction dynamics and spatial changes involved in manipulation. To this end, we adopt a three-branch Mixture-of-Transformer (Tri-MoT) architecture to jointly learn video prediction, motion prediction, and action generation. The motion expert predicts future trajectories from current visual features, allowing motion supervision to shape the representations used for action generation. Because the action expert does not consume predicted trajectories, inference retains the current-observation policy path: a single visual forward pass followed by action denoising. Experiments on RoboCasa-GR1, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus demonstrate strong in-distribution performance and out-of-distribution generalization, with particularly clear gains over Fast-WAM under limited demonstrations and distribution shifts. Introduction sec:intro Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models~ kim2024openvla,pertsch2025fast,intelligence2025pi_ adapt pretrained vision-language representations to robot control, learning to generate actions from visual observations and language instructions. Despite their strong policy-learning capabilities, most VLAs focus on action prediction without explicitly modeling how the scene evolves during execution. World Action Models (WAMs) incorporate this future evolution into policy learning by combining future visual prediction with action generation~ guo2026unified,yuan2026fast . Built on pretrained video models, WAMs transfer rich spatiotemporal priors to robot manipulation by learning from future observations together with action sequences. Yet successful manipulation depends primarily on how the robot and task-relevant objects change over time, whereas future RGB prediction must also model texture, illumination, and background appearance across the entire scene. This difference motivates a complementary target that emphasizes interaction dynamics while retaining the rich visual context learned from future RGB. Recent approaches enrich policy representations by augmenting visual prediction with auxiliary supervision for geometry, semantics, and interaction structure. These objectives include depth and geometric prediction, semantic feature learning, and supervision of affordances and goal regions~ guo2026unified,ma2026geosem,yuan2026dreamwam,zhang2026deva,zheng2026gift,li2026wam4d , encouraging representations to capture spatial layout and task-relevant interaction constraints. A per-frame or region-level target, however, does not by itself identify how the same physical locations evolve throughout an interaction, a distinction also emphasized by 4D-WAM~ yang20264d . This temporal correspondence connects the current scene to the sequence of changes required to complete a manipulation task. We therefore focus on 3D motion as an auxiliary prediction target for WAM representation learning, motivated by two complementary properties. First, each trajectory connects a point in the current observation to its positions at successive future steps, revealing the coordinated motion of the robot and task-relevant objects ( (a)). Second, depth change complements image-plane displacement by describing motion toward or away from the camera. In our annotation census, among point tracks moving by at least 2 of the image diagonal over 32 steps, 79.3 in LIBERO and 32.9 in Piper exhibit depth changes of at least 5 of their initial depth ( (a)). Depth variation therefore accompanies a substantial fraction of visible motion in both simulation and real-world annotations. Its value for policy learning is supported by our depth ablation: retaining the depth component improves LIBERO-Plus success from 82.4 to 84.5 ( (b)). These properties describe the temporal and spatial changes involved in manipulation. Based on this formulation, we propose Trace-WAM, which jointly learns future video prediction, future 3D motion prediction, and action generation. We represent motion using trajectories anchored to a fixed grid in the current image, combining image-plane displacement with depth change relative to each point's initial position. Whereas 4D-WAM~ yang20264d transfers trajectory knowledge by aligning temporal feature changes and source-to-destination relations with those of a pretrained 4D tracking model, Trace-WAM directly predicts motion trajectories under an auxiliary objective. This objective adds explicit supervision for subsequent robot and object motion to video-action representation learning. Concretely, Trace-WAM uses video, motion, and action experts with a structured attention mask ( ). During training, the video, motion, and action objectives jointly optimize the model, using future 3D motion as an additional learning signal for the representations used in action generation. At inference, we retain the Fast-WAM~ yuan2026fast policy path: the video backbone processes current RGB observations once, and the action expert denoises an action chunk using cached visual features, language, and proprioception. As summarized in (a), Trace-WAM requires no future-video or motion prediction at inference. We evaluate Trace-WAM on RoboCasa-GR1, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus, covering both in-distribution control and out-of-distribution generalization. Trace-WAM achieves strong performance across these settings, with particularly clear gains over Fast-WAM when demonstrations are limited and under distribution shifts ( (b)). Experiments on a real robot further show higher success rates across three physical manipulation tasks. These results support 3D motion prediction as an effective auxiliary objective for WAM policy learning. Our contributions are: [leftmargin=*,itemsep=1pt,topsep=2pt] We introduce Trace-WAM, which jointly learns future video prediction, future 3D motion prediction, and action generation within a three-branch architecture. Future 3D motion provides auxiliary supervision for video-action representation learning without requiring future video or motion prediction at inference. Experiments on three manipulation benchmarks demonstrate strong in-distribution performance and out-of-distribution generalization, while real-world evaluations show consistent gains across three physical tasks. Related Work sec:related World Action Models Early approaches formulate manipulation as visual planning, using generative models to propose future observations and learned controllers to translate the resulting visual plans into executable actions~ du2023learning,black2024zero . More recent World Action Models integrate video priors more directly into policy learning, either conditioning actions on predictive video features~ hu2024video,liao2026genie or jointly modeling future visual observations and action sequences~ ma2026dit4dit,yan2026robust,li2026causal,bi2026motus,kim2026cosmos,ye2026world,team2026motubrain . Beyond RGB prediction, recent methods extend predictive supervision to semantic features, depth and 3D geometry, and motion, encouraging policy representations to capture object identity, spatial layout, and scene dynamics~ yuan2026dreamwam,ma2026geosem,yan2026robust,wang2026st,li2026egowam,yan2608flex . Complementary supervision of affordances, object-centric interaction configurations, and goal regions emphasizes which scene elements are involved in the task and where the robot should interact~ zhang2026deva,zheng2026gift . Trace-WAM follows this direction by using auxiliary future 3D motion prediction to supervise temporal point correspondence and depth change jointly with future RGB prediction and action generation. Motion for Policy Learning Motion representations connect action generation to the spatial and temporal structure of manipulation by describing how the robot and objects move throughout an interaction. Incorporating depth further captures displacement along the viewing direction, complementing image-plane motion with spatial information needed for reaching, grasping, and object transport. Existing approaches couple action learning with optical flow or 2D point-motion prediction, using motion features or predicted motion to guide control~ chen2026flowwam,yang2026mt,wang2026mowam , while others incorporate depth and 3D motion to model spatial scene dynamics for action generation~ zhao2026rynnworld,wang2026lamp,lee2026mu_0 . A complementary line of work uses motion supervision to improve policy representations, through distillation from pretrained tracking models~ wang2026track4action,yang20264d or auxiliary 3D motion prediction during human--robot co-training~ li2026egowam . Trace-WAM directly predicts future 3D point trajectories alongside RGB prediction and action generation, using numerical motion targets rather than tracker-feature alignment. The motion objective shapes video-action representations during training; deployed actions use current visual context, language, and proprioception without future-video or motion prediction. Method sec:method Trace-WAM jointly learns future video prediction, future 3D motion prediction, and action generation. Future 3D motion provides auxiliary supervision for video-action representation learning, while the deployed policy generates actions from current observations. summarizes the Tri-MoT architecture and its attention masks. Problem Formulation sec:formulation We consider language-conditioned robot manipulation. At each decision step, the policy receives current RGB observations , a language instruction , and the robot's proprioceptive state . It generates an action chunk where is the action horizon and is the action dimension. The robot executes the first few actions before receiving a new observation and replanning. We follow Fast-WAM~ yuan2026fast in training the policy with future video prediction while generating actions from current observations. Trace-WAM adds future 3D motion prediction as an auxiliary objective. Future RGB and motion labels are used only during training. 3D Motion Representation sec:trajectory Motion Targets. Following the grid-based motion representation of LaMP~ wang2026lamp , we place anchors on a uniform grid covering the current main-camera image and associate each anchor with its positions over future steps. Our reference configuration uses a grid ( ) and , giving 33 positions per anchor when the current frame is included. Anchors follow a fixed row-major order. Although the policy can receive multiple camera views, the motion grid is defined only in the main-camera image. For anchor at step , let contain image coordinates normalized to and depth, measured in meters for simulator annotations and in an aligned relative scene scale for TraceForge annotations. Motion is displacement relative to its current-image position: where . The resulting target combines image-plane displacement with depth change. Every displacement is measured from the current position, rather than accumulated from adjacent frames. All trajectories are expressed in a unified reference-camera frame before conversion to , compensating for camera motion. This screen-aligned representation retains the spatial information provided by depth without depending on a particular robot embodiment, while its coordinates remain compatible with 2D trajectory formats. title: When Black-Box Robot Policies Fail: Online Sensor Diagnosis and Repair with a Transparent Surrogate
comment: Accepted at the Conference on Robot Learning 2026 Workshop on the Science of Physical AI Safety (SPAIS)
summary: Robot foundation models may generalize across tasks and embodiments, but their actions still depend on sensors that can fail. When the policy is frozen or inaccessible, can an external monitor diagnose and repair corrupted inputs without access to its internals? We test a structured surrogate that separates periodic gait from sensor-dependent corrections to guide input repair around a frozen locomotion policy. On simulated Go2, offline diagnosis raises walking success from 259/640 to 429/640 episodes; online repair reaches 382/640, with no triggers in 64 held-out fault-free episodes. A matched boosted-tree surrogate predicts clean actions similarly well but yields no detected repair improvement over no repair. Separate fits improve walking on Go1 and ANYmal C, although phase-aware gradients perform better. Evidence remains limited to one policy and a partly screened simulated fault suite; robot foundation model and hardware validation remain open.
