title: Evaluation-Guided Demonstration Refinement for Vision-Language-Action Policies: The Winning Entry in the MetaFine Open Competition
comment: 1st place in the MetaFine Open Competition, RoboFineMani Workshop @ CoRL 2026
summary: We fine-tuned a separate $π_{0.5}$ policy for each of the five tasks in the MetaFine Open Competition, with a task-specific training mixture and number of actions executed per prediction. Training started from the official demonstrations and expert procedures. Local evaluation exposed recurring grasping, pushing, and insertion failures. We addressed them by revising the demonstrated motions and by adding expert continuations from states the policy reached, while keeping nominal demonstrations in training. Checkpoints were compared on every instruction, so that a gain on one instruction could not hide a loss on another. Our submission, MAI, ranked first overall with a score of 96.66.
full_text: We fine-tuned a separate policy for each of the five tasks in the MetaFine Open Competition, with a task-specific training mixture and number of actions executed per prediction. Training started from the official demonstrations and expert procedures. Local evaluation exposed recurring grasping, pushing, and insertion failures. We addressed them by revising the demonstrated motions and by adding expert continuations from states the policy reached, while keeping nominal demonstrations in training. Checkpoints were compared on every instruction, so that a gain on one instruction could not hide a loss on another. Our submission, MAI, ranked first overall with a score of 96.66. Introduction MetaFine~ xu2026beyond evaluates fine-grained manipulation through instruction understanding, perceptual robustness, and behavior. The MetaFine Open Competition~ metafinechallenge covers five tabletop tasks: bottle-part grasping (T1), mug grasp-and-move (T2), switch toggling (T3), block sorting (T4), and letter insertion (T5). Understanding measures success across instructions; perception averages normalized areas under camera and lighting degradation curves; behavior measures task success, or normalized stage completion for the multi-stage T2 and T4. Each task receives a composite score . We fine-tuned one ~ intelligence2025pi_ policy for each task. We used MetaFine's per-instruction scores, together with our own grouping of episodes by scene layout, to choose which trajectories to inspect, and revised the demonstrations where those trajectories showed recurring errors. The submitted policies scored 96.66 overall and ranked first on the final leaderboard. Technical Approach sec:approach Policy and training setup We fine-tuned all parameters of using OpenPI~ openpi and the flow-matching behavior-cloning objective~ black2024pi_0,Lipman_2022_221002747 . The inputs are the instruction, seven arm and two finger joint positions, and RGB images from the base and wrist cameras. Each predicted action contains seven joint deltas and a gripper command. The policy generates a chunk of 50 actions using ten denoising steps, then executes the first 20 actions for T1, 30 for T3, or 10 for T2/T4/T5 before replanning. We trained with AdamW~ Loshchilov_2017_171105101 , learning-rate warmup, and cosine decay. In the final training rounds, T2 started from the base model and each other task from its previous policy. Checkpoints were selected by local evaluation (Section~ sec:results ). Refining the official demonstrations Training used the official demonstrations and trajectories generated by the official expert procedures. We ran these procedures on additional scenes and revised them in response to the failures found during development. Only successful demonstrations with consistent recorded observations and actions entered training. Where demonstrations contained unnecessary pauses or repeated approaches, as in T1 and T5, we shortened or replanned them. Variation in object pose and task geometry was kept, as were the motions needed to finish the task. Some failed rollouts reached states that nominal demonstrations rarely cover. From such states the expert recorded continuations, following the rationale of dataset aggregation~ ross2011reduction . We also built recovery demonstrations from constructed failure configurations, such as a grasp on the wrong bottle part in T1, and excluded the actions used to set up these configurations from training. Expert procedures could use simulator state; deployed policies received only images, joint positions, and language. When continuations or recovery demonstrations were used, task-specific source quotas kept nominal demonstrations in every training batch. Training for each task Table~ tab:tasks summarizes the observed behavior, training approach, and evaluation checks for each task. T1: grasping the instructed bottle part. Local rollouts showed slips as lifting began. We adjusted the trajectories for both the cap and body instructions, shortening hesitation and beginning a gradual lift during closure. Nominal demonstrations, expert continuations, and recovery demonstrations remained in training. We evaluated the two instructions separately because earlier variants had improved body success at the expense of cap success. T2: mug grasp-and-move. Batches balanced official demonstrations with trajectories generated by the official expert on additional scenes, with equal coverage of the three motion directions. We kept this recipe for the final submission after checking nominal and perturbed conditions. T3: switch toggling. Local failures included missed contact and incomplete toggles at difficult approach angles. We revised the approach and extended the push through the toggle, with recovery demonstrations for failed contact. Later training added approaches that pass above the switch center, alongside the earlier demonstration sources. T4: block sorting. In crowded layouts, the gripper sometimes closed without the target block. We adjusted the expert approach to leave clearance from neighboring blocks and recorded expert continuations from these empty-grasp states. Training mixed these trajectories with the official and earlier expert demonstrations. T5: letter insertion. Earlier rounds replaced the T5 demonstrations with continuous planned trajectories that use one consistent grasp per letter. The remaining failures on o involved lateral offsets and release before seating. We revised the o trajectories to align the letter above the opening and seat it fully before release. The revised o demonstrations included trajectories with varied in-hand offsets, expert continuations from policy rollouts, and recoveries from a letter resting on the board. They replaced the earlier o demonstrations; C/R/L demonstrations were unchanged. Competition Results sec:results Official evaluation Our submission scored 96.66 overall and ranked first on the organizers' final leaderboard; the second- and third-place scores were 94.71 and 91.37~ metafineleaderboard . Table~ tab:official lists the scores for each task. T1 had the lowest score, and overall perception ( ) was lower than understanding ( ). Local development comparisons Local evaluation used the competition's task predicates, action interface, and scoring~ metafinechallenge . Table~ tab:local reports local scores for the submitted policies, with reference comparisons for T1 and T3--T5. Each task used its own evaluation suite; we do not average the local scores across tasks. T1 improved on both instructions, with a larger gain in cap success. On 80 scenes, rose from 88.95 to 93.39. Cap success increased from 88.96 to 97.71, while body success rose from 88.96 to 90.21 and remained the weaker instruction. The scene-clustered 95 interval for the difference in was points. T2 succeeded in all 60 nominal instruction cases; the 480-episode sweep contained two failures, both under visual perturbations of the forward instruction. Under the standard scoring scope (Table~ tab:local ), was 100.00; extending to all three directions gave . The earlier T3 revisions produced large gains, but the final revision did not establish a further improvement. Across two rounds, on the 80-scene development suite rose from 74.9 to 91.6 and then 99.2. That policy is the reference in Table~ tab:local . We compared it with the selected policy on 120 scenes: the development suite, a 20-scene reserve set used to compare checkpoints, and 20 further scenes. With four inference seeds per model, the selected policy scored just 0.24 points higher (computed before rounding). The 95 scene-bootstrap interval, , includes zero, leaving the difference uncertain. T4's clearest gain was in crowded layouts: successes increased from 313/348 to 348/348 on 116 scenes, eliminating the 35 failures observed with the reference. Both policies already had near-ceiling standard-suite (Table~ tab:local ). The selected policy also succeeded in all 720 nominal instruction episodes of the standard 80-scene suite and failed only once in 4,452 episodes on a separate 1,484-scene set. The larger-set result is reported without a reference comparison. T5 improved chiefly on o, the letter targeted by the final revisions. Success on o rose from 82.5 to 97.5 on the development set and from 87.5 to 97.5 on the separate set; also increased on both. The overall gains came with a small regression on C: development-set success fell from 100 to 98.75, despite its demonstrations being unchanged. Lessons Learned and Discussion sec:lessons Per-instruction scores and scene grouping revealed failures hidden by the task score. MetaFine's separate instruction scores distinguished cap from body in T1 and isolated the letter o in T5. In T4 the task score was already high, and our own grouping of episodes by layout showed that the remaining failures concentrated near neighboring blocks. Inspecting the few steps around contact helped distinguish failures that scores alone could not explain. In T1, T3, and T5, we observed a grasp that closed and then slipped, a push that stopped short, and a letter released above the slot, respectively. In response, we revised those segments of the demonstrations: a gradual lift during closure for T1, a longer push for T3, and full seating before release for T5. Targeted revisions could introduce regressions on other instructions or scenes. A T3 variant trained without the earlier sources regressed on the reserve set and was rejected, so the final mixture kept them. Keeping an instruction's demonstrations did not always preserve its performance: earlier T1 variants improved body grasping but lost cap success, and the selected T5 policy declined slightly on C. We therefore checked individual instructions when selecting checkpoints, even when the task score improved. Repeated model selection and combined training changes limit what the local comparisons establish. The local sets served both to guide revisions and to select checkpoints, so their scores describe development performance and the reported intervals do not account for that selection. Official T1 and T5 scores were below their local values, while T2--T4 were within half a point; because the official and local suites use different scenes, these gaps do not identify a cause. Training rounds also combined demonstration and sampling changes, so the local comparisons do not isolate the effect of either. Acknowledgments. We thank the MetaFine authors and organizers for the benchmark and competition resources, and the OpenPI contributors for their code.

title: Tokens of Motion: Primitive Motion Learning for Human-Humanoid Skill Transfer
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models provide a promising paradigm for scalable robotic manipulation, yet their reliance on success-only behavioral cloning leaves them brittle; lacking corrective training signals, minor execution errors rapidly compound into unrecoverable, out-of-distribution failures. To address this limitation, we propose Adaptive Failure-Informed Learning (AFIL), an end-to-end framework that leverages failure trajectories as adaptive negative guidance for diffusion- and flow-based VLA policies. AFIL uses a pretrained VLA to generate failure rollouts online, avoiding the need for handcrafted failure-mode design or human-in-the-loop recovery. It then jointly trains Dual Action Generators (DAGs) for successful and failed behaviors while sharing a common vision-language backbone, enabling efficient failure-aware policy learning with limited parameter overhead. During sampling, the failure generator adaptively steers action generation away from failure-prone regions and toward more reliable success modes, with guidance strength determined by the per-diffusion-step distance between success and failure distributions. Experiments across in-domain and out-of-domain robotic manipulation tasks, covering both short- and long-horizon settings, show that AFIL consistently improves task success rates and robustness over existing VLA baselines, demonstrating its effectiveness, efficiency, and generality.
full_text: 0 Human videos provide a scalable source of manipulation experience, yet transferring them to robots remains challenging because human demonstrations lack robot-compatible actions and differ substantially from robots in embodiment and kinematics. We propose Motion Primitives for Action Composition and Transfer (M-PACT), a framework that addresses this challenge by factorizing primitive motion learning from embodiment-specific motion realization. This separation allows us to learn generalizable and reusable motion primitives from large-scale 3D human hand-pose trajectories, while requiring only limited embodiment-specific robot data to ground these primitives into executable motions. Specifically, we first discover local motion segments from human hand trajectories and learn a compact primitive-motion representation that captures recurring manipulation patterns independently of robot embodiment. Given task and observation context, these primitives are then selected and composed, while a lightweight embodiment-specific decoder maps them to robot motions. Crucially, transferring to a new embodiment preserves the learned primitive representation and requires adapting only the realization model, substantially reducing the dependence on costly robot demonstrations. Experiments across EgoDex, HoloAssist, and HumanoidEveryday demonstrate cross-dataset and cross-embodiment transferability of proposed M-PACT, with lightweight decoder adaptation achieving strong humanoid motion reconstruction using as few as 100 robot demonstrations. These results establish factorized primitive learning as a scalable bridge from large-scale human motion data to humanoid manipulation. Introduction Developing robots capable of diverse manipulation in unstructured environments remains a central goal in robotics and artificial intelligence. Most manipulation policies are learned from robot-centric experience, including demonstrations collected through teleoperation or kinesthetic teaching and interactions acquired through reinforcement learning or autonomous exploration. Although such data provide directly executable actions, collecting them at sufficient scale and diversity remains costly and difficult across tasks, environments, and embodiments rt12022arxiv,o2024open . Human videos offer a compelling alternative: they are abundant and capture diverse object interactions, behavioral strategies, and long-horizon activities in natural settings Ego4D2022CVPR . They can therefore complement limited robot demonstrations and broaden the task and behavioral coverage of robot learning systems kareer2025egomimic . However, human demonstrations lack robot-compatible action supervision, while human and robot effectors differ substantially in morphology, kinematics, appearance, and feasible action spaces kareer2025egomimic,chen2025vidbot . Directly imitating human trajectories can consequently produce ambiguous or kinematically infeasible robot actions. Bridging this embodiment gap requires representations that abstract away embodiment-specific execution while preserving transferable motion structure, for effective and generalizable robot control. Vision-language-action (VLA) models pertsch2025fast,black2024pi_0,intelligence2025pi,liu2025rdtb,rt22023arxiv offer a promising framework for general-purpose manipulation by mapping visual observations and language instructions directly to robot actions. Recent models such as ~ wei2026psi0 , H-RDT~ bi2026hrdt , and Being-H0~ beingbeyond2025beingh0 further pretrain on large-scale egocentric human videos before adapting to specific robot embodiments, demonstrating the potential of human data to broaden behavioral coverage. However, two limitations remain. First, human videos lack robot-executable actions, so converting them into control supervision still requires costly robot demonstrations or computationally intensive human-motion estimation. Second, existing pretraining paradigms often couple human motion with scene appearance and context rather than explicitly isolating transferable motion structure, limiting generalization across scenes, tasks, and embodiments. Existing human-to-robot skill transfer approaches primarily bridge the embodiment gap by geometric alignment of human hand and robot trajectories kareer2025egomimic,chen2025vidbot,shi2025zeromimic,haldar2025pointpolicy,zhou2026traj2action,okami2024 , visual transformation of human demonstrations into robot-centric observations li2025h2r,lepert2025phantomtrainingrobots,chen2026anyworld , or reconstructing hand-object interactions and retargeting to dexterous robot hands wang2024dexcap,mu2026deximit,singh2024hoi_pretraining,chen2026dexterous,paliwal2026doasido,ObjRetarget2026 . However, hand-object manipulation is inherently compositional and behaviorally multimodal: a single task may comprise heterogeneous motions such as grasping, lifting, placing, , each admitting multiple valid executions. Representing such a skill as a monolithic, full-trajectory supervision signal requires an imitation-learning policy to model long and highly variable motion sequences while simultaneously resolving human-robot embodiment differences, making learning difficult and limiting the reuse of shared behaviors across tasks. Recent approaches have begun to introduce temporal hierarchy, however, these methods generally transfer human behavior through complete trajectories singh2024hoi_pretraining,chen2025vidbot , coarse semantic subtasks mu2026deximit,shi2025zeromimic , fixed-horizon trajectory and action predictions haldar2025pointpolicy,zhou2026traj2action . Consequently, recurring local motion patterns can remain coupled to task-level ordering and global scene context, limiting their systematic recomposition and transfer across novel tasks and environments. To this end, we propose to learn Motion Primitives for Action Composition and Transfer (M-PACT), a framework that learns localized primitive motions from human videos by factorizing transferable interaction structure from scene- and embodiment-specific realizations. This factorization allows individual primitives to be transferred across embodiments and compositionally reused across tasks and environments. At its core, a self-supervised motion segmentation module, SkillSeg, partitions 3D human hand trajectories using frame-level kinematic cues, and maps the resulting segments into an embodiment-agnostic vocabulary of primitive-motion tokens, by Embodied Primitive Motion Tokenization (EPMT) module. Learned from web-scale egocentric video corpora, EPMT transforms abundant, behaviorally diverse, and cost-effective human pose trajectories into reusable manipulation primitives. We then condition these primitive representations on contextual features from visual foundation models and perform lightweight fine-tuning using labeled video-motion-action data, enabling M-PACT to select, compose, and realize primitives for diverse manipulation tasks. By separating reusable motion structure from task-specific context and robot-specific control, our approach substantially reduces the need for costly robot demonstrations while improving generalization across tasks and scenes. In summary, our contributions are threefold: [leftmargin=10pt] We propose to learn a motion tokenizer, EPMT that discovers localized, embodiment-agnostic primitive motions from human hand trajectories. Trained on low-cost, web-scale hand-pose data extracted from egocentric videos, EPMT learns primitive tokens that can be reused for skill transfer across embodiments. We introduce M-PACT, a multi-stage transfer framework that integrates EPMT with context-aware visual representations to select and compose primitive tokens and ground them into embodiment-specific, robot-executable actions. This design supports manipulation tasks of varying horizons with lightweight fine-tuning on labeled video-motion-action data. We evaluate motion reconstruction, cross-dataset representation reuse, humanoid decoder adaptation, and contextual primitive prediction across three datasets, complemented by qualitative real-world humanoid demonstrations. Related Work Manipulation from Human Demonstrations. Human demonstrations offer a scalable source of manipulation experience, motivating approaches based on shared representations, geometric alignment, and motion retargeting. EgoMimic jointly trains policies from aligned egocentric human and robot data, while Point Policy predicts keypoint trajectories that are converted into robot actions through geometric constraints kareer2025egomimic,haldar2025pointpolicy . For dexterous manipulation, DexCap transfers captured hand motions through inverse kinematics and imitation learning, whereas DexImit reconstructs hand--object interactions and synthesizes robot demonstrations through subtask decomposition and trajectory generation wang2024dexcap,mu2026deximit . In contrast, we first learn a compact vocabulary of local hand-motion primitives, then separately model contextual selection and embodiment-specific decoding, disentangling reusable motion structure from task context and robot execution. Abstraction and Reusable Skill Discovery. Temporal abstraction organizes demonstrations into reusable behavioral units. CompILE jointly discovers segment boundaries and latent behaviors, while Play-LMP and SPiRL learn latent plans or skill priors from unstructured experience kipf2019compile,lynch2020learning,pertsch2021accelerating . MimicPlay learns a planner through human hand-trajectory prediction and uses it to guide a robot policy trained from teleoperated demonstrations wang2023mimicplay . Our approach instead discovers boundaries from hand kinematics and represents each segment through factorized translation, rotation, and aperture effects. These local primitives are not predefined semantic subtasks and can therefore be reused across demonstrated skills before contextual prediction is learned over the fixed vocabulary. Action Representations and Motion Tokenization. Discrete action representations support categorical prediction and sequence modeling. VQ-BeT uses hierarchical vector quantization to model multimodal actions, while FAST tokenizes transformed robot action sequences for efficient autoregressive learning lee2024behavior,pertsch2025fast . LAPA extends action tokenization to videos without robot labels by learning latent actions between frames and subsequently adapting with robot data ye2025latent . Our framework instead learns from segmented 3D hand trajectories under a shared kinematic convention. Translation and aperture use independent discrete codebooks, rotation remains continuous, and the decoder reconstructs each segment's net effect conditioned on its initial state. This structure enables embodiment-specific adaptation while keeping the motion encoders and codebooks fixed. Method sec:method Framework Overview sec:framework Our central design separates a shared motion representation from embodiment-specific effect decoding. We learn the representation from human hand trajectories and retain it when fitting a compact decoder to robot demonstrations. This allows us to study which motion information can be reused across datasets and embodiments, and which mappings require adaptation. The framework has three stages. SkillSeg first partitions trajectories into local motion segments using self-supervised reconstruction. Embodied Primitive Motion Tokenization (EPMT) then encodes each segment into discrete translation and aperture tokens and a continuous rotation latent, trained jointly with a state-conditioned effect decoder. Finally, target-embodiment adaptation fits a new decoder while freezing the segmentation model, motion encoders, and codebooks. Thus, embodiment adaptation changes the mapping from a shared representation to motion effects while preserving the representation itself. An illustration of the proposed pipeline is shown in Figure~ fig:pipeline . We study two extensions of this core.

title: VLA-Stem: A Lightweight Safety Mechanism for Vision-Language-Action Models via Reinforcement Learning
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models integrate high-level reasoning with low-level action execution for end-to-end robotic control. However, most VLA models target static manipulation in unconstrained environments, overlooking spatial constraints and dynamic obstacles. Fine-tuning VLAs on obstacle-avoidance data is a straightforward solution, but collecting such data is costly, especially for dynamic scenarios, and may degrade their original task capabilities. To address these limitations, we propose VLA-Stem, a lightweight, reinforcement-learning-based safety mechanism for VLA systems. Without fine-tuning the underlying VLA policy, VLA-Stem converts its action chunks into motion references and uses trajectory-level guidance to preserve their spatial intent while allowing flexible motion and timing adjustments. Conditioned on these references, robot proprioception, and local obstacle information, the Stem policy adaptively modifies execution at inference time, preserving the original task intent while enabling responsive adaptation to spatial constraints and dynamic obstacles. For robust and sample-efficient training, we combine teacher-student distillation with curriculum learning. We evaluate VLA-Stem on reference following, static spatial constraints, and dynamic obstacle avoidance. Across six constrained simulation settings, VLA-Stem achieves 52.8% average collision-free task success versus 23.7% for the strongest safety baseline, while preserving base-policy performance in obstacle-free settings; real-world experiments further show consistent collision reductions under static and dynamic obstacles. These results demonstrate that VLA-Stem couples high-level VLA task intent with rapid, reflex-like responses to immediate physical risks, providing a brainstem-inspired mechanism for robust robot execution.
full_text: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a prominent paradigm for end-to-end robotic control, integrating high-level reasoning with low-level action execution. However, most existing VLA models are primarily designed for static manipulation tasks in unconstrained environments, failing to account for safety-critical scenarios that involve spatial constraints or dynamic obstacles. Fine-tuning VLAs on obstacle-avoidance data is a straightforward solution, but collecting such data is costly, especially for dynamic scenarios, and may degrade their original task capabilities. To address these limitations, we propose , a lightweight, reinforcement-learning-based safety mechanism for VLA systems. Without fine-tuning the underlying VLA policy, converts its action chunks into motion references and uses trajectory-level guidance to preserve their spatial intent while allowing flexible motion and timing adjustments. Conditioned on these references, robot proprioception, and local obstacle information, the Stem policy adaptively modifies execution at inference time, preserving the original task intent while enabling responsive adaptation to spatial constraints and dynamic obstacles. To achieve robust and sample-efficient policy learning in complex environments, we adopt a teacher--student distillation framework combined with curriculum learning. We evaluate on reference following, static spatial constraints, and dynamic obstacle avoidance. Across six constrained simulation settings, achieves 52.8 average collision-free task success versus 23.7 for the strongest safety baseline, while preserving base-policy performance in obstacle-free settings; real-world experiments further show consistent collision reductions under static and dynamic obstacles. These results demonstrate that couples high-level VLA task intent with rapid, reflex-like responses to immediate physical risks, providing a brainstem-inspired mechanism for robust robot execution. Introduction Embodied intelligence aims to integrate robotics with artificial intelligence for general real-world interaction, with Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models emerging as a prominent direction. State-of-the-art VLA models~ pi0.5 adopt end-to-end architectures that combine high-level capabilities with low-level action execution. This resembles human behavior, where deliberate reasoning guides bodily actions to accomplish diverse real-world tasks. However, we argue that this paradigm overlooks another fundamental aspect of biological intelligence: basic physiological and sensorimotor functions, such as postural regulation and rapid reflexive responses, which operate through lower-level neural circuits including the brainstem. In contrast, most existing VLA policies lack an explicit counterpart to such lower-level responsive regulation. Therefore, VLA policies should not only learn what to do and how to do it, but also remain responsive to the safety demands of physical interaction. Building on this perspective, we aim to endow VLA systems with the ability to react to immediate physical risks while remaining coordinated with their task-directed behavior (Fig.~ fig:first ). Existing approaches mainly follow two directions. One is to learn collision-aware manipulation behaviors from large-scale avoidance data~ yang2025deep ; however, collecting such data is labor-intensive and costly, especially in dynamic environments, and adapting a pretrained VLA requires additional training of the task policy itself. Another direction is to augment a frozen VLA with a conventional safety module. For example, VLSA~ hu2025vlsa introduces control-theoretic constraints to modify unsafe VLA actions during execution. While this modular design provides an explicit mechanism for satisfying local geometric constraints, it primarily focuses on action-space safety and ignores the coordination between safety responses and the task-directed behavior of the VLA, leading to restricted corrective behaviors, reduced task success, and limited adaptability in complex dynamic environments. This motivates a mechanism that does not treat safety adaptation independently of VLA task intent, but instead tightly integrates safety responses with VLA task execution. To address these limitations, we propose , a lightweight, brainstem-inspired RL-based safety mechanism that couples VLA task intent with rapid responses to physical risks. Specifically, uses the short-horizon trajectory generated by the base VLA as a reference for its intended motion, and jointly conditions on this reference trajectory, robot proprioception, and local obstacle information to generate executable actions. To support such flexible execution, we introduce a trajectory-level guidance objective that preserves the spatial intent of the motion reference while relaxing strict temporal alignment. We further adopt teacher--student distillation with curriculum learning to facilitate structured exploration and improve the learned policy's recovery capability under safety-induced deviations. As a result, improves execution safety and robustness without sacrificing task performance or incurring additional training cost for the base policy. We evaluate across multiple manipulation tasks and scenarios, including obstacle-free execution, static spatial constraints, and dynamic obstacle avoidance. Results show that reduces safety violations while maintaining base-policy task performance, demonstrating its potential as an inference-time safety mechanism for VLA policies. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: We propose , a lightweight, reinforcement-learning-based safety mechanism for VLA models that directly integrates VLA task intent with runtime safety adaptation to physical constraints, without fine-tuning the underlying policy. We design a trajectory-level guidance objective that uses the base VLA trajectory as a reference motion, allowing flexible local motion and timing adjustments while preserving task behavior. We further introduce a teacher--student distillation framework with curriculum learning to improve recovery from obstacle-avoidance-induced deviations. We conduct extensive experiments across multiple manipulation scenarios in both simulation and the real world, demonstrating improved collision-free task success and direct sim-to-real transfer of the Stem policy without real-world training or fine-tuning. Related Work Vision-Language-Action Models Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as an end-to-end paradigm for robot manipulation, conditioning action generation on visual observations and language instructions ye2026c,yip2026sope . Representative systems, including OpenVLA~ kim2024openvla , RT-X~ zitkovich2023rt,brohan2022rt , RDT~ liu2024rdt , ~ black2024pi_0 , and ~ pi0.5 , have continued to improve the scale, generalization, and action-generation capability of robot policies ~ xiong2026cac, geng2026trajwam . Although VLA models demonstrate strong generalization, they remain constrained by high-quality data requirements and limited robustness in out-of-distribution scenarios. Recent work has explored reinforcement learning for VLA adaptation, such as VLA-RL~ lu2025vlarl and ~ amin2025pi . While these methods improve task-level robustness, they still primarily optimize policies for task completion and adaptation, without explicitly treating execution safety in challenging manipulation scenarios as a central objective. Safety for Manipulators Safe trajectory generation has been widely studied through sampling-based planners such as RRT~ lavalle2001rapidly and PRM~ kavraki1996probabilistic , optimization-based methods such as CHOMP~ ratliff2009chomp , TrajOpt~ TrajOpt , and STOMP~ kalakrishnan2011stomp , as well as MPC. Although widely used, these methods often require substantial manual effort due to their complexity and the need for extensive retuning across different scenarios. Learning-based methods~ yu2024ldp , including Motion Planning Diffusion~ carvalho2023motionplanningdiffusion , Deep Reactive Policy~ yang2025deep , and URPlanner~ ying2025urplanner , improve efficiency and generalization through demonstrations or reinforcement learning~ yu2024pathrl . However, they typically act as standalone trajectory generators and are difficult to directly integrate with VLA policies without disrupting the task-directed behavior of the base policy. Beyond trajectory generation, recent work has also explored safety mechanisms for end-to-end policies. CBF-based safe RL methods~ saferl1,saferl2 enforce safety through constrained policy optimization, with SafeVLA~ zhang2026safevla extending this direction to VLA policies, while safety filters such as RAIL~ jung2025rail augment frozen policies with external safety modules. However, filtering-based corrections can become less reliable in complex or dynamic environments and may compromise base-policy performance on challenging tasks. Test-Time VLA Test-time VLA~ deng2025survey is a recent paradigm that adjusts VLA actions during deployment, avoiding costly fine-tuning. VLA-Reasoner~ guo2025vlareasoner improves actions through online MCTS, while V-GPS~ nakamoto2024steering selects candidate actions using a pretrained value function. However, these methods evaluate multiple candidate action sequences at inference time, boosting performance at the expense of real-time efficiency. In contrast, our method performs lightweight VLA-conditioned execution with a compact Stem policy, enabling efficient safety augmentation without candidate search or VLA fine-tuning. Method An overview of the proposed framework is illustrated in Fig.~ fig:overview . We first formulate VLA-conditioned execution, where the frozen VLA provides a task-directed motion reference that conditions the Stem policy ( sec:vla_conditioned_execution ). We then introduce trajectory-level guidance to preserve the spatial intent of this reference while allowing flexible motion and timing adjustments ( sec:trajectory_guidance ). Next, we present teacher--student distillation for learning recovery from execution deviations using privileged task information during training ( sec:distillation ). Finally, we describe the RL objective and curriculum that progressively train the Stem policy from trajectory following to static and dynamic obstacle interactions ( sec:curriculum ). VLA-Conditioned Execution sec:vla_conditioned_execution We formulate as a coupled execution architecture in which the frozen VLA provides a short-horizon task-directed motion reference, while the Stem policy conditions jointly on this reference and the current physical context to generate executable actions. Execution is organized into intervals of control steps, each associated with one VLA action chunk. Let denote such an execution interval and its first control step. At , the frozen VLA policy is queried with its observation and produces an -step action chunk Rather than being executed directly, this action chunk is converted into a motion reference that conditions Stem execution over the current interval. Let denote the end-effector pose in the world frame. We map the VLA action chunk to the corresponding future end-effector poses and express them relative to the end-effector pose at the beginning of the interval: The resulting trajectory serves as the task-directed motion reference until the next VLA query. At each control step within the interval, the Stem policy also receives the current physical context, consisting of robot proprioception and local obstacle information. The proprioceptive state contains the joint positions and end-effector pose. For each obstacle , the local obstacle information consists of its center in the world frame and its bounding-box dimensions . We represent the set of local obstacles as where denotes the number of local obstacles. Conditioned on the active VLA motion reference and the current physical context, the Stem policy generates an executable action at each control step

title: PDRVLA: A Vision-Language-Action Model with Physical Dynamics Representations
summary: Vision--Language--Action (VLA) models generate robot actions from visual observations and language instructions, but their understanding of physical dynamics remains limited. Video world models can capture scene dynamics, yet generating future videos introduces high latency into the control loop. We introduce PDRVLA, whose lightweight Physical Dynamics Module extracts physical tokens from vision--language features to condition action generation without online video generation. The module learns through direct prediction of future RGB, depth, and optical-flow features, with auxiliary supervision through a frozen pretrained video world model. Training relies entirely on publicly available data, expanded through human-to-robot synthesis, subtask annotation, and embodied chain-of-thought (ECoT) annotation. Across four simulation benchmarks, PDRVLA achieves success rates of 99.3% on LIBERO, 89.9% on LIBERO-Plus, 93.6% on RoboTwin~2.0, and 81.5% on SimplerEnv. Ablations show improved future prediction with world-model supervision and evaluate how subtask conditioning, future object-pose supervision, and ECoT training affect action success.
full_text: Corresponding authors: , . Vision--Language--Action (VLA) models generate robot actions from visual observations and language instructions, but their understanding of physical dynamics remains limited. Video world models can capture scene dynamics, yet generating future videos introduces high latency into the control loop. We introduce , whose lightweight Physical Dynamics Module extracts physical tokens from vision--language features to condition action generation without online video generation. The module learns through direct prediction of future RGB, depth, and optical-flow features, with auxiliary supervision through a frozen pretrained video world model. Training relies entirely on publicly available data, expanded through human-to-robot synthesis, subtask annotation, and embodied chain-of-thought (ECoT) annotation. Across four simulation benchmarks, achieves success rates of 99.3 on LIBERO, 89.9 on LIBERO-Plus, 93.6 on RoboTwin~2.0, and 81.5 on SimplerEnv. Ablations show improved future prediction with world-model supervision and evaluate how subtask conditioning, future object-pose supervision, and ECoT training affect action success. 6pt 5pt 3 10000 10000 0 Introduction Vision--Language--Action (VLA) models connect visual observations and language instructions to robot control, drawing on pretrained vision--language models (VLMs) and demonstrations from heterogeneous robots~ black2024pi0,intelligence2025pi05 . Their understanding of the physical world, however, remains limited. For example, a recent analysis reports weak encoding of object physical properties across several VLA policies and unreliable adaptation of their motions to changes in object mass~ xu2026physicalunderstanding . For manipulation, recognizing the current scene is only part of the problem: grasping, moving, and placing objects also change their configurations and spatial relationships. Anticipating how a scene evolves during interaction can provide useful context for action selection, motivating representations that connect current observations with future appearance, geometry, and motion. 0 Pretrained video world models offer a complementary way to learn physical dynamics by predicting how scenes change over time~ wan2025 . Incorporating these models into robot policies can connect future prediction with action generation~ kim2026cosmospolicy . However, generating future videos within the control loop adds latency to action generation. Recent approaches instead use video prediction during training to shape compact representations that can condition a policy without online video generation~ cai2026internvlaa15,tang2026worldtokens . Following this direction, we introduce , a VLA model with a lightweight Physical Dynamics Module (Figure~ fig:intro_overview ). The module extracts a fixed set of physical tokens from intermediate VLM features. The action expert uses these tokens alongside the final-layer VLM features to generate actions. We train the module with two complementary objectives. Direct supervision uses future RGB, depth, and optical-flow latent features as targets, encouraging the tokens to encode future appearance, geometry, and motion. A frozen pretrained video world model conditioned on the physical tokens provides auxiliary supervision for temporal prediction. Joint policy training then combines action and vision--language (VL) objectives with continued direct future prediction. The resulting policy uses physical tokens for action generation without running the video model during control. Our training corpus is built entirely from publicly available datasets. It combines real-robot, handheld UMI, and simulated trajectories with general and robotics-oriented VL data, and is expanded through egocentric human-to-robot synthesis. Subtask and embodied chain-of-thought (ECoT) annotations provide additional supervision for task stages, scene understanding, progress assessment, and next motion. Together, these sources support training across heterogeneous embodiments and complementary forms of action and language supervision. We evaluate on LIBERO~ liu2023libero , LIBERO-Plus~ fei2025liberoplus , RoboTwin 2.0~ chen2025robotwin , and SimplerEnv~ li2025simpler , achieving success rates of 99.3 , 89.9 , 93.6 , and 81.5 , respectively. Ablation studies show that world-model-assisted supervision improves future prediction. Additional experiments examine the effects of subtask conditioning, future object-pose supervision, and ECoT annotations on policy performance. The report makes three contributions: We introduce , whose lightweight Physical Dynamics Module extracts compact physical tokens from intermediate VLM features to complement the final-layer features used for action generation. We train these representations through direct prediction of future RGB, depth, and optical-flow features, with auxiliary supervision from a frozen video world model. Direct future prediction continues during joint policy training, while deployment uses the learned physical tokens without running the video generator. We assemble a cross-embodiment training corpus entirely from publicly available datasets, integrating real-robot, handheld UMI, and simulated demonstrations with general and robotics-oriented VL data. Our data pipeline standardizes heterogeneous trajectories, expands embodiment coverage through egocentric human-to-robot synthesis, and adds subtask and ECoT annotations, supporting joint learning of robot actions and language responses about task stages, scene context, progress, and next motion. We evaluate on four simulation benchmarks and conduct targeted analyses of physical-representation learning and policy performance. The results show improved future prediction with world-model assistance and characterize the effects of subtask conditioning, future object-pose supervision, and ECoT annotations on action success across tasks and inference settings. Data sec:data Corpus Overview Our training corpus combines VLA data with VL data. The VLA portion pairs observations and task instructions with control targets, grounding the model in robot behavior across diverse embodiments and environments. The VL portion extends perceptual, spatial, and task-level reasoning beyond the coverage of action trajectories. We organize the corpus into five categories. The VLA portion comprises real-robot trajectories, UMI demonstrations, and simulated interactions, which provide complementary trade-offs in physical fidelity, collection cost, embodiment coverage, and scale. The VL portion comprises general image- and video-language data together with spatial and embodied examples more closely aligned with manipulation. Table~ tab:data_overview summarizes the composition and scale of each category; individual sources are described in Sections~ sec:vla_data and~ sec:vl_data . In addition to aggregating existing datasets, we derive new training data through synthesis and annotation. Egocentric human-to-robot synthesis converts EgoDex demonstrations~ hoque2026egodex into visually and kinematically adapted trajectories for multiple robot embodiments. Subtask annotation assigns a stage label to each frame and produces subtask-prediction VL examples, while ECoT annotation produces keyframe-level VL examples describing the scene, task progress, and next motion. Table~ tab:augmentation summarizes these derived data. VLA Data sec:vla_data Real-Robot Data sec:real_robot_data Real-robot trajectories expose the model to real-world dynamics, sensor variation, and contact-rich interactions. We aggregate public datasets spanning different robots, environments, and task families. Our single-arm tabletop and in-the-wild manipulation data come from RoboSet~ bharadhwaj2024roboagent , DROID~ khazatsky2024droid , BridgeData V2~ walke2023bridgedata , BC-Z~ jang2022bc , and RH20T~ fang2023rh20t . Together, they cover diverse scenes, objects, operators, and manipulation skills, including pick-and-place, articulated-object interaction, and tool use. We extend the embodiment coverage with bimanual and multi-platform data from RoboMIND V1/V2~ robomind2025,hou2025robomind , RoboCOIN~ wu2025robocoin , and ABC-130K~ abc2026 ; humanoid, arm, and dexterous-hand data from Humanoid Everyday~ zhao2025humanoid and the Unitree UniFoLM releases~ unitree2026unifolmwbt,unitree2026unifolmdex1diverse,unitree2026unifolmdex1,unitree2026unifolmbrainco,unitree2026unifolmz1,unitree2026unifolmdex3 ; and large-scale multi-robot data from AgiBot World Colosseo~ bu2025agibot,contributors2024agibotworldrepo,agibotworld2026 . REASSEMBLE~ sliwowski2025reassemble contributes contact-rich assembly and disassembly trajectories, while FuSe~ jones25fuse and MolmoAct~ molmoact2025 provide additional manipulation trajectories. Selected embodiment-specific subsets from the LeRobot community collections~ hfvlavla2025communityv1,hfvlavla2025communityv2,hfvlavla2025communityv3 add further cross-institution and cross-embodiment coverage. UMI Data UMI data are collected with a handheld gripper and wrist-mounted camera rather than by teleoperating a particular robot~ chi2024umi . The resulting demonstrations record real-world interaction as camera observations and end-effector pose trajectories without tying the motion to a robot's joint configuration. We use six UMI datasets with different scales, capture systems, and task coverage: UMI~ chi2024umi , FastUMI~ wu2024fast , FastUMI-100K~ liu2025fastumi100k , Hy-Embodied-0.5-VLA-Data~ zhang2026hyembodied05vlavisionlanguageactionmodelsrealworld , HiFi-UMI-2K~ simpleai2026hifiumi , and RealOmni-Open Data~ genrobot2025realomni . After source-specific filtering, they contribute approximately 1.22 million episodes and 10 , 259 hours. Because UMI demonstrations do not provide robot joint-space commands, we use their temporally aligned end-effector poses directly to construct the unified Cartesian action representation in Section~ sec:data_processing . Simulation Data Simulation complements real-world data with controllable, reproducible interaction and access to ground-truth states and success signals. It also makes it practical to vary tasks and embodiments without additional hardware collection. The simulation corpus covers three complementary settings: standardized skills and long-horizon tasks from ManiSkill2~ maniskill22023 , Meta-World~ metaworld2021 , and RoboCasa~ robocasa2024 ; large-scale cross-embodiment trajectories from InternData-A1~ tian2026interndata , GR00T-X-Embodiment-Sim~ nvidia2025gr00txsim , and InternVLA-M1~ internvlam12025 ; and bimanual or dexterous manipulation from RoboTwin 2.0~ chen2025robotwin and DexMimicGen~ dexmimicgen2025 . VL Data sec:vl_data General VL Data The general VL mixture includes vision-centric instruction data from Cambrian-1~ tong2024cambrian ; captioning and open-ended visual question answering from COCO-Caption~ lmmslab2026cococaption and VQAv2~ huggingfacem42026vqav2 ; and image- and video-reasoning examples from OneThinker~ onethinker2026 . Spatial and Embodied VL Data Spatial and embodied VL data bring the supervision closer to manipulation. We divide them into spatial reasoning over general imagery and embodied or procedural reasoning drawn from robot data, simulation, and web video. The spatial-reasoning group covers spatial question answering, geometric relations, coordinate-aware grounding, referring-expression localization, and multi-view or 3D reasoning. It includes SpaceThinker~ remyxai2026spacethinker , OpenSpaces~ remyxai2026openspaces , SpaceOm~ remyxai2026spaceom , RefSpatial~ jingkunan2026refspatial , data released with Scaling Spatial Intelligence with Multimodal Foundation Models~ sensenova_si2025 , and cross-view correspondence examples linking egocentric, third-person, and robot-camera observations~ crossviewpoint2026 . The embodied and procedural group includes point supervision for object, free-space, and affordance localization from RoboPoint~ yuan2024robopoint ; visual quest

title: Evolving Agent Teams
summary: The rapid progress of software engineering agents drives interest in applying them to open-ended problems such as GPU kernel optimization. However, we find that existing coding agents converge to local optima on real-world, expert-written kernels (e.g., FlashInfer). We introduce Evolving Agent Teams, a multi-agent framework that escapes such local optima. It features (1) a central supervisor that diagnoses each local optimum and restructures a team of agents; and (2) a persistent file system that comprises a learning document, an evolution history, and per-team artifacts, grounding restructuring with accumulated experience. Under a matched token budget, Evolving Agent Teams consistently outperforms strong coding-agent baselines. With an extended token budget, Evolving Agent Teams generates a CUDA kernel that reaches 1.2x mean speedup over the production FlashInfer MLA paged decode kernel from scratch and wins on 36 of 47 production workloads from FlashInfer-Bench (0.86-0.99x on the remaining 11). It also demonstrates superior performance on tasks such as KDA prefill on AMD MI350X (3.01x over vLLM) and NVIDIA B200 (3.44x over FlashKDA), MoE expert-offload serving on Apple silicon (30.3 tokens/s decode for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next in MLX 4-bit on a 48 GB M4 Pro), and RoboDojo robot manipulation (62.1 on held-out seeds vs. 55.3 for the best leaderboard entry). Code is available at https://github.com/caoshiyi/EAT.

Introduction The rapid progress of coding agents on software engineering tasks~ jimenez2024swebench, yang2024swe, wang2024openhands has driven interest in applying them to open-ended discovery tasks such as GPU kernel optimization. Here, the goal is not just to produce a correct kernel but to search a large, hardware-dependent design space for high performance. Expert-written kernels such as ~ ye2025flashinfer and ~ shah2024flashattention3 navigate this space across two levels: low-level primitive use (e.g., WGMMA tensor cores, swizzled shared-memory layouts) and high-level architectural design (e.g., dispatch strategies, warp specialization, dataflow). While low-level primitive use can substantially improve performance within a chosen design, high-level architectural choices often determine which hardware bottlenecks remain and thus largely shape the attainable performance ceiling. Unfortunately, even strong coding agents struggle to write challenging GPU kernels. They often make rapid initial progress, but then converge to local optima far below expert-written baselines. A common failure mode is that agents select design directions that are initially easier to implement but architecturally limited, spend most of their budget tuning within those directions, and fail to revisit harder alternatives that require substantial debugging or architectural rethinking. For example, when writing the MLA decode kernel used in DeepSeek-V3 inference~ deepseekv3 , single-agent runs often abandoned difficult WGMMA-based implementations after repeated correctness failures, and instead optimized simpler but less efficient WMMA-based designs. The trajectory illustrates three distinct phases that require qualitatively different capabilities. Versions 1--5 focus on correctness: the team debugs WGMMA register layouts and IPC cache coherence for multi-GPU communication, producing a working but slow two-phase kernel ( ). Versions 6--10 introduce TMA asynchronous loads and a warp-specialized pipeline that first exceeds the baseline ( ). Versions 15--22 shift to a fundamentally different architecture: the team replaces cuBLAS with a custom WGMMA kernel fused with NVLink multicast for the all-reduce, culminating in cluster-level TMA multicast ( ). Optimizing an Already-Optimized Implementation sec:flash-kmeans The four tasks above start from na\"ive reference kernels. To test whether can also improve code that has already been carefully optimized by domain experts, we apply it to Flash-KMeans~ yang2026flash , a recent GPU-optimized exact K-Means implementation. Flash-KMeans fuses distance computation with online argmin (FlashAssign) to bypass HBM materialization of the distance matrix and introduces a sort-inverse update that transforms high-contention atomic scatters into segment-level localized reductions, achieving up to end-to-end speedup over prior GPU baselines on H200. The released implementation uses hand-tuned Triton kernels. We task the with rewriting the assignment kernel in CUDA, starting from the Triton source as a reference rather than a na\"ive PyTorch baseline. As shown in Figure~ fig:flash-kmeans , the system produces a CUDA WGMMA kernel that reaches speedup over the Triton kernel on the default workload, and achieves up to lower latency on compute-bound configurations (high ) across the full benchmark grid (Figure~ fig:flash-kmeans-bench ). title: Autonomous fixed-wing interception using reinforcement learning
comment: MSc thesis, Faculty of Aerospace Engineering, Delft University of Technology, 2026. 24 pages, 29 figures, 4 tables
summary: Medium altitude, long endurance unmanned aerial systems such as Shahed-type strike drones are an unanswered threat in modern conflicts. Conventional air defense systems are too expensive to provide a feasible large-scale solution. Quadcopter interceptors are a cheap, battle-proven alternative, but their extremely limited flight time restricts them to low altitude targets at short range, whereas fixed-wing platforms have the endurance to reach higher altitude targets from longer distances. However, such interceptors are still operated manually. Recent developments in learning-based controllers show potential for automation. In this work, a fixed-wing interceptor is presented that is controlled by a neural network that maps filtered monocular vision observations directly to actuator commands. The policy was trained in a custom Python environment using reinforcement learning and proximal policy optimization. The policy was then deployed on a fixed-wing platform and tested in real interception scenarios. As a baseline, two classical guidance controllers were also developed and tested in simulation. The policy is able to intercept targets both in simulation and in real flight. In simulation, the policy outperforms the classical controllers under most conditions. The interceptor was ultimately successfully validated in real flight by intercepting maneuvering fixed-wing targets. This novel system shows the potential of artificial intelligence for autonomous control of fixed-wing interceptor drones.

The policy was trained in a custom Python environment using reinforcement learning and proximal policy optimization. The policy was then deployed on a fixed-wing platform and tested in real interception scenarios. As a baseline, two classical guidance controllers were also developed and tested in simulation. The policy is able to intercept targets both in simulation and in real flight. In simulation, the policy outperforms the classical controllers under most conditions. The interceptor was ultimately successfully validated in real flight by intercepting maneuvering fixed-wing targets. This novel system shows the potential of artificial intelligence for autonomous control of fixed-wing interceptor drones. interception, CUAS, reinforcement learning, artificial intelligence, terminal guidance, computer vision, fixed-wing Introduction Medium Altitude Long Endurance (MALE) Unmanned Aerial Systems (UAS) pose a credible threat in modern warfare Kunertova2023DronesUkraine Bilousova2023SanctionsDrones . In both the Ukraine-Russia conflict as well as the recent Iran-Israel/US war, the systems used can be classified into two broad groups. Firstly, intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance drones, which are generally fixed-wing UAS with varying imaging capabilities. They typically fly at 2-3 km altitude at speeds up to 150 km/h. Secondly, Shahed-type strike drones, which are delta-wing kamikaze drones that typically fly at 1-2 km altitude at speeds reaching above 250 km/h. They carry a large explosive payload and have high endurance, allowing for long-range (up to 2000 km) targeted ground strikes. To answer these threats, low cost interceptor drones are emerging as an alternative to expensive conventional air defenses such as fighter jets and missiles. Interceptors carry an explosive payload which is detonated when close enough to neutralize the target. Hence, such systems are single-use, meaning a minimal onboard sensor suite is preferred for affordability. A ground-based radar system can typically provide a mid-course guidance target lock with a few hundred meters error. However, terminal guidance requires meter-level accuracy and hence is currently mainly vision-based, as monocular cameras are inexpensive and easy to source. Traditional guidance laws such as Proportional Navigation (PN) and Pure Pursuit (PP) shneydor1998missile yanushevsky2018modern zarchan2012tactical need a constant Line Of Sight (LOS) and struggle against maneuvering targets. Consequently, current interceptors are mostly manually controlled during terminal guidance. Vision-based relative state estimation can be done in many ways for a variety of applications, including drone racing Kaufmann2023Champion , target tracking pothuri2025learningapproachefficientvisionbased , aerial refueling Martinez2013VisionAerialRefueling and also interception jana2022interception patel2025generalpurposemethodrobotic vanderAa2024IBVSquadcopterInterception . For interception purposes, the bounding-box Barisic_2019 KFegoMotionGroundTargets2025Kim vanderAa2024IBVSquadcopterInterception is an effective and easy to implement proxy to a relative state. Turning visual observation into effective guidance for interception has been done using classical control approaches such as PP jana2022interception and PN yan2025preciseinterceptionflighttargets . Recently, Reinforcement Learning (RL) has been successfully applied to UAS control tasks such as stabilization Hwangbo2017QuadrotorRL , attitude control Koch2018RLUAV , acrobatics kaufmann2020deepdroneacrobatics , drone racing bahnam2026monoracewinningchampionleveldrone Kaufmann2023Champion and also interception pothuri2025learningapproachefficientvisionbased Capelle2025DroneInterception GIRAL2026110985 , with controller authority varying from high level planning to direct actuator command. While promising, for interception the real challenge lies in transferring these results from simulation to a real, uncontrolled environment. Recent work suggests that end-to-end learning-based controllers can achieve high sim-to-real transfer robustness by implementing domain randomization Ferede2025OneNet . In MALE interception scenarios, fixed-wing drones can be superior to quadrotors due to their better endurance, allowing them to intercept targets from longer ranges and at higher altitudes. Studies on RL controllers for fixed-wing platforms are sparse. However, obstacle avoidance Chai2024MonocularObstacleAvoidance , path following Marquis2025RARLFixedWing evasion Zhuang2024 and interception with perfect state knowledge GIRAL2026110985 have been carried out in simulation. In real environments, studies have demonstrated successful attitude holding B_hn_2024 and landing Fletcher2021PerchedLandingRL . Fixed-wing, vision-based interception using a learning-based controller in a real environment is lacking in the literature. Most interception studies are done in simulation and using a quadrotor model, whilst realistic perception and sim-to-real transfer are usually not addressed. In this work, a learning-and monocular vision-based fixed-wing interceptor is presented and demonstrated to successfully intercept MALE targets in a real environment. Shown in figure fig_Banking , the interceptor is built entirely with off-the-shelf components. An RL controller is trained in simulation which replaces the guidance and control of a conventional autopilot. A neural network directly maps filtered visual and flight controller information to actuator commands. The performance of the RL controller is validated against baseline PN and PP controllers in simulation. Finally, the RL controller is tested on real flight interceptions of fixed-wing, MALE UAS. The main contributions of this work are therefore: Development of an end-to-end neural network enabling autonomous fixed-wing interception of maneuvering targets with limited onboard sensing. Development of a monocular vision- and learning-based, autonomous, fixed-wing interceptor able to intercept MALE targets in a real environment. Development of a RL framework inspired by Capelle2025DroneInterception , incorporating fixed-wing dynamics and a real computer-vision algorithm. The final controller is tested in real flight interceptions and assessed in terms of performance and constraints. title: LingGS: Decoupling Feed-Forward Geometry Prediction from Camera Tracking for High-Fidelity Gaussian SLAM
summary: Achieving high-quality reconstruction and responsive camera tracking remains challenging for monocular RGB Gaussian splatting SLAM under a limited optimization budget. We present an online system that addresses this challenge by combining learned geometric priors with explicit geometric camera tracking, which can substantially outperform learned camera prediction in terms of tracking accuracy. A frozen streaming 3D foundation model serves as a virtual RGB-D sensor, providing depth estimation from monocular video. An explicit geometric solver then estimates camera motion through feature reprojection, and a streaming Gaussian mapper integrates the resulting observations into a dense scene representation. We further show that geometric tracking improves camera pose accuracy across representative streaming geometry backbones, demonstrating the broader applicability of our approach. Extensive experiments on indoor and outdoor datasets show that our method significantly improves reconstruction quality over existing approaches, achieving about 7 FPS on a single RTX 4090 and delivering 2-3 times the throughput of the evaluated prior SLAM systems.
full_text: Introduction sec:intro Monocular Gaussian SLAM aims to estimate the camera pose and build a renderable scene map online using only an RGB image stream. This capability supports immersive interaction, live scene capture, and remote interaction in AR/VR and robotics. 3D Gaussian splatting (GS)~ kerbl2023gs provides an explicit scene representation with efficient rendering and differentiable mapping, making it a useful representation for dense SLAM. However, unlike RGB-D Gaussian SLAM methods~ keetha2024splatam, yan2024gsslam, yugay2023gaussianslam, peng2024rtgslam, ha2024gsicp, zhu2025loopsplat , without measured depth, the monocular GS SLAM system must jointly recover camera pose, scene geometry, and the appearance, within a limited computational budget. Methods that rely on sparse feature points or incremental map optimization struggle to achieve high-fidelity mapping~ matsuki2024monogs,huang2024photoslam . Learned dense priors help fill this gap, but integrating them into a consistent map introduces further challenges. Dense depth prediction and camera joint optimization add online computational cost~ homeyer2024droidsplat,cheng2025s3po , while per-frame depth predictions do not ensure cross-frame scale consistency and require additional scale recovery and geometric alignment~ deng2025gigaslam,yu2026robust . Consistent depth and camera poses are both essential to this task. Depth determines where Gaussians are initialized, while camera poses determine whether observations from different frames align. Poor initialization requires additional map refinement, and inaccurate poses introduce conflicting observations that can blur the reconstructed scene. The challenge is therefore to obtain consistent dense depth and camera poses together within a limited online computational budget. Streaming 3D foundation models offer a promising starting point. By maintaining temporal context, they predict consistent dense depth and camera poses as images arrive~ su2026xstreamvggt,zhuo2026streamvggt, chen2026ttt3r,chen2026lingbotmap . Their depth predictions provide dense surface estimates for the Gaussian initialization, reducing the need to recover the scene structure from sparse feature points. Yet this advantage depends on the quality of the accompanying poses. We observe that directly using the models' predicted poses can lead to cross-frame misalignment, limiting reconstruction quality even when useful depth estimates are available. To this end, we introduce an explicit geometry pose solver that combines 2D feature points with predicted depth and utilizes them to jointly constrain camera pose estimation. Our system requires no additional training and runs at 7~FPS on a single RTX~4090 GPU. It achieves higher rendering quality than the previous baselines across indoor and outdoor datasets, with the lowest depth error and competitive tracking error. Overall, our main contributions are: Depth-assisted geometric tracking for streaming 3D models. We introduce an explicit geometry solver for camera tracking that combines 2D feature points with predicted depth. Intensive experiments show that our geometry solver can provide better tracking than the learned streaming camera head. An efficient monocular Gaussian SLAM system. We build a faster high-fidelity monocular GS SLAM system combining the geometric solver, a frozen streaming model, and a Gaussian mapper, leading to higher appearance quality. Across evaluated datasets, our system can improve rendering PSNR by up to 3.1~dB. Generalization of geometry solver across streaming models. We apply our geometry solver to multiple representative streaming models. We show that the geometry solver reduces trajectory error by up to 97 relative to the models' native camera head, demonstrating its effectiveness across different backbones and providing insight for future streaming model design. Related Work sec:related:gsslam Visual tracking without depth prior. These methods recover scene geometry from RGB observations through visual tracking and map optimization. MonoGS~ matsuki2024monogs estimates poses by photometric alignment with the Gaussian map, making tracking dependent on the quality of the evolving reconstruction. Photo-SLAM~ huang2024photoslam combines ORB-SLAM3~ campos2021orbslam3 with Gaussian mapping. CaRtGS~ feng2025cartgs , RP-SLAM~ bai2024rpslam , and SEGS-SLAM~ wen2025segs further develop this architecture through improvements to computation allocation, map updates, and scene modeling. MGSO~ hu2024mgso instead initializes Gaussians from geometry recovered by direct photometric odometry. Without learned dense geometric priors, surface recovery relies on multi-view image observations and parallax. Regions with weak visual constraints may remain insufficiently reconstructed at initialization, requiring interpolation or further geometric refinement during mapping. Learned geometry for tracking and mapping. Learned depth and pointmap predictions provide richer surface information for tracking and mapping. Splat-SLAM~ sandstrom2024splatslam , DROID-Splat~ homeyer2024droidsplat , and HI-SLAM2~ zhang2025hi integrate learned dense depth and trajectory refinement. MGS-SLAM~ zhu2024mgsslam uses multi-view depth supervision, while SplatMAP~ hu2025splatmap updates Gaussian positions using refined poses and depths from dense SLAM, and uses reliability masks to prune or add Gaussians. Some methods strengthen geometric consistency through map-to-tracker feedback or optical flow constraints ~ zhu2026mygosplat,seo2026gaussianflow , and suppress unreliable observations in dynamic scenes ~ zheng2025wildgs,li2025dy3dgs . These designs improve geometric estimation, but dense tracking and iterative refinement add computation to the online pipeline, limiting their application. Feed-forward prediction offers a way to reduce this burden. StreamGS~ li2025streamgs and Flash-Mono~ zhang2026flash predict poses and Gaussian attributes before limited map refinement, but require intensive model retraining. Pointmap and multi-view foundation models also support tracking and mapping in OpenGS-SLAM~ yu2025opengsslam , ARTDECO~ li2025artdeco and S3PO-GS~ cheng2025s3po , but with a high tracking cost. GeoGS-SLAM~ gao2026geogs , VGGT-GS SLAM~ han2026vggtgsslam , and M ~ ren2026m3 combine learned predictions with geometric or photometric optimization to refine poses and scene estimates by processing frames in batches. OTF~ meuleman2025onthefly explores efficient incremental Gaussian construction, but loses the consistent geometry reconstruction. Combining predicted geometry with explicit pose estimation is particularly relevant to our work. GigaSLAM~ deng2025gigaslam and KiloGS-SLAM~ yu2026robust use predicted depth with geometric solvers, while KiloGS-SLAM additionally activates learned pixel matching when needed, but they suffer from the scale drift. MonoEM-GS~ kruzhkov2026monoemgs uses the iterative closest point (ICP) to align predicted pointmap with the Gaussian representation. These approaches demonstrate the value of learned geometry for explicit camera estimation. Our work focuses on using streaming consistent depth predictions for camera tracking and Gaussian mapping. Method As illustrated in Figure~ fig:overview , given a monocular RGB sequence , our system combines learned geometric priors with explicit geometric camera tracking to incrementally estimate camera poses and build a Gaussian scene representation. The LingBot-Map~ chen2026lingbotmap first establishes a fixed camera calibration from the initial frames and subsequently provides depth as a virtual depth sensor. The geometric solver (Sec.~ sec:geometry_solver ) combines these geometric measurements with image features to estimate camera poses by minimizing reprojection error. The Gaussian mapper (Sec.~ sec:gaussian_mapper ) integrates through keyframe selection, Laplacian-guided Gaussian insertion, and 30 refinement steps using RGB and depth losses with keyframe replay.
