title: Ego-CEVR: Learning Cross-Embodiment Visual Representations from Human Egocentric Videos
summary: As egocentric video becomes increasingly available for embodied learning, an important research question is how to turn this low-cost, scalable source of data into robot manipulation capabilities. Egocentric videos naturally provide rich context for high-level task understanding, while real-robot demonstrations with wrist observations and action annotations provide supervision for fine-grained action alignment. We present Ego-CEVR, a data-native framework for hierarchical visual representation learning that assigns distinct learning objectives to global and interaction representations. The global module learns object relations, task state, and temporal progress through future prediction on egocentric video. The Interaction module interprets wrist observations in global context and learns local alignment and contact cues through robot action supervision. Separate residual paths expose both representations to the action policy, preserving direct access to task context alongside fine-grained execution information. Ego-CEVR supports independent pretraining of its global video module on large-scale human egocentric videos and videos from diverse robot embodiments, without requiring robot action labels or paired wrist observations.
full_text: Introduction sec:intro In recent years, a series of works rt2,openvla,pi0,pi05 and their applications have marked the rapid development of embodied manipulation. More and more embodied data from various sources such as egocentric video (Ego), Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) and cross embodiments data have been applied to the training of models. egomimic,chi2024universal,collaboration2023open As embodied data scale up, different types of data are expected to play distinct roles in robot learning. ye2026data An important challenge is to systematically use data from diverse sources with varying forms of supervision. liu2026roboicl,cheng2026context,fang2026emerge . However, how can we design data-native models that are specifically tailored to these various data sources in order to make better use of the data from these different sources? This issue has not yet been fully discussed. VLA policies transfer visual and linguistic priors to robot control, yet semantic generalization does not always translate into faithful execution on unseen tasks~ chen2026instructions,fang2026vision,zhang2026flatness . Predictive world models learn how scenes evolve during manipulation, but using this knowledge for precise local control remains challenging~ vpp,genie_envisioner,geact2 . Integrating semantic understanding, world modeling, and action generation is therefore a promising direction~ jepa_vla,uniwam . To benefit from heterogeneous video and robot data, such integration must also specify which representations can be learned without actions and how robot supervision should ground them in local control. Reusing manipulation experience from humans or other robots requires handling differences in morphology, action space, and local interaction geometry~ human_to_robot,dreamzero . Despite differences in embodiment, similar manipulation tasks often involve similar changes in the spatial and functional relationships between objects. Egocentric videos and robot head-camera videos can therefore both provide supervision for learning task-level visual representations~ egomimic,ego4wam . Wrist observations provide a closer view of the end effector and its target, revealing local cues for action alignment and contact. Video prediction alone may not sufficiently ground these cues in robot actions. We therefore learn global task context through video prediction and local interaction representations through robot action supervision. Following this principle, we introduce , a data-native framework for hierarchical visual representation learning ( ). It learns global task context from human egocentric and robot head-camera videos through future prediction, and learns local interaction representations from wrist observations under robot action supervision. Wrist features query the global representation, establishing a hierarchy in which local interaction draws on task context while the global representation is computed independently of the interaction module. Experiments on LIBERO~ libero , LIBERO-Plus~ libero_plus , RoboTwin 2.0~ robotwin2 , and real robots show improvements in task success and robustness. Ablations further examine the contributions of hierarchical representation learning and multi-source video pretraining. Our main contributions are: We propose a data-native framework that incorporates multi-source egocentric videos and action-labeled robot demonstrations at different training stages to learn task-level and local execution knowledge. We develop a few-shot cross-embodiment adaptation procedure that combines task knowledge learned from video with a few demonstrations from the target robot. We design a hierarchical representation learning architecture that learns distinct yet complementary representations for high-level task understanding and fine-grained action alignment. Related Work sec:related_work Vision-language-action policies. Vision-language-action (VLA) models transfer pretrained visual and linguistic knowledge to robot control, achieving substantial progress in semantic generalization, multitask manipulation, and deployment across environments rt2,openvla,pi0,pi05,gr00t_n1,gemini_robotics . However, object recognition and semantic understanding acquired from image-text data do not directly specify how object states should evolve during manipulation or how actions should realize an instruction. On unseen tasks, policies may reproduce familiar training behaviors, causing their execution to deviate from the intended instruction dreamzero . These limitations motivate incorporating future visual prediction into policy learning, providing temporal supervision through state transitions and enabling learning from video experience beyond action-labeled robot demonstrations gr1,gr2 . Predictive world models for robot control. Video foundation models provide rich spatiotemporal priors for learning manipulation processes and their visual consequences wan,cosmos_wfm . Predictive policies guide action generation using future visual states or internal video-model representations, while world-action models further couple visual state evolution with robot actions vpp,genie_envisioner,lingbot_va,dreamzero . These approaches expand the use of video knowledge for control, but visual generation quality does not necessarily ensure the spatial precision required for fine manipulation. Visually plausible predictions may fail to preserve the relative positions, alignment, and contact relationships needed for accurate execution, and prediction errors can propagate into action errors on unseen tasks and scenes. Consequently, recent work more directly addresses the control relevance of predictive representations. GE-Act 2.0 develops a control-oriented latent space, while VPP2 improves predictive and action generalization through manipulation-video pretraining and subsequent adaptation geact2,vpp2,lingbot_va2 . Fast-WAM further demonstrates that predictive supervision can shape control representations during training without requiring explicit future-video generation at deployment fastwam . These advances raise a central question: how should manipulation knowledge acquired from video be organized into policy conditions that support precise execution? Integrating vision-language understanding and world modeling. The complementary requirements of task semantics, manipulation dynamics, and local control motivate integrating vision-language understanding, world prediction, and action generation. One line of work jointly models video and actions or coordinates semantic understanding, visual prediction, and control through multiple experts uva,uwm,motus,uniwam . Another incorporates predictive information into VLA policies through future-latent alignment or attention-based conditioning flare,jepa_vla,vla_jepa . These studies show that temporal knowledge learned through video prediction can complement the visual-language context of a base policy. For manipulation policies with both Head and Wrist observations, this integration also requires determining the learning roles of different views: how to acquire transferable task knowledge, how embodiment-dependent local interaction should use that knowledge, and how both should support action generation. Ego-CEVR addresses these questions through a representational hierarchy with an explicit conditional dependency. Head video prediction learns global representations, which condition the learning of execution-relevant interaction representations. The action expert accesses both through separate conditioning paths alongside the base-policy context. Cross-embodiment learning from heterogeneous egocentric data. Human egocentric videos capture diverse object interactions and task variations, providing coverage that is difficult to obtain through robot teleoperation alone. Early work uses such videos to learn transferable visual representations and rewards r3m,vip . Subsequent methods transfer human manipulation experience to robot policies through human-robot data alignment, hand-motion estimation, or action retargeting egomimic,egovla,egoscale . These approaches demonstrate the value of human experience, while their motion-estimation and alignment requirements also affect the range of usable data and the quality of available supervision. EgoWAM and Ego4WAM further investigate how prediction targets, data alignment, and supervision influence transfer, showing that video-only supervision can provide an effective foundation for subsequent robot learning egowam,ego4wam . These findings highlight the need to match model learning objectives to the observations and supervision available across data sources. Ego-CEVR incorporates this requirement into a shared Head/Ego video learning interface spanning humans and heterogeneous robot embodiments. The global module supports independent learning without a common action space or paired Wrist observations, while robot demonstrations ground the learned knowledge in local interaction and the target robot's action mapping. Method sec:method Overview and Data Formulation We use egocentric data to refer to first-person videos from either humans or robots. When the source needs to be specified, we use human egocentric videos and robot head-camera videos, respectively. Both are captured with non-fisheye RGB cameras. For egocentric data, only the first-person camera view is used, without paired wrist observations or robot action annotations. Real-robot demonstrations, in contrast, include observations from a head camera and two wrist cameras, together with robot action annotations. We denote the egocentric observation at time by and the pair of wrist observations by . The action sequence used for policy training is denoted by . We use for the language instruction when describing the language-conditioned modules below. As illustrated in , consists of a global video representation module, an interaction representation module, and a representation-augmented action expert. The global module learns from egocentric video through future prediction and produces a representation . The interaction module uses wrist observations and to produce an interaction representation under robot action supervision. The global module can therefore be pretrained on egocentric data independently of wrist observations and action annotations. We use ~ pi05 as the base policy and retain its original encoding of observations, language instructions, and robot state. Two additional attention branches provide and to the action expert. The following subsections describe the representation learning objectives and action conditioning in detail. Predictive Global Representation Learning We use the diffusion transformer (DiT)~ dit of the pretrained Wan2.2 video model~ wan,wan22 as our visual backbone. Given the current egocentric observation and language instruction , a frozen VAE encoder maps the observation to a latent . The language-conditioned video DiT processes at a zero noise timestep. We extract attention value tokens from selected intermediate layers and concatenate them along the token dimension to form the global representation . The resulting tokens retain spatial information from these layers for interaction modeling and action prediction. At inference, extracting does not require generating future video. We supervise the video backbone through conditional flow matching~ flow_matching over future video latents. The frozen VAE encoder maps the current egocentric frame to and the subsequent video frames to future latents , where denotes the prediction horizon in latent timesteps. During training, we keep clean and construct noisy future latents through linear interpolation: Given the noisy future latents and noise timestep , the video DiT predicts the vector field , conditioned on and the language instruction . The prediction objective is where is the timestep-dependent loss weight, and the mean squared error is computed only over valid future latent positions.

title: World Dreamer v5-lite: A Multi-Robot World Action Model with One Dreamer
comment: 10 pages, 4 figures. Guoning Wu and Zijian Cai share first authorship. Yongbin Zheng is the corresponding author
summary: Multi-robot control requires integrating distributed camera views while predicting separate action sequences. Most vision-language-action and world-action models target one robot. Combining multiple views alone does not establish spatial correspondence between them. World Dreamer v5-lite is a multi-robot world-action model built around a shared world state for robot-specific action prediction. Calibrated features from a pretrained video encoder populate this state in workspace coordinates; its spatial size remains fixed as views are added. A vision-language model provides scene context and one query per robot. The queries read the shared state and exchange pose-aware information, while their action streams remain separate. Masked-view cooperative training withholds selected camera views from both visual branches while retaining all action targets. This encourages the use of observations shared by other robots. Pretraining uses more than 10,000 hours of trajectories from 20 simulated robot types, RoboFactory, and real robots. On RoboFactory, World Dreamer v5-lite achieves 74.0% mean success, 23.7 percentage points above the strongest evaluated baseline. Across four real-robot tasks, it reaches 78.8% mean success, a margin of 13.8 points. It also reaches 58.08% overall on RoboCasa365.

It also reaches overall on RoboCasa365. Introduction sec:intro Vision--language--action (VLA) models adapt pretrained multimodal backbones to robot control~ brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,black2024pi0,black2025pi05,bjorck2025groot , and world-action models further couple action prediction with predicted visual dynamics~ du2023universal,li2025uva,zhu2025uwm . These models inherit semantic knowledge from vision--language pretraining and, in the case of world-action models, knowledge of how scenes evolve from video pretraining. Most of these models predict actions for a single robot. Many manipulation tasks instead require several robots to work in a shared workspace, for example, when one robot holds an object while another operates on it~ qin2025robofactory . This setting differs from single-robot control in three respects. First, observations are distributed: each robot typically carries its own cameras, which move with it and capture only part of the workspace, and image patches from different cameras do not correspond to the same physical locations. Second, control is separate while decisions are coupled: the robots may differ in embodiment and action space, yet the action of each robot depends on where the other robots are and what they are doing. Third, observations are often incomplete: the camera of one robot may be occluded by another robot or by the manipulated object, so a robot must sometimes act on what other cameras observe. Extending single-robot models to this setting is not straightforward. Concatenating camera tokens does not, by itself, establish correspondence between views in workspace coordinates. Separate policies preserve robot-specific controls, but a policy restricted to its own cameras cannot use observations from teammates. Existing multi-agent policies can share information across robots~ wang2025gaudp,park2026clsdp . Even with this capacity, training with complete observations gives a robot little incentive to use another view when its own cameras already suffice. addresses these requirements with a shared world state built from calibrated video features in workspace coordinates. A vision--language model conditions one query per robot on the current images and instruction; the queries read and exchange pose-aware information while their action streams remain separate. Only observed video features enter the state used for action prediction, while an auxiliary future-video latent objective trains the video encoder. During training, selected camera views are withheld from both visual branches, but every robot retains its action target, exposing the model to incomplete visual coverage. Evaluation spans the multi-robot benchmark RoboFactory~ qin2025robofactory The camera configuration of RoboFactory is modified so that each agent receives observations from its own cameras. All methods are evaluated under this setting. , the household benchmark RoboCasa365~ nasiriany2024robocasa,nasiriany2026robocasa365 , and four real-robot tasks. The real-robot tasks use homogeneous LeKiwi teams~ lekiwi2025 and heterogeneous LeKiwi--OpenArm teams~ openarm2025 . The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows: [leftmargin=*] A multi-robot manipulation framework, , is proposed. Calibrated multi-view features from a pretrained video encoder form a shared world state read by all robots. Pose-aware agent queries exchange information across robots. A masked-view cooperative training strategy is introduced. It withholds robot views from both visual branches while retaining all action supervision. This encourages each robot to act on observations shared by the others. achieves leading performance among the evaluated methods on RoboFactory and four real-robot tasks. Its mean success rate exceeds the strongest baselines by 23.7 and 13.8 percentage points, respectively. On RoboCasa365, it achieves competitive performance. Related Work sec:related Vision--language--action models. Vision--language--action (VLA) policies map language and images to robot actions with pretrained multimodal backbones. RT-2 co-fine-tunes web-pretrained vision--language models (VLMs) on robot trajectories and represents actions as text tokens~ brohan2023rt2 . OpenVLA builds on the Prismatic VLM and predicts discretized action tokens after training on about 970k demonstrations from Open~X-Embodiment~ kim2024openvla , and Octo is a transformer policy pretrained on 800k Open~X-Embodiment trajectories and instructed by language or goal images~ team2024octo . attaches a flow-matching action expert to a PaliGemma backbone~ black2024pi0 , and extends its training to heterogeneous data sources for open-world mobile manipulation~ black2025pi05 . GR00T~N1 pairs a vision--language module with a diffusion transformer that generates continuous actions~ bjorck2025groot . These policies process the observations of one robot as a sequence of image tokens. retains the VLM as a source of semantic context and agent queries, but additionally aggregates the views of all robots in a calibrated shared world state. World-action models. World-action models couple action prediction with predicted visual dynamics. UniPi generates a future video from an image and a language goal and extracts actions with an inverse-dynamics model~ du2023universal . UWM integrates action diffusion and video diffusion in one transformer with an independent diffusion timestep for each modality~ zhu2025uwm . Several recent models use video prediction mainly as a training signal: UVA decodes video and actions from a joint latent with separate diffusion heads and bypasses video generation at inference~ li2025uva , and Fast-WAM~ yuan2026fastwam and GigaWorld-Policy~ ye2026gigaworldpolicy likewise retain video co-training while skipping future-frame generation when acting. also uses future-frame prediction only during training, but it lifts the observed features of the video encoder into a shared world state in workspace coordinates instead of using them as image-indexed tokens of a single robot. Multi-robot policies. RoboFactory provides compositional multi-agent manipulation tasks for studying embodied collaboration~ qin2025robofactory . On this benchmark, GauDP reconstructs a 3D Gaussian field from the RGB observations of all agents and redistributes it to each agent within a diffusion policy~ wang2025gaudp . CLS-DP instead targets decentralized execution without communication: privileged multi-agent dynamics are distilled into a latent space during training, and each agent infers this latent from its own camera at deployment~ park2026clsdp . differs from these methods in three respects: it builds on pretrained vision--language and video models, it lets robots exchange information explicitly through pose-aware agent queries, and its masked-view training encourages robots to act on shared observations when their own views are withheld. 3D visuomotor policies. Explicit 3D representations provide spatial structure for visuomotor policies. DP3 conditions a diffusion policy on a compact representation extracted from sparse point clouds~ ze2024dp3 . PDFactor factorizes a point cloud into three orthogonal feature planes~ tian2025pdfactor , a plane factorization also used for 3D-aware generation in EG3D~ chan2022eg3d . The shared world state adopts a similar plane layout but is built from the features of a pretrained video encoder across multiple moving cameras, handles patches without depth through candidate points along their viewing rays, and is accumulated over observed frames with a visibility-gated update. Method sec:method In this section, we present , a framework for language-conditioned control of multiple robots that share a workspace. At each decision step, given a language instruction, the current and recent RGB observations of calibrated cameras, and the proprioception of each robot, predicts an action chunk for every robot. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:arch , draws shared context from two sources. A vision--language model (VLM) processes the instruction and the current images together with one learnable query per robot (Sec.~ sec:vlm ). In parallel, a video encoder processes the recent observations of all cameras (Sec.~ sec:video ), and its features are placed in workspace coordinates to build the shared world state (Sec.~ sec:worldstate ). The Action Decoder combines these signals with the proprioception of each robot and the relative poses between robots to predict the controls of every robot (Sec.~ sec:action ). Finally, Sec.~ sec:training-objective introduces masked-view cooperative training, which encourages the robots to act on each other's observations. Vision--language conditioning sec:vlm The instruction and the current images of the available views form a shared prefix of language and image tokens for the VLM (Fig.~ fig:arch ). A fixed layout reserves robot slots, and an agent mask selects the robots present at the decision step. One learnable agent query per robot slot follows the prefix. The input embedding of the query for slot is where is a learnable embedding common to all robots and is a learnable embedding of slot . Because all queries follow the same prefix, one VLM pass conditions the robot queries on the same scene without rerunning the backbone separately for each robot. The VLM provides two outputs to the Action Decoder. First, the VLM processes the input query embedding with the shared scene prefix and produces a contextualized hidden state at robot query position . This hidden state is projected and normalized to form the initial decoder query , where is the decoder width. Second, the layer-wise keys and values of the prefix tokens form a shared scene-prefix cache, which supplies the instruction and image context to every robot without another VLM pass (Sec.~ sec:action ). Outputs of unused slots are zero-padded. Video encoder sec:video While the VLM provides semantic context from the current images, the video encoder supplies the spatial evidence from which is built. Recent RGB histories occupy camera slots, which are separate from the robot slots: a robot may provide several views, and a workspace camera may provide another. A view mask selects the available cameras; the same mask determines which current images enter the VLM. A causal video variational autoencoder (VAE) converts each RGB history into latents, and the encoder of a pretrained video model processes observed latent steps. During training, noised future steps are additionally provided for an auxiliary video-flow prediction task. A prefix-asymmetric attention mask prevents observed tokens from attending to the future steps. The observed outputs, and therefore , depend only on observations, so no video generation is required at inference. Shared world state phi sec:worldstate The video encoder prod

title: Which Hand Was Late? Diagnosis for Robot Failure Recovery in Bimanual Tool Use
summary: Failure diagnosers for robot manipulation are increasingly vision--language models (VLMs), trained and evaluated on single-arm failures produced by perturbing a successful demonstration. Bimanual tool use adds failures of other kinds: a tool that slips out of its socket while still held, two correct gestures made at different times, and attempts that fail for two reasons at once. On a simulated bimanual tool-use task whose failure causes are read from the recorded trace, we measure what each sensing channel lets a diagnoser tell. The tool's slip is read on the tool hand; which hand was late is read on both arms, while a sensor on one hand reads its own hand's delay and at most part of the other's; and whether a late attempt was also pushed too weakly is not identifiable from passive sensing when the tool hand is late. Within two attempts, a repair policy that escalates when the cause is not identifiable repairs as many failures as one told the true cause. A VLM's internal state carries the late hand almost perfectly, along a direction no closer to the one its answer reads than a random one; whether the answer reports it depends on the wording of the question.
full_text: Failure diagnosers for robot manipulation are increasingly vision--language models (VLMs), trained and evaluated on single-arm failures produced by perturbing a successful demonstration. Bimanual tool use adds failures of other kinds: a tool that slips out of its socket while still held, two correct gestures made at different times, and attempts that fail for two reasons at once. On a simulated bimanual tool-use task whose failure causes are read from the recorded trace, we measure what each sensing channel lets a diagnoser tell. The tool's slip is read on the tool hand; which hand was late is read on both arms, while a sensor on one hand reads its own hand's delay and at most part of the other's; and whether a late attempt was also pushed too weakly is not identifiable from passive sensing when the tool hand is late. Within two attempts, a repair policy that escalates when the cause is not identifiable repairs as many failures as one told the true cause. A VLM's internal state carries the late hand almost perfectly, along a direction no closer to the one its answer reads than a random one; whether the answer reports it depends on the wording of the question. Introduction Imitation learning and recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have enabled impressive advances in robotic manipulation kim2024openvla, black2025pi and with them the question of what a robot should do when an attempt fails. Deployed in an open world, a robot will encounter mechanisms it has never interacted with before~ tedrake2024manipulation , and it will inevitably fail on some of them. Some of what a mechanism requires can only be found out by trying: a robot that has never opened a stiff lock cannot know in advance how much force it requires. What matters is whether it can learn from the attempt. Failures can also occur on familiar tasks when the robot misestimates quantities that are not directly observable, such as the force required to push a locked door open or the timing of the other hand's action. In either case, a failure is useful only if its cause can be identified: to recover from a failure and learn from it, a robot must detect it, attribute it to its cause, and act on that cause. A growing body of work addresses this problem through visual failure reasoning by asking a vision--language model (VLM). AHA~ duan2025aha takes an image sequence and returns a natural-language explanation of the failure; RoboFAC~ lu2025RoboFac evaluates detection, identification and localisation from video; ViFailback~ Zeng2026Diagnose turns the diagnosis into visual corrections for a policy; and ARMOR~ qi2026selfrefining jointly refines detection and open-ended reasoning. These systems address detection, did the attempt fail?, and diagnosis, why did it fail? Both are learned from failures of a particular kind: each involves one arm acting on one object, is produced by perturbing a successful demonstration, and has a cause that is visible in the scene. Bimanual tool use breaks each of these assumptions. Consider unlocking a utility cabinet with a square key: one hand seats the key in the lock and turns it, while the other pushes the door. The attempt can fail because a gesture was wrong (the key was never seated), because the tool slipped out of its socket under torque while still firmly held, because the lock needed more force than was applied, or because both hands did the right thing at different times. The last case is not a mistake of either arm but a relation between them. For such a failure, ``why did it fail?'' becomes ``which hand was late?'', a question no single-arm taxonomy can ask (Figure fig:diag ). In this paper, we ask: What must a failure diagnoser observe to tell which hand caused a bimanual tool-use failure, and do VLM diagnosers report it when they observe it? When a failure has no visible evidence, can vision detect it without being able to diagnose its cause? To answer this, we need a task in which the cause of each failure is known without relying on an annotator's reading of the video. We build a bimanual, tool-mediated lock in simulation, inject one fault per attempt with a scripted controller, and read the class of every failure from the recorded trace of the mechanism. We then apply the same probe to one sensing channel at a time, and to the internal representation and the language output of the same VLM. We do not propose a new diagnoser, we instead measure what a diagnoser needs. Our contributions are the following: [leftmargin=*] A tool-use task with known failure causes (Sec.~ sec:task ), where the cause of each failure can be recovered from the trace, including failures with multiple simultaneous causes. What can be diagnosed, and from where (Sec.~ sec:where ): the tool's slip is read on the tool hand and which hand was late on both arms, while whether a late push was also too weak is on no passive sensor when the tool hand is late. Sensor placement determines which of these signals are available. Diagnosis determines repair (Sec.~ sec:repair ): failures with two causes are repaired only when both causes are corrected. A policy that asks only whether the hands overlapped, applies the matching correction and, if it fails, both (escalation) repairs as many failures within two attempts as one told the true cause. The model represents the late hand (Sec.~ sec:readout ): the VLM’s state encodes which hand was late, even though this information is not read out by its answer. Related work Failure diagnosis with vision--language models is a recent line of work, almost entirely concerned with a single arm and with judging an explanation by its text. We review these diagnosers, how their answers are scored, and the two tools our study borrows: bimanual platforms and representation probes. Failure reasoning with VLMs. Beyond the systems above, post-trained failure detectors such as I-FailSense~ ifailsense2026 fine-tune a VLM (here PaliGemma-2) specifically for robot failure detection. REFLECT liu2023reflect is the closest to our setting in that it uses non-visual modalities, but it treats them as evidence for a scene-level explanation rather than asking which modality carries which cause. How answers are scored. These systems score an explanation with a classifier head or by its similarity to a reference: ROUGE-L~ lin2004rouge , embedding similarity or an LLM judge. To our knowledge, none compares the answer with what the model's own state contains, which is what our readout analysis does (Section~ sec:readout ). Bimanual platforms and probes. Low-cost bimanual platforms~ zhao2023aloha have made two-arm tasks easy to use, yet we know of no diagnosis benchmark whose taxonomy includes a relation between two arms. Linear probes on frozen features~ alain2017understanding separate what a representation contains from what a model reports. We use the same probe on every sensing channel and on the VLM's own states. A tool-use task with known failure causes sec:task We need failures whose cause is known without an annotator (contribution~1). We first describe the scene and its lock (Section~ sec:scene ), then how the cause of each failure is read from the recorded trace, including failures with two causes (Section~ sec:labels ), and finally the probe we apply to every sensing channel and to the VLM (Section~ sec:protocol ). Scene and mechanism sec:scene Two Franka Panda arms face a door fitted with a lock (Figure~ fig:task ). One arm fetches a square key-tool from a stand, seats it in the lock's socket and turns it; the other pushes the door. The tool transmits torque through its shape, so the hand never touches the mechanism, and a tool that is not seated deep enough slips out of the socket while still held: a cam-out, which emerges from the contact geometry. The key springs back when released, so both hands must act at once: the door opens only if the key is held turned while the push exceeds a hidden threshold , drawn for every attempt and absent from every observation. Details of empirical experiments are in Appendix~ app:task . Causes read from the trace sec:labels A scripted controller plays a fixed plan for each arm and injects one fault per attempt: the tool inserted short, a hand aimed off axis, the key under-turned, the push too shallow, or one arm's schedule delayed. We label each failure according to the recorded trace (Figure~ fig:sankey ): wrong indicates that a gesture was not delivered; timing indicates that both gestures were delivered and the push reached the threshold, but never while the key was held as the coordination failure; and force indicates that the push was on while the key was held, but never reached the threshold. Failures with two causes. An attempt can also fail for two reasons at once: the push was never on while the key was held, and it never reached the threshold. Replayed in the same world, re-timing the late hand alone opens the door in of attempts and a lower threshold alone in none; doing both opens it in all . These attempts ( with the tool hand late, with the push hand late) are neither a timing failure nor a force block, and we keep them as a class of their own. Data and questions. The campaign has attempts on doors: successes, wrong ( of them cam-outs), timing, force and failures with two causes; every attempt replays bit for bit. Each question is asked on the population where it makes sense: detection, failed against succeeded; diagnosis, blocked against wrong; coordination, timing against force blocks, also split by which hand was late (tool hand late, against , push hand late against ); and cam-out, a slipped tool against a force block with the tool held ( against ). And for failures with two causes, timing against two causes (Section~ sec:twocauses ) Probing protocol sec:protocol We fit the same probe to one input channel at a time: on the tool hand, its wrist torque, the contact between tool and socket, and the joint that turns the key; on the push hand, its wrist force and its contact with the door; joint positions and velocities of both arms (arm poses); the commands of both arms; and images from the front and both wrist cameras through a frozen ResNet-50. The lock angle, the barrel's own joint and the latch's input, is reported as a mechanism reading, and the latch state (door angle, push over the threshold , their conjunction) as an oracle ceiling, never as evidence. Each channel is summarised by its first and last frame in the window and their difference. The probe is an -regularised logistic regression, its strength chosen by cross-validation on the training doors; splits are grouped by door in five folds; AUC is computed within each door and pooled by pairs; intervals are bootstraps over doors, and comparisons between channels are paired on the same resampled doors. The trial window runs from the moment the key should be turned to the end of the push hold on the nominal schedule; the approach window ends before either arm reaches anything and serves as a negative control. Details are in Appendix app:protocol . What can be diagnosed, and from where sec:where This section applies the probe of Section~ sec:protocol to each sensing channel, one question of Section~ sec:labels at a time (contribution~2). Every number is a within-door AUC: the probability that the probe ranks an attempt of the first class above one of the second on the same door, so that is chance and a perfect separation. Table~ tab:channels gathers them, one row per input and one column per question, next to what each input costs per attempt. Every channel that reads both arms separates a blocked attempt from a wrong gesture (arm poses , commands , images ): the wrong gestures are geometric, and the arms display them. What remains is to locate the cause of a blocked attempt: on one arm (Section~ sec:camout ), between the two arms (Section~ sec:bilateral ), or on no sensor (Section~ sec:twocauses ). title: Rendering-Free Event Frame Simulation for Fast Reinforcement Learning of Autonomous Robot Navigation
summary: Event cameras offer low latency, high dynamic range, and milliwatt-level power consumption, making them ideal for agile robots such as tiny drones navigating through cluttered environments. However, existing simulators generally render photorealistic images before converting them into events, making large-scale reinforcement learning prohibitively slow. We propose an analytic event simulator that exploits what event cameras fundamentally measure - moving contrast edges - to synthesize event streams directly from scene geometry and ego-motion without visual rendering. Our simulator generates a 64x64 event observation in 17 microseconds on a single GPU - over 400x faster than a state-of-the-art rendering pipeline - enabling end-to-end reinforcement learning for goal-directed obstacle avoidance to converge in under 30 minutes - three orders of magnitude faster than training on rendered events. Policies transfer zero-shot to physically based event simulations (ray-traced Isaac Sim). Our policy reaches 83% success in cluttered courses unseen during training (mid-difficulty, traversability probability approx. 0.57), at 2.4 m/s average goal velocity, and retains 70% in a simulated texture-dense indoor hall. Furthermore, we quantized the policy to a 1.2 MB int8 network running fully onboard a 56-gram Crazyflie equipped with a Prophesee GenX320 event camera and an OpenMV N6 microcontroller board. Without any fine-tuning, external processing, or positioning, the policy achieves an average success rate of 82% (5/5, 5/6, 4/6 flights) across three real-world obstacle courses of increasing difficulty. Code: Introduction Flying robots such as tiny drones are attractive for search-and-rescue, inspection, and monitoring in confined, GPS-denied spaces, yet reliable autonomous navigation in such settings remains a fundamental challenge. Conventional navigation stacks such as Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) cadena_past_2016 demand heavy sensing suites and power-hungry onboard computers that small platforms cannot carry. Recently, an extremely lightweight approach to navigation, Bee-Nav, has been introduced that achieves long-range navigation with minimal sensing and compute~ ou_efficient_2026 . But for obstacle avoidance, it still relies on depth sensing. Stereo depth cameras such as the Intel RealSense D435i (72\,g, \,W) deliver dense, reliable range images and are routinely carried by drones in the 500--1000\,g class---but the camera alone approaches a Crazyflie's entire takeoff weight. Multi-zone Time-of-Flight arrays, by contrast, are light enough for any nano-drone (sub-gram), yet resolve only zones---too coarse for thin wires, slender poles, or fine vegetative clutter. On sub-100-gram nano-drones such as the Bitcraze Crazyflie, the Size, Weight, and Power envelope binds tighter still, bounding the entire sensing, processing, and carrier payload to a few dozen grams and roughly a watt. This rules out not only dedicated depth cameras but also the embedded GPU computers on which conventional event-processing stacks rely (e.g., an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX module: --100\,g, 10--25\,W). Clutter-resilient obstacle avoidance within this envelope requires rethinking the sensing paradigm. Event cameras are biologically inspired sensors that have emerged as a compelling modality for autonomous robots~ gallego_event-based_2022 . Operating asynchronously at microsecond temporal resolution with high dynamic range ( \,dB) and milliwatt-level power consumption, these neuromorphic sensors capture logarithmic brightness changes with negligible motion blur. These characteristics are particularly advantageous for agile drones, where aggressive rotational maneuvers and unpredictable lighting frequently defeat frame-based cameras. Event-based obstacle avoidance has accordingly been explored through optical-flow pipelines~ dinaux_faith_2021 and direct end-to-end learning~ bhattacharya_monocular_2024 (Sec.~ sec:related ). Training robust visuomotor policies with reinforcement learning (RL), however, remains fundamentally bottlenecked by event simulation: standard simulators synthesize events by interpolating pixel intensities across high-frame-rate rendered image sequences~ Rebecq18corl, hu_v2e_2021 , and even recent GPU-accelerated renderers~ shi_evis_2026 throttle the millions of closed-loop environment transitions that end-to-end RL demands. In this work, we propose an approach to sidestepping rendering entirely. Observing that event cameras fundamentally respond to moving contrast edges, we propose an analytic event proxy that synthesizes event streams directly from scene geometry and ego-motion. Event generation costs s per frame, and end-to-end RL for goal-directed obstacle avoidance converges in under 30 minutes. The learned policy transfers zero-shot to a physically based event simulation (83 success in unseen cluttered rooms). Quantized to a 1.2\,MB int8 network running fully onboard a 56-gram Crazyflie with a Prophesee GenX320 event camera, it further achieves 100 , 83 , and 67 success (5/5, 5/6, 4/6 flights) in three distinct, increasingly difficult real environments, with all sensing, processing, and state estimation onboard. The main contributions of this work are: an ultra-fast, rendering-free analytic event proxy for navigation tasks that trains avoidance policies three orders of magnitude faster than rendered-event pipelines; a sim-to-sim-to-real transfer study showing that policies trained purely in the proxy transfer zero-shot to photorealistic Isaac Sim and to a real Prophesee GenX320; the first fully onboard, event-driven goal-directed navigation on a 56-gram Crazyflie, with all perception and inference on a sub-watt microcontroller. Related Work sec:related Event-based drone flight Prior work on event-based flight spans indirect pipelines---which first reconstruct an intermediate quantity such as optical flow, time-to-contact, or depth, and act on it---and direct methods that map event streams to commands. On the indirect side, Falanga~et~al.~ falanga_dynamic_2020 demonstrated dodging of fast dynamic obstacles with a hand-designed ego-motion-compensated detection pipeline (learned variants followed~ sanket2020evdodgenet ), Dinaux~et~al.~ dinaux_faith_2021 pioneered onboard static-obstacle avoidance by estimating the focus of expansion from event-based optic flow (80 on a frontal pole), and Hagenaars~et~al.~ hagenaars_-device_2025 learn monocular event-based depth self-supervised, on board a small drone, for obstacle avoidance. On the direct side, Bhattacharya~et~al.~ bhattacharya_monocular_2024 presented a static-obstacle avoidance for quadrotors from a monocular event camera, pre-training an events-to-control policy on approximated simulated events and fine-tuning its perception component with real events-and-depth data. Messikommer~et~al.~ messikommer_approximate_2026 learned commanded-direction avoidance in clutter by imitating a privileged teacher while minimizing event rendering, deploying on an NVIDIA Jetson. These systems convincingly demonstrate the latency and dynamic-range advantages of events, but they execute their networks off-board or on onboard computers drawing typically 10\,W or more (NVIDIA Jetson family), an order of magnitude beyond the power and payload budget of a nano-drone. At the extreme low-power end, Paredes-Vall\'es~et~al.~ paredes-valles_fully_2024 achieved the first fully neuromorphic vision-to-control loop on a flying drone, running spiking networks on the Intel Loihi research chip for optical-flow-based flight, landing, and hovering. Goal-directed navigation through cluttered environments, computed fully on board a commercially available microcontroller, has remained open---this is the capability we demonstrate. Event camera simulation Event datasets exist for driving and agile flight~ zhu_multi_2018, gehrig_dsec_2021, zhong_event-based_2026 , but fixed recordings cannot provide the interactive experience that closed-loop reinforcement learning requires; simulation therefore plays a central role, and existing event simulators are generally render-and-convert pipelines. One family converts conventional video, optionally with frame interpolation: v2e~ hu_v2e_2021 , Vid2E~ gehrig_video_2020 , and V2CE~ zhang_v2ce_2024 produce realistic events but replay fixed footage and cannot react to an agent's actions. A second family couples an event model to a rendering engine: ESIM~ Rebecq18corl drives an adaptive log-intensity interpolator from a renderer, a DVS plugin brings events to Gazebo~ kaiser_towards_2016 , and circuit-level models such as IEBCS~ joubert_iebcs_2021 add characterized sensor noise to rendered frames. Most recently, EVIS~ shi_evis_2026 accelerates the render stage inside Isaac Sim with motion-vector warping, approaching real-time throughput; we adopt it as the physically based reference simulation for our sim-to-sim transfer evaluation. All of these must produce images before events. Render-free event generation remains largely unexplored. GERD~ pedersen2024gerd synthesizes events from controlled 2D affine transforms of prototypical objects for equivariance studies, without 3D scenes or a closed loop. Messikommer~et~al.~ messikommer_approximate_2026 attacked the same bottleneck by routing around event simulation rather than cheapening it: event rendering is confined to a one-time offline dataset used to learn a task representation, and during policy search a network approximates that representation directly from lightweight privileged state, so no events are rendered at all (a speedup). In contrast, we make closed-loop event generation itself analytic---no images or offline rendered dataset anywhere---and train end-to-end with RL on event inputs rather than imitating a privileged expert; the approximation is validated by transfer to a physically based event simulation and to a real sensor, zero-shot and without fine-tuning. Autonomous nano-drones and learned flight Autonomous nano-drones. Full autonomy under a gram-and-milliwatt budget has so far been reached with minimal, carefully engineered pipelines. The DelFly Explorer~ de_wagter_autonomous_2014 achieved autonomous obstacle avoidance on a 20\,g flapping-wing MAV, which included a 4\,g onboard stereo system. Sniffy Bug~ duisterhof_sniffy_2021 achieved fully autonomous gas-source seeking with a swarm of 37.5-gram nano-quadcopters in cluttered, GPS-denied spaces. On the perception side, the PULP line squeezed deep networks onto milliwatt processors: PULP-DroNet~ palossi_64-mw_2019 demonstrated closed-loop DNN-based visual navigation at 64\,mW, follow-up work brought sim-to-real nano-drone racing~ lamberti_sim--real_2024 , fully onboard human-pose estimation~ palossi_fully_2022 , and NanoFlowNet~ bouwmeester_nanoflownet_2022 computes dense optical flow in real time for obstacle avoidance. All of these rely on frame-based or range sensing and on supervised perception modules or hand-designed controllers tuned in simulation---none learns control end-to-end, and none uses events. Learned vision-based flight. On standard-size quadrotors, simulation-trained policies have achieved remarkable results: Loquercio~et~al.~ loquercio_learning_2021 learn high-speed flight in the wild from depth images by imitating a privileged expert; Song~et~al.~ song_learning_2023 add perception awareness through learning-by-cheating; Kulkarni~et~al.~ kulkarni_semantically-enhanced_2023 and MAVRL~ yu_mavrl_2024 learn depth-latent collision prediction and complexity-adaptive speed. Closer to our end-to-end setting, SkyDreamer~ verraest_skydreamer_2025 maps pixel-level representations directly to motor commands with model-based RL, achieving onboard sim-to-real drone racing; the direct event-based methods discussed above~ bhattacharya_monocular_2024, messikommer_approximate_2026 bring this paradigm to event cameras. title: Learning Visuomotor Quadrotor Flight Through Dynamic Narrow Gaps via Differentiable Simulation
summary: Threading a quadrotor through a moving narrow gap is a demanding test of agile flight, requiring centimeter-level spatial alignment and precise temporal execution. We address this challenge using a control policy that operates directly on onboard visual and inertial measurements to output collective thrust and body-rate commands. The task is difficult because success lies on a thin feasible manifold: small errors in timing, position, attitude, or visual observability cause collision. Prior planning and learning methods rely on privileged state, teachers, planners, or distillation; learning dynamic narrow-gap traversal directly, from scratch, remains open. We introduce a differentiable moving-gap formulation that gates centering, alignment, and smooth collision terms by signed distance to a time-varying gap plane, turning a sparse traversal event into a dense pathwise objective. We integrate this formulation into a visual-feature-to-command policy trained in one stage from random initialization, without a teacher, planner, or distillation. We validate our approach in both synthetic and real-world experiments. In controlled benchmarks, we demonstrate that pathwise gradients significantly outperform score-function gradients for precision-critical tasks, yielding a 99.3% success rate in simulation after only a few minutes of training on a single GPU. Furthermore, the policy transfers directly to a real quadrotor, successfully crossing a dynamic narrow gap from varied initial conditions using onboard sensing and inertial measurements, achieving an 80% success rate over 10 physical trials.

We address this challenge using a control policy that operates directly on onboard visual and inertial measurements to output collective thrust and body-rate commands. The task is difficult because success lies on a thin feasible manifold: small errors in timing, position, attitude, or visual observability cause collision. Prior planning and learning methods rely on privileged state, teachers, planners, or distillation; learning dynamic narrow-gap traversal directly, from scratch, remains open. We introduce a differentiable moving-gap formulation that gates centering, alignment, and smooth collision terms by signed distance to a time-varying gap plane, turning a sparse traversal event into a dense pathwise objective. We integrate this formulation into a visual-feature-to-command policy trained in one stage from random initialization, without a teacher, planner, or distillation. We validate our approach in both synthetic and real-world experiments. In controlled benchmarks, we demonstrate that pathwise gradients significantly outperform score-function gradients for precision-critical tasks, yielding a success rate in simulation after only a few minutes of training on a single GPU. Furthermore, the policy transfers directly to a real quadrotor, successfully crossing a dynamic narrow gap from varied initial conditions using onboard sensing and inertial measurements, achieving an success rate over 10 physical trials. \\ ~Video: \\ ~Code: Introduction sec:introduction Agile quadrotors can move quickly through confined spaces, but useful motion is often constrained by windows, frames, shelves, machinery, debris, and other structures that leave only narrow passages. Narrow-gap traversal is therefore a representative primitive for agile flight, requiring the vehicle to coordinate speed with whole-body geometric precision. Dynamic gaps make the primitive harder: the quadrotor must fit through the aperture and arrive when it is traversable. We study the onboard visual-inertial version of this problem, learning policies that use vision and inertial measurements to output collective-thrust-and-body-rate (CTBR) commands for static and moving gap traversal. This setting combines thin spatio-temporal feasibility, partial onboard observations near crossing, and aggressive low-level control. Prior work has made strong progress on agile quadrotor planning and narrow-gap traversal through model-based trajectory optimization~ falanga2017,liu2018sb,wang2022minco,han2021fastracing,yang2021wholebody,ren2023mr , learning-based control~ lin2019nn,xie2023learning,xiao2023rl,loquercio2021learning,kaufmann23champion,wu2026sensorimotor , and differentiable simulation~ wiedemann2023apg,heeg2025visualdiffsim,zhang2025nmi,zhang2026irreg . Yet most of these methods rely on static apertures, privileged geometry, or teacher/planner pipelines. This leaves open whether precision-critical moving-gap traversal can be learned end-to-end from random initialization, without a planner, teacher, or distillation. A moving aperture changes the problem qualitatively: the policy must decide not only how to cross, but also when to commit to the crossing. We argue that a central bottleneck is the quality of the learning signal. Model-free RL methods such as PPO~ schulman2017ppo estimate score-function (SF) gradients by treating the simulator as a black box, which can be too noisy on thin-manifold tasks. Pathwise (PW) gradients differentiate through closed-loop rollouts~ kingma2014vae,mohamed2020mcg , but can become unreliable under stiffness, discontinuities, contacts, or chaotic dynamics~ mora2021pods,suh2022pods,metz2021grads . Our key observation is that narrow-gap flight is unforgiving but still smooth: with differentiable quadrotor dynamics and smooth task costs, even failed rollouts indicate how to adjust centering, attitude, and timing. We build on this observation with a differentiable moving-gap formulation that gates centering, alignment, and smooth collision terms by signed distance to a time-varying gap plane. Integrated into a visual-feature-to-CTBR policy trained in one stage from random initialization, this formulation turns a sparse traversal event into a dense pathwise objective. The framework supports privileged-state and onboard visual-inertial observations and requires no demonstrations, trajectory labels, privileged teacher, planner, or distillation. We validate our approach in simulation and real-world flight. In simulation, policies train in -- minutes on a single GPU and reach success with centimeter-level crossing accuracy. In matched 1,000-environment, five-seed state-task runs, tuned PPO used more transitions and more training time than BPTT on moving gaps when averaging its four converged seeds. Controlled benchmarks show that PW optimization succeeds with a single rollout per update, whereas SF optimization fails even with one thousand times more samples. Deployed in the real world, a 10 38\, cm quadrotor traverses a 25 80\, cm moving gap using onboard sensing and inertial measurements, achieving an 80 success rate over 10 trials. Contributions: In summary, the contributions of this work are: [leftmargin=*, nosep, topsep=0pt] We demonstrate precision-critical vision-based static and moving traversal can be learned end-to-end through differentiable simulation without demonstrations, a teacher, a planner, or distillation. We release an open-source differentiable-simulation framework for learning observation-to-CTBR policies under both privileged-state and onboard visual-inertial observations, converging in minutes on a single GPU. We show that pathwise gradients provide useful learning signals on thin-manifold tasks where score-function gradients fail even with orders of magnitude more samples. We deploy the visual-inertial moving-gap policy on a real quadrotor, closing the loop from differentiable training to physical agile flight. Related Work sec:related_work Narrow-Gap Quadrotor Flight. Traversing narrow gaps is a long-standing SE(3)-aware control benchmark, requiring precise attitude commitment under centimeter-level clearance. Optimization-based methods decompose free space into convex corridors and solve constrained SE(3) trajectory optimizations~ liu2018sb,wang2022minco,han2021fastracing,yang2021wholebody,ren2023mr ; falanga2017 first demonstrated onboard traversal with active vision but assumed known gap geometry and a hand-crafted estimator. On the learning side, lin2019nn trained an end-to-end planner-controller still requiring known gap pose; xiao2023rl,chen2023tiv apply deep RL with curriculum learning and safety-aware exploration but rely on privileged pose information; and xie2023learning demonstrate the importance of closing the perception-control loop for static-gap onboard-sensing traversal. Two concurrent works are closest: wu2026sensorimotor bootstrap a model-free RL policy from a model-based planner and distill it end-to-end, and zhang2026irreg learn from raw depth via differentiable simulation for irregular static gaps. We differ by (i)~treating moving gaps as a first-class trained task rather than a reactive byproduct; (ii)~learning end-to-end from random initialization without a teacher, planner, or distillation, in minutes rather than over \,h in wu2026sensorimotor ; and (iii)~isolating why pathwise gradients succeed where score-function gradients fail. End-to-End Visuomotor Quadrotor Policies. Vision-conditioned quadrotor control has advanced through policy distillation and large-scale RL: loquercio2021learning fly through cluttered forests by distilling a privileged planner into a vision policy, and kaufmann23champion reach champion-level racing via deep RL with high-frequency state estimation. Recent work explores lighter perception interfaces~ xing2024bootstrap, xing2024contrastive , onboard sensing for angled narrow gaps~ xie2023learning , and whole-body gap traversal from image masks~ wu2025wholebody . These policies can match or surpass model-based methods in time-optimal regimes, but typically require expert demonstrations, privileged teachers, or large sample budgets---which our low-variance pathwise gradients from differentiable simulation avoid. Differentiable Simulation for Robot Learning. Differentiable simulators optimize control policies directly via analytic gradients. wiedemann2023apg showed that analytic policy gradients can train competitive low-level quadrotor controllers, with extensions to vision-conditioned flight~ zhang2025nmi,pan2026learning, ren2026learning, xing2026continual , locomotion~ song2024quadrupeddiff , and high-throughput GPU-accelerated frameworks~ diffaero2025,aerialgym2025,visfly2025 . The closest concurrent work, zhang2026irreg , applies differentiable simulation with a depth-image renderer to irregular static gaps. We target a complementary regime---static and dynamic gaps---evaluated against PPO under matched parallelism. Methodology sec:methodology Problem Formulation sec:problem_formulation We consider closed-loop quadrotor traversal through narrow rectangular gaps in two settings: (i) static gaps and (ii) moving gaps with time-varying pose. We approximate the quadrotor body as an ellipsoid. A rollout is successful if the ellipsoid projection onto the gap plane is fully contained within the rectangular aperture during traversal. Control Architecture. We use a hierarchical control stack: a low-level onboard controller runs at 1000\,Hz and tracks mass-normalized collective thrust and body-rate commands. A learned policy runs at 60\,Hz and maps observations to commands, , where is the collective thrust command and are desired body rates expressed in the body frame. To model command latency, the policy output is applied to the simulated dynamics with a one-step delay, i.e., the dynamics at step use rather than the newly computed . The quadrotor (approx.\ \,cm) must traverse a rectangular gap of size \,cm without collision (Fig.~ task_geometry_A ). A gap frame is centered at the aperture, with normal to the gap plane and aligned with width and height. We consider static gaps, rotated about by , and moving gaps following planar pendulum motion with randomized amplitude and length (Fig.~ task_geometry_BC ), resulting in a time-varying pose . The task geometry and observation modalities are illustrated in Fig.~ fig:dims . Observation Settings. sec:obs_settings We consider state-based and visual-feature-based observations. The state-based observation provides privileged quadrotor and gap information: where flattens rotation matrices, denotes a target behind the gap, and is a queue of past actions. For moving gaps, is defined relative to the nominal pose. The visual-feature-based observation excludes global pose information and instead uses onboard inertial quantities together with normalized 2D gap-corner projections (Fig.~ task_geometry_D ) and additional features derived from projected gap corners. These features (e.g., projected center, area, aspect ratio, visibility) are deterministic functions of the corner projections and are augmented with short-term temporal differences. The observation also includes the action history . Full details are provided in Appendix~ sec:appendix_observations . title: GraftRay: Physically Based Mesh Insertion into Gaussian Splatting Scenes via Path Tracing
summary: Inserting virtual objects into scenes reconstructed via 2D or 3D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS/3DGS) is a key capability for content creation, AR, and synthetic data generation. However, realistic insertion requires the object to be seamlessly lit by the scene and, conversely, to cast physically plausible shadows onto it. Existing approaches either harmonize appearance in image space, sacrificing multi-view consistency, or approximate scene illumination with an environment map at the insertion point, which cannot represent near-field area lights such as windows and lamps that dominate indoor lighting. To address this, we present GraftRay, a unified method for physically consistent insertion of mesh objects into indoor scenes represented by either 2D or 3D Gaussians. We recover scene materials and surface normals with diffusion-based priors, and explicitly model spatially-extended emitters, solving their radiance in closed form. A hybrid renderer then jointly path-traces the scene Gaussians and inserted meshes, producing view-consistent shading, interreflections, and soft shadows. On FIPT, GraftRay sets a new state of the art, outperforming recent baselines such as ComGS and EAG-PT in rendering fidelity and shadow accuracy, while maintaining highly competitive rendering efficiency.
full_text: [] #1 GraftRay inserts mesh objects into a 3D Gaussian Splatting scene with physically consistent shading and shadows. fig:teaser ] Inserting virtual objects into scenes reconstructed via 2D or 3D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS/3DGS) is a key capability for content creation, AR, and synthetic data generation. However, realistic insertion requires the object to be seamlessly lit by the scene and, conversely, to cast physically plausible shadows onto it. Existing approaches either harmonize appearance in image space, sacrificing multi-view consistency, or approximate scene illumination with an environment map at the insertion point, which cannot represent near-field area lights such as windows and lamps that dominate indoor lighting. To address this, we present GraftRay, a unified method for physically consistent insertion of mesh objects into indoor scenes represented by either 2D or 3D Gaussians. We recover scene materials and surface normals with diffusion-based priors, and explicitly model spatially-extended emitters, solving their radiance in closed form. A hybrid renderer then jointly path-traces the scene Gaussians and inserted meshes, producing view-consistent shading, interreflections, and soft shadows. On FIPT, GraftRay sets a new state of the art, outperforming recent baselines such as ComGS and EAG-PT in rendering fidelity and shadow accuracy, while maintaining highly competitive rendering efficiency. Introduction sec:intro 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl20233d and its 2D counterpart~ huang20242d enable high-quality, real-time rendering of reconstructed scenes. However, inserting a virtual object into such scenes remains challenging. Beyond matching its appearance to the background, the inserted object must respond to the scene's illumination, cast geometrically consistent shadows, and contribute indirect light to surrounding surfaces. Achieving these effects requires explicit light transport while preserving the visual fidelity of the original reconstruction. Existing approaches address this problem from three main directions. Environment-map-based methods estimate local illumination from HDR environment maps~ bolduc2025gaslight,liang2024photorealistic,huang2026lightharmony3d . Although effective for approximating incident illumination, environment maps do not explicitly represent the spatial positions of local emitters or their interactions with scene geometry, limiting their ability to reproduce spatially varying illumination and geometrically consistent shadows. Inverse-rendering methods jointly recover scene materials and illumination~ liang2024gs,du2025gs,gu2025irgs,zhang2023neilf++,lin2025iris,sabae2026aegir,chen2024gi . While physically grounded, these methods introduce additional unknowns beyond those strictly required for object insertion. Moreover, low-dynamic-range (LDR) observations weaken the photometric constraints needed to distinguish emissive sources from highly reflective surfaces. Finally, image-space harmonization methods use generative models to refine the appearance of composited objects~ ren2026mv,violante2026lighting,skorokhodov2025diffusion,li2025freeinsert . Despite producing visually plausible results, they do not explicitly model scene-level light transport and therefore cannot guarantee consistent relighting when the object or illumination changes. We propose GraftRay, a unified framework for physically consistent object insertion into 2D and 3D Gaussian scenes ( ). Because our pipeline extracts material priors directly from rendered views rather than relying on original capture data, it uniquely supports physically-based insertion even for synthetically generated Gaussian scenes where original training images are unavailable. We first render multi-view images from the Gaussian scene and estimate material properties, including albedo, roughness, metallicity, and normals, using robust 2D estimators such as RGB-X or diffusion-based models. These predictions are then unprojected onto individual 2D/3D Gaussians to provide scene-level material attributes, bypassing the complex joint optimization of traditional inverse rendering. Building on these attributes, we extend an OptiX-accelerated path tracer to support Gaussian primitives with stochastic transparency~ enderton2010stochastic and axis-aligned bounding boxes, traced jointly with inserted meshes. The extended path tracer incorporates a Mitsuba-style path integration scheme~ Mitsuba3 , analytic area emitters, multiple importance sampling (MIS), and explicit shadow rays to enable light transport directly on Gaussian scenes. We further recover scene illumination from LDR observations by treating saturated pixels as lower-bound constraints and using unsaturated surfaces to constrain emitter intensities. Since light transport is linear in emitter intensities with fixed geometry and materials, we precompute unit-radiance basis images and formulate light estimation as a nonnegative least-squares (NNLS) problem. Finally, we use differential rendering~ debevec2008rendering to introduce the inserted object's shadows and indirect illumination while preserving the original background reconstruction. Our contributions are summarized as follows: From LDR images alone, we unproject multi-view 2D material and normal predictions onto individual 2D/3D Gaussians, providing scene-level material attributes for physically based insertion without joint inverse rendering. We extend an OptiX path tracer to trace stochastic-transparency Gaussians jointly with meshes, computing illumination, shadows, and indirect light between Gaussian scenes and mesh objects, while differential rendering preserves the reconstruction. We formulate light-intensity estimation using censored observations and path-traced radiance bases, exploiting unsaturated illumination cues to distinguish true emitters from bright reflectors and efficiently estimate nonnegative emitter intensities. Related Work sec:related Lighting estimation for object insertion. Classical object insertion relies on differential rendering~ debevec2008rendering , which combines a captured scene with an estimate of its illumination; Karsch ~ karsch2011rendering extended this paradigm to single photographs. Subsequent methods estimate illumination from images using learned HDR environment maps~ gardner2017learning , spatially varying lighting~ garon2019fast,li2020inverse , or lighting volumes~ srinivasan2020lighthouse . Diffusion-based approaches further improve illumination estimation and adaptation: DiffusionLight~ phongthawee2024diffusionlight synthesizes environment-map observations through a rendered chrome ball, while DiPIR~ liang2024photorealistic uses a diffusion model as a critic for lighting optimization. GaSLight~ bolduc2025gaslight lifts ordinary images into HDR Gaussian splats, LightHarmony3D~ huang2026lightharmony3d predicts environment maps for hybrid Gaussian--mesh rendering, and LuxRemix~ liang2026luxremix decomposes indoor illumination into editable components. Unlike approaches that primarily estimate environment maps or distribute emissive radiance across scene representations, GraftRay explicitly parameterizes local area emitters and uses them in path-traced light transport, allowing their spatial extent and scene occlusion to affect illumination and shadows. Compositing and harmonization in 3D. Recent methods use generative priors to improve the visual consistency of inserted objects in reconstructed scenes. MV-CoLight~ ren2026mv generates multi-view-consistent lighting and shadows, while Violante ~ violante2026lighting harmonize composite images with diffusion models and consolidate the results into 3DGS. D3DR~ skorokhodov2025diffusion similarly uses diffusion priors for zero-shot 3DGS harmonization. Other approaches explore alternative scene representations and insertion strategies: ComGS~ gao2026comgs composes objects using surface octahedral probes, and FreeInsert~ li2025freeinsert inserts text-specified objects without requiring explicit spatial priors. Related 2D methods include image harmonization~ cong2020dovenet , diffusion-based object relighting~ neuralgaffer , token-space relighting from sparse views~ chen2026lumitokens , and geometry-guided video insertion with GO-Renderer~ gu2026go . GaussianEditor~ chen2024gaussianeditor explores direct editing of 3DGS scenes. These methods primarily target perceptual consistency or generative scene editing, whereas GraftRay explicitly models light transport to produce view-consistent shadows and indirect illumination for inserted objects. Inverse rendering on Gaussian splats. Neural inverse rendering initially developed around radiance fields~ mildenhall2020nerf , factorizing geometry, reflectance, and illumination~ zhang2021nerfactor,jin2023tensoir with ray tracing for indoor scenes~ zhu20232 . For Gaussians, GS-IR~ liang2024gs and GS-ID~ du2025gs recover per-Gaussian BRDFs under environment maps or spherical Gaussians. GI-GS~ chen2024gi and IRGS~ gu2025irgs incorporate global illumination, with IRGS employing differentiable 2D Gaussian ray tracing. NeILF++~ zhang2023neilf++ couples incident and outgoing light fields, while IRIS~ lin2025iris addresses indoor LDR reconstruction by estimating camera responses. Intrinsic diffusion priors~ zeng2024rgb,kocsis2024intrinsic and factorized inverse path tracing~ wu2023factorized offer alternative material decomposition strategies. Among these, AEGIR~ sabae2026aegir is closely related, jointly optimizing area emitters, materials, and geometry via a differentiable deferred renderer. Similarly, EAG-PT~ yang2026eag reconstructs emission-aware 2DGS with albedo only for path-traced editing. Unlike these joint factorizations, GraftRay targets object insertion with a constrained optimization: we initialize scene materials from priors and optimize emitter radiances while keeping geometry and materials fixed, reducing coupled unknowns and enabling explicit handling of saturated LDR observations. Ray tracing Gaussian primitives. Recent methods have extended ray tracing to Gaussian and particle-based representations. 3DGRT~ moenne20243d traces particle scenes using ray-tracing hardware, bounding individual primitives and evaluating their responses along rays. EVER~ mai2025ever supports exact ellipsoid rendering for view synthesis, while GHPT~ bo2026ghpt combines rasterization and path tracing for real-time relightable Gaussian splats. Building on these efforts, we extend an OptiX-accelerated path tracer to support light transport directly on Gaussian scenes. Our approach shares the peak-response intersection strategy with 3DGRT but targets physical illumination rather than view synthesis. Stochastic hit acceptance sun2025stochastic accounts for Gaussian transparency during ray traversal, enabling Monte Carlo light-transport estimation with analytic area emitters, multiple importance sampling, and next-event estimation. Method sec:method Given a reconstructed Gaussian Splatting scene and user-marked light regions, our method estimates scene illumination and inserts objects with consistent direct and indirect lighting. As illustrated in , we first estimate per-Gaussian materials and normals from multi-view intrinsic-image predictions. We then initialize analytic area-light candidates from the marked regions and estimate their radiances using a Gaussian-aware path tracer and unit-radiance basis renders. Finally, differential compositing transfers the lighting changes induced by the inserted objects to the original 3DGS rendering while preserving its view-dependent appearance. Physically based light transport additionally requires a surface normal and BRDF parameters, including albedo , roughness , and metallic , which are not explicitly provided by the reconstruction. title: Vision-Language-Action or World-Action? Just Action Models
summary: The vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action model (WAM) communities debate whether control policies should inherit pretrained knowledge from vision-language models or from visual generators. The debate, however, bundles three separable choices: backbone initialization, the objective applied to future observations, and whether the machinery for that future loss is kept at inference. A gap between a VLA and a WAM therefore cannot simply be attributed to any one of them. We show that decoupling these choices yields a common framework for both families, which we term Just Action Model (JAM): a pretrained visual backbone with an action expert, trained with an action loss and a foresight loss. The foresight loss trains current-observation features to predict frozen encodings of the recorded future through a prediction head discarded after training, so no visual generation is involved in either training or inference, and the backbone can be chosen freely. We first compare objectives within fixed policy architectures, then evaluate the foresight recipe across backbone families. The resulting JAM policies outperform their matched FastWAM and ImageWAM counterparts on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, and achieve similar or slightly higher success rates on RoboTwin. Compared with FastWAM, JAM improves the success rates from 97.0%/55.3%/91.2% to 98.2%/64.5%/91.4%, respectively. With cached foresight targets, JAM reduces estimated online training FLOPs per sample per update by 73% relative to FastWAM. Our results show that future supervision improves control without visual generation or additional inference machinery, and strong foresight performance is attainable with either generator-initialized or vision-language backbones.
