title: Hierarchical Sparse Graph for Multi-dimensional Assignment in Event-based Tracking
summary: Existing event-based tracking methods typically operate in an online manner, associating tracklets across adjacent batches. However, this limited temporal window often leads to failures in challenging scenarios, such as long-term occlusions or missed detections, where broader temporal context should be incorporated for high-precision tracking. To achieve robust and accurate tracking, this paper concentrates on the event-based multi-dimensional assignment that associates tracklets across multiple batches simultaneously. Unlike image-based detectors, event-based detectors can generate multiple correct yet spatially distinct tracklets for a single object per batch. This violates the one-to-one rule in classic data association, making event-based association an underdetermined many-to-many matching problem. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to tackle this NP-hard problem. To address its underdetermined nature, we formulate the assignment problem via fuzzy logic, where pairwise tracklet correlations are quantified through multiple long-range kinematic metrics. This fuzzy design eliminates the need for hard tracking thresholds and enables multiple heterogeneous metrics to be integrated into a unified correlation. By treating tracklets as nodes and their fuzzy correlations as edges, we construct a Hierarchical Sparse Graph (HSG). Building upon the HSG, we pose assignment as a graph partition task, and employ a heuristic solution that measures vertex affinity for partitioning adaptively. The entire pipeline is training-free. Comprehensive experiments on two challenging event datasets, eTram and Ev-UAV, show that our method outperforms existing event-based and most image-based association models. Particularly, it achieves over 2$\times$ the performance of OC-SORT across all metrics in the many-to-many association scenario.

This fuzzy design eliminates the need for hard tracking thresholds and enables multiple heterogeneous metrics to be integrated into a unified correlation. By treating tracklets as nodes and their fuzzy correlations as edges, we construct a Hierarchical Sparse Graph (HSG). Building upon the HSG, we pose assignment as a graph partition task, and employ a heuristic solution that measures vertex affinity for partitioning adaptively. The entire pipeline is training-free. Comprehensive experiments on two challenging event datasets, eTram and Ev-UAV, show that our method outperforms existing event-based and most image-based association models. Particularly, it achieves over 2 the performance of OC-SORT across all metrics in the many-to-many association scenario. Data association, event-based vision, multiple object tracking. Introduction section:Intro ata assignment is a critical step in Multiple Object Tracking (MOT)~ baeRobustOnlineMultiobject2014, gaoRobustTrackingLearning2023, rakaiDataAssociationMultiple2022, wangMambaEVTEventStreamBased2026 , especially in the tracking-by-detection paradigm. It is a classic combinatorial optimization problem aimed at identifying matching pairs among detections (or tracklets). Depending on the number of frames considered, image-based data association can be roughly categorized into two types: linear assignment for online tracking and multi-dimensional assignment for offline tracking. Although linear assignment methods~ tokmakovLearningTrackObject2021, liuMultiObjectTrackingMeets2022, caoObservationCentricSORTRethinking2023 have shown strong performance, certain challenges, such as long-term occlusions or missed detections~ zhangGlobalDataAssociation2008, linLTTrackRethinkingTracking2024 , can lead to a performance drop. To address this problem, a few works~ buttMultitargetTrackingLagrangian2013, ochsHigherOrderMotion2012 incorporate multiple frames into the association process. These approaches are termed multi-dimensional assignment. Event cameras are a notable class of bio-inspired sensors that work differently from conventional image-based cameras. Rather than outputting images at a fixed rate, they asynchronously capture per-pixel brightness changes as a stream of binary events. This unique working principle offers distinctive properties compared to image-based cameras, including high temporal resolution (1 ), high dynamic range ( 120 dB), and high sensitivity to dynamic stimuli~ gallegoEventbasedVisionSurvey2022, huangEventGuidedStructuredOutput2018a . These characteristics make event cameras particularly suitable for object tracking~ wangPriorKnowledgeDrivenHybrid2025, liuEMTrackEfficientMultimodal2025, mengBRMoEBlindMultiModal2025 in challenging conditions, like fast motion, extreme illumination, or low-texture targets, where image-based cameras often fail. In such scenarios, achieving high tracking accuracy and robust performance becomes the priority. This motivates a rethinking of the prevailing event-based efficiency-oriented tracking design and calls for more accurate event-based tracking approaches. Event-based association is a critical tracking component but has received limited attention. In this paper, we study event-based multi-dimensional assignment to improve the overall tracking performance. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig1_1 (a) and (b), upstream detections lead to two distinct association scenarios. The former resembles image-based association, where each object corresponds to exactly one detection per batch. We refer to this as one-to-one association. But for the other scenario, this one-to-one characteristic does not hold since asynchronous events can yield multiple spatially distinct yet valid detections for a single object. While image-based detectors can also produce multiple detections per object, this matching ambiguity can be eliminated via Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS) or other strategies. In event-based vision, multiple detections for an object can all be correct and cannot be suppressed, as they may be different temporal segments of the event trajectory. In this case, event-based association becomes an underdetermined many-to-many matching problem. As the association period increases, the processing difficulty grows substantially. Unlike the one-to-one bipartite matching with binary outcomes, event-based association is an inherently fuzzy problem due to the non-unique correspondence between objects and tracklets. Therefore, we construct a fuzzy modeling pipeline that takes two motion-based metrics as input and yields a fuzzy correlation value in as output. Since no explicit mathematical mapping exists between these inputs and the output, we develop a hierarchical quantization method to bridge them, and subsequently propose a heuristic solution to seek the optimal assignment. The overall framework is shown in Fig.~ fig3_1 . The assignment problem is underdetermined, so we design a heuristic search-merge approach to find the optimal solution, which iteratively groups tracklets into cohesive partitions of HSG. Each partition corresponds to a set of tracklets of the same object. Central to this approach is a connection similarity measure, which leverages topological and weight information to assess the vertex affinity for merging. As this measure depends on multiple factors, manually setting a merging threshold is impractical. We derive an adaptive threshold under a null model to make the whole optimization automatic. Our method is evaluated by comparing with multiple event-based and image-based association methods on eTram~ vermaETraMEventbasedTraffic2024 and Ev-UAV~ chenEventbasedTinyObject2025 datasets for the above two association cases. Contributions are summarized as follows: This is the first work on event-based multi-dimensional assignment. We model the problem via fuzzy logic to integrate multiple kinematic metrics into unified tracklet correlations and construct a HSG for assignment optimization. To model unpredictable and non-linear long-range event trajectories, we devise two kinematic metrics, B\' e zier curve-based position smoothness and direction-displacement-based variation consistency. These metrics capture the spatio-temporal coherence of tracklets in positional and directional domains, respectively. A hyperparameter-free graph partition solution is proposed. It quantifies vertex affinities and partitions the graph adaptively for optimal assignment. Despite being training-free, our method consistently outperforms existing event-based and motion-based methods, while remaining competitive with leading image-based association networks. Notably, it also demonstrates robust performance in tracking tiny objects (6.8 5.4 pixels) under large spatio-temporal gaps, surpassing OC-SORT~ caoObservationCentricSORTRethinking2023 by over 2 across all metrics. The remainder is as follows. Section~ section:Rew reviews related work. Section~ section:HSG presents our fuzzy modeling pipeline and HSG construction, followed by the graph partition solution in Section~ section:Solu . Experimental results and analysis are reported in Section~ section:exps , and Section~ section:Con concludes the paper. Related works section:Rew To date, event-based multi-dimensional assignment remains largely unexplored. Existing event-based tracking methods often associate detections from adjacent batches or continuous timestamps for efficiency. Accordingly, we review both event-based association methods and relevant image-based multi-dimensional assignment techniques. Event-based association Existing event-based association methods can be broadly grouped into two paradigms, direct association and tracking-by-detection. Direct association methods~ dietschePowerlineTrackingEvent2021, everdingLowLatencyLineTracking2018, legentilIDOLFrameworkIMUDVS2020 usually assign individual events to existing clusters, which is a unique paradigm benefiting from asynchronously triggered events. Tracking-by-detection is the classic paradigm in the image-based tracking domain. Therefore, most existing event-based association methods are derived from the image-based counterparts. These methods typically employ Kalman Filter with the Hungarian algorithm~ zhuEventBasedVisualInertial2017, jiangObjectTrackingEvent2020, wangEventBlobTracking2023, barranco2018real , neighbor searching~ alzugarayAsynchronousCornerDetection2018, lagorceAsynchronousEventBasedMultikernel2015, alzugarayHASTEMultiHypothesisAsynchronous2020, hu2022ecdt, rameshETLDEventbasedFramework2020 , or Intersection over Union (IoU)-based matching~ chenAsynchronousTrackingDetectionAdaptive2019, chenEndtoEndLearningObject2020 . For instance, Alzugaray et al.~ alzugarayHASTEMultiHypothesisAsynchronous2020 use a multi-hypothesis framework where the alignment score of each hypothesis is updated incrementally to track features in adjacent batches. Hu et al.~ hu2022ecdt generate head and tail descriptors from each tracklet, then match head descriptors of the previous batch with tail descriptors of the current batch. Jiang et al.~ jiangObjectTrackingEvent2020 use an offline-trained detector and an online-trained tracker, where a Kalman fusion scheme has been proposed to incorporate measurements from the detector and the tracker for real-time intervention-free operations. Barranco et al.~ barranco2018real utilize Mean Shift to cluster event tracklets in X-Y-T space and employ Kalman Filter with Hungarian algorithm to associate them in adjacent batches. Chen et al.~ chenAsynchronousTrackingDetectionAdaptive2019 detect objects by bounding boxes in event frames and use IoU to evaluate association candidates. Despite their diversity in implementation, all these methods operate on adjacent batches, making them unable to associate fragmented tracklets with large spatio-temporal gaps. Image-based multi-dimensional assignment A fundamental constraint in image-based association is the one-to-one constraint. It states that each object must correspond to exactly one detection and one detection must belong to only one object. This results in a bijective mapping between detections and objects. In image-based multi-dimensional assignment, although the increasing number of candidates elevates the complexity of the problem, this constraint renders this NP-hard problem well-posed. Some works have formulated multi-dimensional assignments as a network flow problem~ berclazMultipleObjectTracking2011, zhangGlobalDataAssociation2008, pirsiavashGloballyoptimalGreedyAlgorithms2011, collinsMultitargetData

title: CTBakeGS: training-free baking of photorealistic CT volume renderings into 3D Gaussian splats
summary: Photorealistic volume rendering of computed tomography (CT) may convey anatomy intuitively, but it needs the CT data, dedicated software and a powerful graphics processor. Three-dimensional Gaussian splatting (3DGS) displays photorealistic scenes in real time on less powerful devices, but existing medical approaches train each scene for minutes to hours. We aimed to convert a CT volume rendering directly into a 3DGS model without training. Splats were placed on an adaptive octree of millimetre-sized cells. Their colour and opacity were computed on the graphics processor with the renderer's lighting, cell opacity was converted analytically into splat opacity, and faint splats were retained stochastically above the 1/255 opacity floor of standard 3DGS rasterisers. Six public CT scans (1.5-mm voxels) were converted with three transfer functions and compared with converged references by peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), structural similarity and a learned perceptual metric. Two-million-splat models reached a PSNR of 32.6 +/- 0.9 dB for bone, 30.1 +/- 1.0 dB for contrast-enhanced vessels and 32.3 +/- 1.5 dB for skin and bone. A conversion pass (usually two or three per model) took 4-30 s on a current laptop and 9-60 s on a desktop with a 4-GB graphics card. On the laptop, the models rendered at 68 frames per second at 800 x 800 pixels. Training-free conversion produced real-time 3DGS models of photorealistic CT renderings in about a minute or less per conversion pass on ordinary computers, with fidelity that we consider sufficient for interactive viewing.
full_text: Photorealistic volume rendering of computed tomography (CT) may convey anatomy intuitively, but it needs the CT data, dedicated software and a powerful graphics processor. Three-dimensional Gaussian splatting (3DGS) displays photorealistic scenes in real time on less powerful devices, but existing medical approaches train each scene for minutes to hours. We aimed to convert a CT volume rendering directly into a 3DGS model without training. Splats were placed on an adaptive octree of millimetre-sized cells. Six public CT scans (1.5-mm voxels) were converted with three transfer functions and compared with converged references by peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), structural similarity and a learned perceptual metric. Two-million-splat models reached a PSNR of 32.6 +/- 0.9 dB for bone, 30.1 +/- 1.0 dB for contrast-enhanced vessels and 32.3 +/- 1.5 dB for skin and bone. A conversion pass (usually two or three per model) took 4-30 s on a current laptop and 9-60 s on a desktop with a 4-GB graphics card. On the laptop, the models rendered at 68 frames per second at 800 x 800 pixels. Training-free conversion produced real-time 3DGS models of photorealistic CT renderings in about a minute or less per conversion pass on ordinary computers, with fidelity that we consider sufficient for interactive viewing. Background Photorealistic volume rendering of computed tomography (CT) simulates light scattering in tissue and has the capacity to depict anatomy with apparent lifelike depth and shading kroes2012,jonsson2014,dappa2016,eid2017 . It speeds anatomical understanding compared with conventional CT images and serves surgical planning, teaching, patient communication and documentation elshafei2019,binder2021,pachowsky2022,ebert2017 . However, it needs the CT data, dedicated software and a powerful graphics processing unit (GPU), so results are usually shared as still images or videos. Three-dimensional Gaussian splatting (3DGS) represents a scene as millions of semi-transparent Gaussians rasterised in real time kerbl2023 . Standard 3DGS viewers display such models directly, so a 3DGS model of a CT rendering could be viewed, also in head-mounted displays, without the CT data or renderer. For medical and scientific volumes, most methods optimise Gaussians iteratively against tens to over a thousand rendered views per scene, for minutes to over an hour on a dedicated GPU niedermayr2024,kleinbeck2025,li2025clipgs,gao2025sixdgs,tang2025,dyken2026,gao2026factorsplat ; one refines an analytic initialisation li2026vbm . Feed-forward networks predict Gaussians within seconds but must first be trained on about 100--1,000 volumes with rendered views gao2026renderfm,wang2026vvgt . Most optimised models must be rebuilt, or extended dyken2026,gao2026factorsplat , when the transfer function changes. A volume, however, already defines what a Gaussian representation needs: where the material is, how opaque it is and, once lit, its colour. Gaussian kernels have long served direct volume rendering, notably in elliptical weighted average (EWA) splatting zwicker2001 . Instead of optimising or learning Gaussians from rendered images, we aimed to bake the appearance of a lit CT rendering directly into Gaussians, so that conversion is immediate on ordinary hardware. The contribution is not a new rendering model but the removal of the prerequisites of existing 3DGS pipelines: rendered training views, a dedicated GPU and per-scene training time. We describe CTBakeGS and measure how faithfully it reproduces the original rendering. Methods Conversion Principle. A CT volume stores voxel-wise radiodensity values in Hounsfield units. A direct volume rendering is fully defined by three inputs: the CT data, a transfer function that maps Hounsfield units to colour and opacity max1995 , and the virtual lighting. A 3DGS model, in turn, is a set of Gaussian splats. Each splat is a small, ``soft'', semi-transparent blob in space, described by a position, a size and orientation (scale and rotation; a sphere or a stretched ellipsoid), an opacity and a colour; its opacity is highest at the centre and fades smoothly with distance from it kerbl2023 . A splat differs from a voxel in three respects. First, a voxel is one sample of a regular grid, so its position and size are fixed by the grid, whereas a splat can be placed anywhere and have any size. Second, a voxel stores a measured quantity, in CT the X-ray attenuation in Hounsfield units, and says nothing about appearance; a splat stores the appearance itself, that is, how that piece of the scene looks. Third, a voxel volume becomes an image only through volume rendering (transfer function, lighting and ray casting) max1995 , whereas splats are simply projected onto the screen and blended in depth order kerbl2023,zwicker2001 , which graphics processors do very quickly. CTBakeGS derives splats directly from the volume: the volume is divided into small cells, each cell becomes one splat, and each splat receives the colour and opacity that the lit volume rendering gives to its cell. This takes five steps, described in turn below (Fig.~ fig:method ): (1) virtual lighting is precomputed, so that it can be stored in the splat colours; (2) the volume is divided into cells, which set the positions and sizes of the splats; (3) colour and opacity are sampled within each cell; (4) cell opacity is converted into splat opacity, as neighbouring splats overlap to generate a smooth realistic appearance; and (5) faint splats, which would vanish below the 1/255 opacity floor of standard rasterisers, are retained stochastically with raised opacity. An anti-aliasing compensation is applied when the splats are drawn. The result is written as a standard 3DGS file (.ply or .spz). Step 1: lighting. In CTBakeGS, each splat has a single view-independent colour that does not change with the viewing direction, whereas 3DGS models trained from images usually store view-dependent colour. Lighting and shadows must therefore be computed before conversion and stored (baked) in that colour. CTBakeGS uses the lighting of its own photorealistic volume renderer, which approximates global illumination with a precomputed light volume of about 112 cells along the longest axis. For each light-volume cell, rays cast through the transfer-function opacity give the visibility of a sky dome in 24 directions and the transmittance towards a key light, which produces soft shadows. A sample's colour is multiplied by the visibility-weighted sky light plus the transmittance-weighted key light and then tone-mapped. The renderer has a real-time view (one pass per frame), which supplies the colours for conversion, and a progressive view, which averages jittered frames until the image converges. Step 2: cells. The cells determine where splats are placed and how large they are. Cells of one voxel each would spend many splats on homogeneous regions and would tie the splat count to the voxel count. Cells are therefore organised as an adaptive octree that is refined only where opacity changes. Starting from cells four voxels wide, a cell is split into eight when its opacity varies strongly, that is, when the maximum transfer-function opacity over its Hounsfield-unit range, , exceeds the smaller of the opacities at the two ends of that range by more than /2 (and > 0.01). Homogeneous regions thus keep one large splat, whereas boundaries receive small splats, down to sub-voxel size. The split test extends 1.5 cell widths beyond the cell, so that large splats do not protrude through nearby surfaces. Cells are cubes measured in millimetres (unit: the finest voxel spacing), so that thick-slice data do not produce elongated cells. The number of splats follows from the finest permitted cell size. To reach a chosen target count, this size is adjusted, assuming a power law between cell size and splat count, and the conversion is repeated until the count is within 8 of the target, usually after two or three conversion passes. If the target falls between two octree levels, as happened once (case~3, bone, one-million target), the count overshoots. Step 3: colour and opacity. Each cell is now reduced to one colour and one opacity. The cell is sampled on the GPU at 27 stratified points ( ). At each point, the transfer function gives the extinction, and the colour is shaded with the lighting model and light volume of the real-time view (Step~1). The point colours are averaged with weights for extinction and for the transmittance towards the most open axis direction, so that points lying deep inside the cell do not darken it. From the mean extinction and the cell size , the cell opacity is Step 4: opacity mapping. Each cell is replaced by an isotropic Gaussian splat with standard deviation s. title: ThinkWorld: World Imagination Reinforces Chain-of-Dynamics Reasoning
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have made substantial progress in robotic manipulation, but their generalization remains constrained by the diversity and coverage of action-labeled robot demonstrations. Human videos provide much broader behavioral and environmental experience, while learning from them faces a fundamental trade-off between scalable data and explicit action grounding. We introduce ThinkWorld, a VLA learning framework that grounds action reasoning in world dynamics and strengthens it through reinforcement learning with world imagination. ThinkWorld represents each action thought as a Chain-of-Dynamics (CoD), a sequence of discrete motion tokens that captures the intermediate dynamics connecting the current world to a future state and serves as a common action representation across embodiments. We first initialize CoD with action-labeled demonstrations, then predict the future induced by each CoD and reinforce those whose predictions better match the observed outcome. This enables videos without action annotations to provide direct supervision from observed state transitions, allowing human and robot experience to refine the same reasoning space. Experiments in simulation and on real robots demonstrate effective human-to-robot transfer and strong generalization to unseen tasks and environments.
full_text: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have made substantial progress in robotic manipulation, but their generalization remains constrained by the diversity and coverage of action-labeled robot demonstrations. Human videos provide much broader behavioral and environmental experience, while learning from them faces a fundamental trade-off between scalable data and explicit action grounding. We introduce ThinkWorld, a VLA learning framework that grounds action reasoning in world dynamics and strengthens it through reinforcement learning with world imagination. ThinkWorld represents each action thought as a Chain-of-Dynamics (CoD), a sequence of discrete motion tokens that captures the intermediate dynamics connecting the current world to a future state and serves as a common action representation across embodiments. We first initialize CoD with action-labeled demonstrations, then predict the future induced by each CoD and reinforce those whose predictions better match the observed outcome. This enables videos without action annotations to provide direct supervision from observed state transitions, allowing human and robot experience to refine the same reasoning space. Experiments in simulation and on real robots demonstrate effective human-to-robot transfer and strong generalization to unseen tasks and environments.\\ Links: Project Page Introduction Building general-purpose action models that transfer across tasks, objects, environments, and embodiments is a central goal of robot learning. Recent vision-language-action models (VLAs)~ brohan2023rt,o2024open,team2024octo,kim24openvla,black2024pi_0,intelligence2025pi0,bjorck2025gr00t have made substantial progress by transferring pretrained vision-language knowledge and scaling across heterogeneous robot demonstrations. Nevertheless, their policy learning and behavioral coverage remain largely tied to action-labeled robot trajectories, whose collection requires physical platforms, embodiment-specific interfaces, and substantial human effort. Human videos offer a complementary source of experience with far greater behavioral and environmental diversity, but do not provide directly executable robot actions. Existing approaches seek to extract actionable supervision from human videos along two main directions. Latent action models~ ye2025latent,bu2025univla,dai2026conla,sun2026vla infer transition variables from pairs or sequences of frames and use them for representation or policy learning. While naturally scalable to action-unlabeled videos, these inferred variables are underconstrained and may capture appearance changes or camera motion rather than controllable behavior. In contrast, fully supervised approaches recover hand poses, object interactions, or retargeted trajectories to provide explicit motion supervision~ kareer2025egomimic,zheng2026egoscale,liu2026egoengine . Such supervision provides direct physical grounding, but relies on accurate pose estimation and human-to-robot correspondence. Human-video learning therefore yields a trade-off between stronger action grounding from explicit supervision and broader behavioral coverage from unlabeled videos. Future observations provide a natural supervisory signal to bridge this gap as every video records the consequences that follow a behavior, regardless of embodiment. Predictive world models~ agarwal2026cosmos,zhou2024dino,assran2025vjepa2 and foresight-based VLAs~ zhang2026dreamvla,sun2026vla,cai2026internvla,li2026fomovla exploit this signal by forecasting future pixels, visual features, or trajectories, providing a direct account of what changes in the world. However, inferring the intermediate dynamics that result in these changes remains challenging, particularly from large-scale human videos without action annotations. Recent reasoning-augmented VLAs offer a useful perspective by introducing intermediate tokens, such as textual plans~ zawalski2024robotic,huang2026thinkact , visual guidance~ lee2025molmoact,fang2026molmoact2 , continuous latents~ huang2026fast , or coarse action trajectories~ zhong2026acot , to structure action generation. This raises a natural question of whether such intermediate representations can instead be grounded in the dynamics they induce in the world, providing a shared action interface across embodiments. Motivated by this perspective, we introduce ThinkWorld, a VLA learning framework that formulates action thoughts as Chain-of-Dynamics (CoD) and reinforces them through world imagination. CoD represents an action as a sequence of discrete motion tokens that captures how the world evolves over time, providing a common reasoning interface across human and robot behaviors. We first initialize this space with action-labeled demonstrations, grounding CoD in physically meaningful behavior. ThinkWorld then predicts the future world representation induced by each CoD and compares it with the future observation, using their alignment to reinforce action reasoning. As a result, videos even without motion annotations provide a learning signal, allowing large-scale human videos and robot trajectories to jointly refine the same CoD space. This training objective propagates through the shared VLM, enriching the representations for action prediction with knowledge of how motion transforms the world. Across simulation benchmarks and real-robot evaluations, we demonstrate that ThinkWorld enables human-to-robot skill composition and generalization to unseen scenarios. Our contributions are as follows: We introduce ThinkWorld, a VLA learning framework that couples a common VLM-native action-reasoning interface for both human and robot with internal world imagination. We propose consequence-grounded reinforcement learning, which rewards CoD according to its consistency with observed future consequences and thereby enables action reasoning to improve from videos without action labels. We show that ThinkWorld benefits from scaling action-unlabeled human video and enables human-to-robot skill transfer, allowing robots to execute complete tasks demonstrated in human videos while receiving robot supervision only for the constituent atomic skills. Related Works sec:related_works Generalist Robot Policies. Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models~ kim24openvla,bjorck2025gr00t,black2024pi_0,intelligence2025pi0,wang2026qwen,chen2025internvla,team2025gemini build upon advances in vision-language models (VLMs)~ bai2025qwen3,li2025eagle,chen2026eagle,liu2025nvila,ye2026omnivinci to learn generalist manipulation policies that map visual observations and language instructions to executable actions.. Despite acquiring broad capabilities from large-scale robot demonstrations, end-to-end imitation remains bounded by the behaviors observed during training. Recent embodied reasoning methods introduce intermediate reasoning between perception and control~ zawalski2024robotic,huang2026thinkact,lee2025molmoact,huang2026fast,fang2026molmoact2,zhong2026acot,lu2026tacitvla,liu2026long . ThinkAct~ huang2026thinkact reinforces textual and visual plans with action-aligned rewards, MolmoAct~ lee2025molmoact reasons through spatial traces, Fast-ThinkAct~ huang2026fast compresses reasoning into latent thoughts, and ACoT-VLA~ zhong2026acot predicts coarse reference actions to guide policy generation. However, these methods largely augment robot demonstrations with intermediate reasoning, without explicitly grounding the learned thoughts in the task-relevant changes they induce in the world. Their generalization to novel scenes and skills therefore remains constrained by the behavioral coverage of the underlying robot data. Learning Robot Policies from Human Videos. Improving generalization also requires expanding the behavioral coverage of the training data. Human videos capture substantially greater diversity in scenes, objects, and skills than robot demonstrations, motivating their use for scaling robot learning~ yang2025egovla,zheng2026egoscale,kim2026ego,li2026egowam . Supervised methods convert human interactions into robot-compatible representations, as in EgoScale~ zheng2026egoscale and EgoWAM~ li2026egowam , but require costly cross-embodiment supervision. Latent action models instead infer action-like variables from visual transitions without explicit control labels~ ye2025latent,chen2025moto,routray2026vipra , with LAPA~ ye2025latent learning discrete latent actions before grounding them into robot control. Such representations may capture appearance or embodiment cues rather than task-relevant dynamics. ThinkWorld grounds shared motion tokens and refines them by matching predicted and observed futures in videos. World Models and Visual Foresight for Embodied Control. Recent advances in generative video models~ wan2025wan,agarwal2025cosmos have enabled their application to a wide range of tasks~ xu2023open,tosi2024diffusion,huang2025videomage,kim2025seg4diff . World models learn action-conditioned dynamics to support planning and policy optimization. Dreamer-style agents optimize policies through imagined rollouts~ hafner2023mastering,hafner2025training , while recent large-scale models acquire broad physical priors from diverse video data~ agarwal2026cosmos,gao2026dreamdojo,li2026hydra . In robotics, visual-foresight methods generate video plans or image subgoals to guide control~ du2023learning,black2024zero,bharadhwaj2024gen2act,zhao2025cot , while predictive VLAs forecast future pixels or latent features for planning and representation learning~ zhang2026dreamvla,sun2026vla,cai2026internvla,li2026fomovla,kim2026pri4r . More recent world-action models jointly model future-world evolution and robot actions~ ye2026world,pai2025mimic,cen2025worldvla,kim2026cosmos . In contrast, ThinkWorld does not use future prediction as the control output or an imagined rollout for policy optimization. Instead, it treats agreement between predicted and observed futures as a training-time signal to reinforce action-grounded Chain-of-Dynamics within the VLM. This directly turns observed world changes, including those in action-unlabeled videos, into supervision for action reasoning, while future prediction is discarded at deployment. Method sec:method Problem Formulation sec:problem Given a language instruction , a current visual observation , sampled history frames , and proprioceptive state in case of robot, our goal is to predict a continuous robot action sequence . Rather than treating actions solely as supervision for continuous control, ThinkWorld turns them into a reasoning interface for modeling how an action should unfold and transform the world. Through supervised fine-tuning, we instantiate this interface as a Chain-of-Dynamics (CoD) , grounding its discrete motion vocabulary with action-labeled demonstrations across human and robot embodiments while learning CoD-conditioned future imagination through learnable queries that predict the future visual state (Sec.~ sec:cod ). We then reinforce CoD reasoning through world imagination, using the alignment between the imagined future and the observed future after a physical horizon as a learning signal that does not require motion annotations (Sec.~ sec:world_rl ). Together, action grounding and reinforcement through world imagination refine the model representations used for continuous control while extending learning to action-unlabeled videos at scale. Chain-of-Dynamics for Embodied Action Reasoning sec:cod Robot actions are typically represented in embodiment-specific control spaces, such as joint positions or end-effector poses. Although directly executable, these control targets keep action supervision tied to individual embodiments, limiting transfer across robots and from human demonstrations. We therefore introduce Chain-of-Dynamics (CoD), a sequence of discrete motion tokens that provides a shared action language for human and robot motion, as illustrated in Fig.~ fig:architecture (a).
